## docs/DISJOINT_EXPERT_CACHE.md

# Avoid duplicate expert slots across helper and primary GPUs

## Why this helps

On a PC with two small GPUs, helper experts start out separate from the primary
cache. Later, the adaptive primary cache can promote an expert that the helper
already holds. Both cards then spend memory on the same expert.

We observed about 1,900-2,000 duplicate slots during sustained requests.
This opt-in change keeps helper-owned experts out of primary promotion candidates,
in both the server and command-line generation paths.

## Use

Set `STRATA_DISJOINT_ADAPT=1` before starting the engine. It is off by default.
It leaves the existing peer-tier check and expert arithmetic unchanged.
The check is live: each promotion candidate is asked of the helper's own cache (`RemoteExperts::holds`), so an expert
the helper's tier swaps in or out later is followed (a mask copied at load would go stale). Needs the helper-share
change (#854) for `holds`.

## Validation environment

- Two modified RTX 3080 20 GB cards; CUDA SM86, CUDA 13.1, Linux.
- Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 (18 cores / 36 threads), about 94 GiB usable RAM.
- PCIe 3.0, no GPU peer-to-peer access; 17 expert-pool workers.
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S, 131,072-token context, INT8 KV,
  32,768 resident KV cells.
- Medium thinking: 2,048-token reasoning cap, 8,192-token output cap.
- Physical GPU power limits stayed at 250 W and 280 W. No power increase.
- Historical performance tests used an isolated engine based on official
  v0.1.38 plus reviewed architectds/Strata changes (best, 05c0f36).
  This PR contains only our change, ported to official main (99f3dbd).
  The historical timings are NOT a measured speedup of this pure-upstream port.

## Historical benefit

Same binary and helper capacity, six complete JSON tasks per arm:

| 32K cached request | Original | Ownership guard |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Generation | 81.5 tokens/s | 94.1 tokens/s |
| Complete request | 12.997 s | 11.417 s |

Generation improved by 15.5%; request time fell by 12.2%.
The tasks returned complete 100-record arrays and correct source facts.
All 18 checks passed across the original, guarded, and larger-cache arms.
The larger-helper arm is not included in the comparison above.
These repetitive tasks do not represent all agent workloads.

## Validation and remaining work

- Standalone ownership test passes, including disabled, empty, unowned,
  owned, and out-of-range entries, plus candidate filtering.
- Linux compile/link against pure official main (99f3dbd) passed. No engine
  was started and no production settings were changed.
- Pure-upstream GPU performance and session/vision/cancellation regression
  checks still need to be run. Keep this PR as a draft until then.
- Historical combined builds passed those safety checks, but that is not a
  substitute for validating this independent port.


## docs/DOCKER.md

# Strata in Docker

Run Strata as a container: one command, nothing to install on the computer except Docker and your graphics card's driver.
The images come with Strata's engine already built for your card, so nothing is compiled on your side. The model is
downloaded on the first start into a volume (a download that stops continues where it stopped), and every later start goes
straight to serving.

> **On this page:** [Which image](#which-image-for-which-card) · [One command per card](#one-command-per-card) ·
> [Docker Compose](#docker-compose) · [Settings](#settings) · [The API key](#the-api-key) · [Connect your apps](#connect-your-coding-apps) ·
> [Watch and stop](#watch-it-and-stop-it) · [Update](#updating) · [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) ·
> [From the older image](#from-the-older-image) · [Build it yourself](#build-it-yourself)

Docker on a **Mac** has no access to the Mac's graphics chip (no Metal): use the Mac app or the Terminal
([MAC.md](MAC.md), [TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md](TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md)). Docker Desktop on **Windows** passes NVIDIA cards through
(WSL 2) but not Radeon or Arc cards; on Windows the app is the easier way for every card.

## Which image for which card

| Your graphics card | Image tag | Needs on the computer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA **RTX 20, 30, 40, 50** series (and the matching RTX A / Quadro cards) | `0.2.3-cuda13` | NVIDIA driver **580 or newer**, [NVIDIA Container Toolkit](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/container-toolkit/latest/install-guide.html) |
| NVIDIA **GTX 10 (Pascal), Tesla P100, V100 (Volta)**, or any NVIDIA card whose driver is **575 to 579** | `0.2.3-cuda12` | NVIDIA driver **575 or newer**, the same toolkit |
| AMD **RX 9000** series and Radeon AI PRO R9700 (RDNA 4, gfx1200 / gfx1201) | `0.2.3-rocm-gfx120x` | the `amdgpu` kernel driver (Linux 6.8+) |
| AMD **RX 7000** series (RDNA 3, gfx1100 / gfx1101 / gfx1102) | `0.2.3-rocm-gfx110x` | the `amdgpu` kernel driver |
| AMD **Ryzen AI Max** ("Strix Halo", Radeon 8060S, gfx1151) | `0.2.3-rocm-gfx1151` | the `amdgpu` kernel driver |
| Intel **Arc** A-series and B-series (including Arc Pro B70) | `0.2.3-sycl` (only for a release that carries the Intel engine package; otherwise [build it](#build-it-yourself)) | the `i915` or `xe` kernel driver; **prepared model files** (see [Intel](#intel-arc)) |

Size of the images on disk (built from the engine packages of the 0.2.0-beta release): `cuda13` 2.2 GB, `cuda12` 2.9 GB, `rocm-gfx120x` 2.8 GB,
`rocm-gfx110x` 2.4 GB, `rocm-gfx1151` 1.5 GB; the download is about a third of that (measured on the 0.1.45 packages: `cuda13` 640 MB, `cuda12` 845 MB,
`rocm-gfx120x` 505 MB, `rocm-gfx110x` 330 MB, `sycl` 450 MB). The model comes on top, on the first start.

Not sure which NVIDIA image? Take `cuda13` when `nvidia-smi` shows driver 580 or newer and the card is an RTX; otherwise `cuda12`.
A wrong pick does no harm: the container starts, says in plain words that the engine does not fit this card, and stops.

**Ready-made images are published from version 0.2.1 on**, to the GitHub Container Registry: `ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:<version>-<flavor>`
(for example `0.2.3-cuda13`), and `ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:latest-<flavor>` for the newest release of that flavor. Pin the version
tag if you want updates only when you decide. The examples below use these images. If you built an image yourself
([Build it yourself](#build-it-yourself)), use the tag you gave it (for example `strata:0.2.3-cuda13`) in their place.

## One command per card

Each command runs Strata in the background, keeps your files in the volume `strata-data`, and listens only on this computer
(`127.0.0.1:8080`). Replace `MODEL` and the key. The first start downloads the model (tens of GB): watch it with
`docker logs -f strata`. Already have the model's GGUF files? Add `-e MODEL_PATH=/models -v /your/folder:/models:ro` and nothing is
downloaded for the model itself ([Files you already have](#files-you-already-have)).

**NVIDIA**

```sh
docker run -d --name strata --gpus all -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  --ulimit memlock=-1:-1 --shm-size 2g --stop-timeout 120 \
  -v strata-data:/data -e MODEL=IQ3_XXS -e API_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 24) \
  ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:0.2.3-cuda13
```

**AMD**

```sh
docker run -d --name strata --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri \
  --group-add video --group-add $(getent group render | cut -d: -f3) -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  --ulimit memlock=-1:-1 --shm-size 2g --stop-timeout 120 \
  -v strata-data:/data -e MODEL=IQ3_XXS -e API_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 24) \
  ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:0.2.3-rocm-gfx120x
```

**Intel Arc**

```sh
docker run -d --name strata --device /dev/dri --group-add $(getent group render | cut -d: -f3) \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 --ulimit memlock=-1:-1 --shm-size 2g --stop-timeout 120 \
  -v strata-data:/data -e MODEL=IQ3_S -e MODEL_PATH=/models -v /srv/gguf/IQ3_S:/models:ro \
  -e API_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 24) ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:0.2.3-sycl
```

What the options are for: `--ulimit memlock=-1:-1` lets the engine pin the RAM it uses for the model, `--shm-size 2g` gives
it shared memory, and `--stop-timeout 120` gives the model two minutes to unload when you stop the container (Docker's
default 10 seconds is too short for a big model). Do not put a memory limit on the container: Strata plans from the whole
computer's RAM and loads tens of GB.

To print the key you made: `echo` it before you start (it is in your shell history otherwise), or ask the running container:
`docker exec strata strata launch --show-key --preset docker`.

### Intel Arc

Strata's downloader prepares NVIDIA and AMD cards. For an Arc card the container **uses prepared model files**: the model's
GGUF files in a folder you mount (`-v /srv/gguf/IQ3_S:/models:ro` and `-e MODEL_PATH=/models`), and the prepared pack and MTP
layer in the data volume (`/data/Strata-data/packs/<model>` and `/data/Strata-data/mtp/rt`, made by the Intel installer on
this or another computer, see [INTEL.md](INTEL.md)). Without them the container tells you which file is missing and stops.
Nothing is downloaded or prepared for Arc inside the container. Arc B-series cards (xe driver) stream the experts from the
GGUF files, so the GGUF folder should be on a fast SSD.

## Docker Compose

Ready-made files are in [docker/compose/](../docker/compose): `docker-compose.nvidia.yml`, `docker-compose.amd.yml`,
`docker-compose.intel.yml` and `.env.example`. Copy the one for your card and its `.env.example`, edit, start:

```sh
cd docker/compose
cp .env.example .env              # set MODEL=..., API_KEY=...
docker compose -f docker-compose.nvidia.yml up -d
docker compose -f docker-compose.nvidia.yml logs -f
```

They set what the commands above set: the GPU (`deploy.resources.reservations.devices` for NVIDIA, `/dev/kfd` and
`/dev/dri` plus the `video` and `render` groups for AMD, `/dev/dri` for Intel), `ulimits.memlock`, `shm_size`, a two-minute
`stop_grace_period`, the `strata-data` volume, and the port bound to `127.0.0.1`. To let other computers reach it, set
`STRATA_BIND=0.0.0.0` in `.env` and keep a real `API_KEY`.

## Settings

Everything is an environment variable (`-e NAME=value`, or in compose). They are the same questions `strata launch` asks on its
screens; leave out what you do not care about.

| Variable | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MODEL` | model size: `IQ2_XS`, `IQ3_XXS`, `IQ3_S`, `Q2_0`, `UD-Q4_K_XL`, ... ([MODELS.md](MODELS.md)) | Strata picks what suits the card, and says so in the log |
| `FAMILY` | `qwen`, `swift`, `coder`, ... when a size exists in several families | the usual one |
| `MODEL_PATH` | GGUF files you already have: a folder or one `.gguf`, **inside the container** (mount it with `-v`, `:ro` is fine) | download |
| `CONTEXT` | how much text it remembers at once: `32k`, `64k`, `128k`, `256k` or a number | the largest that fits |
| `PARALLEL` | requests answered at the same time, 1 to 8 | fitted to the card |
| `VISION` | `off`, `on` (the model reads pictures), `gpu`, `cpu`; the picture-reader file (about 0.9 GB) is downloaded with the model | `off` |
| `KV` | conversation memory format: `int8`, `q4_0` (half the memory), `k8v4`, `fp16` | `int8` |
| `GPU` / `GPUS` | card numbers as the monitor lists them, `0` or `0,1`; empty or `all` = the engine's choice. Changing it later makes the model's run settings again (the files stay) | all that fit |
| `GPU_ROLES` | a role for each card, `1=main,0=helper` (`main`, `helper`, `off`; cards you do not name are off; not together with `GPU` / `GPUS`). Passed to `launch --gpu-roles`; see [MULTI_GPU.md](MULTI_GPU.md) |
| `TUNE` | `quick` (up to about 20 minutes, once), `thorough`, `skip`; done once and kept in the preset (`RETUNE=1` tunes again) | `skip` |
| `API_KEY` / `API_KEY_FILE` | the key clients must send ([below](#the-api-key)); the file form is for Docker secrets | made for you |
| `PORT` | the port inside the container | `8080` |
| `PRESET` | the preset name in `/data` | `docker` |
| `STRATA_SET` | advanced engine settings, space separated, like `strata launch --set` (`"prefill=65536 STRATA_PIN_BY_NEED=1"`) | none |

Your choices are saved as a preset in the volume. Start again with no settings and the saved preset is used; start with
settings and they replace the saved ones (tuning results are kept). To change one thing, recreate the container with the new
variable; the model and tuning stay in `/data`. Anything else: `docker exec strata strata launch --help`, or
`docker run --rm IMAGE strata launch --plan --model q2_0` to see what a choice would do without starting anything.

What is in the volume `/data`: `Strata-data/` (model files, the prepared pack), `state/` (presets, tuning, the key), `install/`
(run settings and logs), `home/`. The engine and the Terminal are in the image, so updating the image never touches your files.

To keep it all on a big disk, mount a folder there instead of the named volume: `-v /mnt/big/strata:/data` (the folder must be writable by the
container's user). Nothing large is written anywhere else in the container.

### Files you already have

Mount the folder with the model's GGUF files read-only and name it: `-v /srv/gguf/IQ3_XXS:/models:ro -e MODEL_PATH=/models
-e MODEL=IQ3_XXS`. Nothing is downloaded for the model itself; the prepared pack is made in the volume.

- The folder holds the shards of one model directly (`...-00001-of-00002.gguf`, `...-00002-of-00002.gguf`), not a folder of folders.
  If you mount a parent folder, the container says which sub-folder to name in `MODEL_PATH`.
- The folder has to be mounted: a `MODEL_PATH` that is not in the container, or a folder with no `.gguf` files, stops the start at
  once with a message, and nothing is downloaded.
- Read-only (`:ro`) is fine. The pack (about 40 GB for IQ3_XXS) and the draft layer (about 6 GB, fetched once) are written to the
  volume, so it needs that room. With pictures on (the default) the picture reader (0.9 GB) is fetched too; `VISION=off` skips it.
- Links to the files work when the links' targets are mounted too, and `MODEL` is set (without `MODEL`, Strata identifies the files itself
  and does not follow links).
- Without `MODEL_PATH`, files you put into the volume by hand (`/data/Strata-data/models/<model folder>/`) are found as well, if they have the
  published names.

## The API key

The server listens on every address **inside** the container (that is what lets the published port work), and Strata does not
serve beyond this computer without a key. So a key is always on:

- **You set it** with `API_KEY` (16 characters or more; `openssl rand -hex 24` makes one) or `API_KEY_FILE`.
- **You do not**: the first start makes one, keeps it in the volume, and the log tells you how to show it:
  `docker exec strata strata launch --show-key --preset docker`.

Publish the port as `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080` to keep it on this computer. Publish it as `-p 8080:8080` (or bind `0.0.0.0`) only
when other computers should reach it, and then use a key you chose. Strata warns in the log when the key is short. Every
request must send `Authorization: Bearer <key>`; `GET /health` answers without one.

## Connect your coding apps

From outside the container, the address is the published port and the key is yours:

- OpenAI-compatible apps: base URL `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`, API key = your key, model name from `GET /v1/models`.
- Anthropic-compatible apps (Claude Code): base URL `http://127.0.0.1:8080`, same key.

`strata connect` writes the settings file for OpenCode, Codex CLI, Claude Code, oh-my-pi, pi, Hermes Agent and OpenClaw, and
checks that a prompt and a tool call work. **Inside** the container it fills in the key and the model for you:

```sh
docker exec strata strata connect opencode          # prints the file and the environment
docker exec strata strata connect opencode --check  # one prompt and one tool call, the way that app sends them
```

It prints `http://127.0.0.1:8080`, which is the address *inside* the container; on your computer use the published address
(`-p 127.0.0.1:9000:8080` makes it `http://127.0.0.1:9000`). If your coding app runs on your computer, install the `strata`
Terminal there ([TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md](TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md)) and run `strata connect opencode --url http://HOST:8080 --key <your key>`.

## Watch it and stop it

```sh
docker logs -f strata                       # what it is doing (the first start: the download)
docker exec -it strata strata monitor       # the live monitor (q leaves it, the server keeps running)
docker exec strata strata monitor --once    # one snapshot, for scripts
docker ps                                   # "healthy" once the model is loaded; "starting" while it downloads or loads
docker stop strata                          # drains, unloads the model, frees the graphics memory, exits 0
docker start strata                         # serving again in about a minute: the model and your choices are in the volume
```

The health check asks `GET /v1/models` with the key. During the first download the container shows `starting`, not `unhealthy`.
`docker stop` sends SIGTERM; the container runs `strata launch --stop`, so the engine releases its memory properly. Give it time
(`--stop-timeout 120` or compose's `stop_grace_period: 2m`): with the default 10 seconds a big model can be killed (exit 137).

## Updating

```sh
docker pull ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:0.2.3-cuda13      # the new tag (with a self-built image, build it again instead)
docker stop strata && docker rm strata
# run the same docker run command again with the new tag (compose: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d)
```

The models, the prepared pack, your preset and tuning stay in the volume `strata-data`; nothing is downloaded again. A new
engine can make an old tuning result less useful: start once with `-e TUNE=quick -e RETUNE=1` to tune again.
`strata update` inside the container is not the way to update: the engine is part of the image.

## Troubleshooting

**"The engine in this image does not match this computer's graphics card"** or the container stops right at the start.
The card is not visible to the container, or the image is for another card. Check the options for your card in
[the commands](#one-command-per-card) and the table in [Which image](#which-image-for-which-card).

**NVIDIA: `could not select device driver "" with capabilities: [[gpu]]`, or `docker: Error response from daemon: unknown or
invalid runtime name: nvidia`.** The NVIDIA Container Toolkit is missing or Docker was not told about it:

```sh
sudo apt install nvidia-container-toolkit          # or your distribution's package; see NVIDIA's install guide
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
sudo systemctl restart docker
docker run --rm --gpus all ubuntu nvidia-smi       # must list your card
```

On Fedora / RHEL with Podman, use CDI: `sudo nvidia-ctk cdi generate --output=/etc/cdi/nvidia.yaml`, then `--device nvidia.com/gpu=all`.
If `nvidia-smi` inside the container works but Strata says the driver is too old, you picked `cuda13` with a driver below 580:
use the `cuda12` image or update the driver.

**AMD: `Permission denied` on `/dev/kfd`, or no card found.** The container needs the device files and your user (or the
container's user) must be allowed to use them. Add `--device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri` and the groups
`--group-add video --group-add $(getent group render | cut -d: -f3)` (the render group's number differs from computer to
computer, so use the number, not the name). `ls -l /dev/kfd /dev/dri/renderD*` shows who owns them. On a computer with
SELinux (Fedora, RHEL) that still refuses the device files, add `--security-opt label=disable` to the `docker run`.

**Intel: no device found.** Pass `--device /dev/dri` and `--group-add <render group number>` as above. An Arc card needs the
`i915` or `xe` driver on the host (`ls /dev/dri/renderD*` must show a device; `lspci -k | grep -A3 -i arc` shows the driver in use).

**SELinux (Fedora, RHEL, Rocky): `Permission denied` on a folder you mounted.** Add `:z` (shared) or `:Z` (private) to the
mount: `-v /srv/gguf/IQ3_XXS:/models:ro,z`. A named volume like `strata-data` needs nothing.

**The container is killed or the computer swaps.** Strata loads tens of GB into RAM: leave the container without a memory
limit, close other big programs, and pick a smaller `MODEL` ([MODELS.md](MODELS.md)). The log prints a warning when it sees a
memory limit.

**`docker stop` took long or ended with exit code 137.** The model was still unloading when Docker's time ran out. Use
`--stop-timeout 120` (compose: `stop_grace_period: 2m`).

**Port already in use.** Publish another host port: `-p 127.0.0.1:9000:8080` (inside the container it stays 8080).

**The first start says it is downloading but nothing moves.** `docker logs -f strata` shows the percentage every few seconds;
an interrupted download continues where it stopped when you start the container again. The volume needs the model's size free
(the log names it).

**"No MODEL was set"** warning: fine, Strata chose a model for your card; set `MODEL` to choose yourself.

## From the older image

The 0.1.x image compiled the engine inside `docker build` and was set up with `setup.py`. The new ones are built from the engine
package and start through `strata launch`. Mapping:

| Older variable | Now |
| --- | --- |
| `MODEL`, `FAMILY`, `CONTEXT`, `API_KEY`, `PORT`, `KV`, `GPU`, `GPUS`, `VISION` | the same (`VISION` takes `off\|on\|gpu\|cpu`; `no` / `yes` still work) |
| `GGUF_DIR` | `MODEL_PATH` (the old name still works) |
| `HOST` | not needed: the server listens on every address inside the container; choose where it is reachable with `-p` |
| `LOW_RAM`, `RESIDENT_BUDGET_GIB`, `KV_STREAMING`, `LAYER_SPLIT`, `CONFIG`, `REINSTALL` | ignored with a warning; use `STRATA_SET` for engine settings and `strata launch --help` for the rest |

A volume from the older image is picked up: the first start moves `/data/models`, `/data/packs` and `/data/mtp` into
`/data/Strata-data` (a rename inside the volume: nothing is copied or downloaded again, and the prepared pack is kept). The old
`/data/config` is not read; the run settings are made again from the files. A folder you mounted yourself at one of those places
is left alone: point `MODEL_PATH` at it. The container name, the volume and the port can stay as they were.

## Build it yourself

This is the way to get an image for a computer without registry access or after changing Strata. You need an engine package
folder (made by `packaging/package_engine.py`, or fetched by `strata update` into a components folder) and Docker on Linux:

```sh
docker/build.sh --flavor cuda --engine ~/components/engine/0.1.45.3-linux-x86_64-cuda-cuda13 --tag strata:0.2.3-cuda13
docker/build.sh --flavor hip  --engine ~/components/engine/0.1.45.3-linux-x86_64-hip-rx9070 --tag strata:0.2.3-rocm-gfx120x
docker/build.sh --flavor sycl --engine ~/components/engine/<a-sycl-package-folder> --tag strata:0.2.3-sycl
```

`build.sh` assembles the build context (the Terminal's files and the package) and runs `docker build`. The build makes the
Terminal exactly as the release archive (Python 3.12 and the locked packages, fetched at build time only), then checks the
engine package before it may enter the image: every file's SHA-256, and that every library it imports is bundled or belongs
to the system or the graphics driver (`packaging/binary_deps.py`); finally it checks that the dynamic linker resolves every
library inside the finished image. A package that fails any of these stops the build. Nothing is pushed anywhere.
`docker/smoke-test.sh` runs the checks we ran on real cards (serves, key, chat, tool call, monitor, clean stop, memory freed, restart); see its first lines for the variables.

**From source.** `docker build -t strata:src .` in the repository compiles the CUDA 13 engine inside Docker, makes the package
and puts it in the same kind of image (`--build-arg CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89` for one card only, much faster). For a GTX 10, P100 or
V100 build the CUDA 12 variant: `docker build -t strata:src-cuda12 --build-arg CUDA_IMAGE=nvidia/cuda:12.9.1-devel-ubuntu24.04
--build-arg CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="60;61;70;75;80;86;89" --build-arg BUILD_VISION=0 .` (the build turns on the Pascal / Volta code by itself
when an architecture below 75 is listed, and names the package `cuda12` with driver 575.51). For AMD and Intel
builds from source see [AMD_HIP.md](AMD_HIP.md) and [INTEL.md](INTEL.md); then package the result with
`packaging/package_engine.py` and use `docker/build.sh`.

## Publishing the images (for maintainers)

The images are built from the **engine packages of a release**, never from a build on the runner, so an image holds exactly the
files the signed update feed names. Nothing publishes by itself: a maintainer starts the workflow, after the owner's OK.

1. Make the release first (its `strata-feed.json`, `strata-feed.json.sig` and the engine archives must be on the GitHub release).
2. GitHub, **Actions, Docker images, Run workflow** ([.github/workflows/docker-images.yml](../.github/workflows/docker-images.yml); the file has to be on
   the default branch to show up). Inputs: the release tag (`v0.2.3`), the flavors (empty: every flavor the release has a package
   for), **push** and **latest**. Run it once with **push off**: it builds every image and publishes nothing (a dry run).
3. Run it again with **push on**. It logs in to `ghcr.io` with the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` (`packages: write`) and pushes
   `ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:0.2.3-<flavor>` and `latest-<flavor>`. Turn **latest** off for a pre-release.
4. The first push creates each package as private. In the repository's Packages, open every package, **Package settings, Change
   visibility, Public**, and check it is linked to the repository (the image carries the `org.opencontainers.image.source` label).
5. Check one pull from a computer that is not logged in: `docker pull ghcr.io/niko1221/strata:0.2.3-cuda13`.

For each flavor the job runs [docker/fetch-engines.py](../docker/fetch-engines.py), which reads the release's signed feed (the
Ed25519 key in `strata_control/update_keys.json`), downloads the package, and checks the archive's size and SHA-256, the manifest
hash, the package signature and every file's hash, exactly as `strata update` does; a package that fails stops the job before
anything is built. [docker/build.sh](../docker/build.sh) then builds the image (and checks the package again inside the build), and
the job starts the image once to see that the Terminal inside it runs.

| Flavor (tag suffix) | Engine package in the release feed |
| --- | --- |
| `cuda13` | `linux-x86_64`, cuda, variant `cuda13` |
| `cuda12` | `linux-x86_64`, cuda, variant `cuda12` |
| `rocm-gfx120x` | `linux-x86_64`, hip, variant `rx9070` (gfx1200 / gfx1201) |
| `rocm-gfx110x` | `linux-x86_64`, hip, variant `rx7900` (gfx1100 / gfx1101 / gfx1102) |
| `rocm-gfx1151` | `linux-x86_64`, hip, variant `halo` (Strix Halo, gfx1151) |
| `sycl` | `linux-x86_64`, sycl; **only when the feed lists one** (the 0.2.0-beta feed has none, so no Intel image is built from it) |

A flavor the feed has no package for is left out, with a line in the log. The same steps run from a Linux computer with Docker:
`docker/publish.sh --release-tag v0.2.3` builds everything and pushes nothing; add `--push` (after `docker login ghcr.io`) to publish.
The images run on the runner without a graphics card, so the card checks (`docker/smoke-test.sh`) stay a manual step on a computer with the card.

## Tested

2026-10-19, images built from the engine packages of the 0.2.0-beta release (engine 0.1.45.3), fetched and checked against the signed feed by
`docker/fetch-engines.py` (the packages are the ones `strata update` installs). Run on real cards with the checks below (`docker/smoke-test.sh`): `cuda13`
and `cuda12` on one RTX A4000 (driver 580), `rocm-gfx120x` on one Radeon AI PRO R9700. All passed: serving 71-161 s after `docker run` with the prepared
files, `docker stop` took 4-5 s with exit code 0, the card's memory was free again, and the second start reused the saved preset. `rocm-gfx110x` and
`rocm-gfx1151` (Strix Halo) were built and passed the package and library checks but have not run on a card. On a computer without an AMD card the
`rocm-gfx120x` container says in plain words that the engine does not match the card and exits with code 3.

2026-10-17, images built from the 0.1.45 engine packages, on real cards: NVIDIA RTX 3060 (`cuda13`
and `cuda12`), Radeon AI PRO R9700 (`rocm-gfx120x`), Intel Arc Pro B70 (`sycl`). On each: the container serves, `GET /v1/models` answers (and
refuses a request without the key), a one-word chat and a tool call work, `docker exec strata monitor --once` works,
`docker stop` ends it with exit code 0 and the graphics memory is free again, and a second start reuses the saved preset.
Not run on a card: `cuda12` on Pascal / Volta (it ran on the RTX 3060), `rocm-gfx110x` (RX 7000). They are built and checked the same way.

## Known limits

- Linux x86-64 hosts only. Docker on Windows reaches NVIDIA cards only; Docker on a Mac cannot use the GPU.
- The images run as `root` inside the container (GPU device files, page-locked memory). Run the container on a computer you
  trust the way you would run the app; do not mount folders you do not want it to read.
- An Arc card needs prepared model files (see [Intel](#intel-arc)).
- AMD **RX 7000** (gfx110x) and RDNA 3 iGPUs: the gfx110X image is built for gfx1100 / 1101 / 1102 (RX 7900, 7800, 7700, 7600). The
  Radeon 780M (gfx1103) is experimental and has its own engine package, not in these images.


## docs/EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md

# Resident expert exchange buffer rotation

When the resident RAM complement exchanges an expert with the GPU cache, the
evicted expert lands in a temporary host buffer. The existing path then copies
those bytes into the promoted expert's old RAM slot. Rotation removes that last
host copy: the temporary buffer becomes resident, and the old RAM slot becomes
the next temporary buffer.

## Enable

Rotation is **off by default**. Set `STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE=1` before starting the
engine with your existing arguments:

```bash
export STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE=1
```

```powershell
$env:STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE = '1'
```

Only the exact value `1` opts in. Set it to `0` or remove it to restore the copy
path. This setting does not select resident RAM mode or change any preset.
It applies only when the resident complement is fully pinned and GPU-mapped
and the exchange buffers can also be pinned and mapped. Other layouts keep the
copy path and log why rotation could not be enabled. Configurations without a
resident complement do not use it. Layers may differ in expert block size (a
GGUF with mixed quantizations per layer): see
[Layers of different block sizes](#layers-of-different-block-sizes).

The startup diagnostic confirms activation:

```text
FileExpertSource: exchange buffer rotation enabled: ...; no host commit memcpy
```

Serving diagnostics report the cumulative rotated block count and avoided
`memcpy` payload bytes. This counts the copied payload once, not read plus write
traffic, and does not include the GPU transfers, which still occur.

## Ownership and synchronization

The original allocations own their memory until `FileExpertSource::close()`.
Rotation updates slot ownership and keeps each host pointer paired with its GPU
alias. Atomic slot IDs let background residency queries observe those immutable
pairs. Compute readers and GPU transfers must still finish before the existing
serialized commit; rotation adds no overlapping compute or new synchronization
policy. Reserve the maximum exchange capacity before rotation starts: growing a
live exchange arena is rejected because it can now hold resident experts.

## Layers of different block sizes

A swap exchanges two experts of the same layer, so the RAM slot the promoted
expert leaves has exactly the size of the block the evicted one needs. Rotation
therefore keeps its spare buffers per block size: an exchange of a layer takes
a spare of that layer's size and hands back one of the same size, and every
size keeps its number of spares for good. The first version required one size
for all layers and fell back to the copy path on any other pack; Swift 1.5
IQ3_S has seven sizes (1,510,400 to 2,662,400 bytes) and IQ3_XXS has nine
too, so neither could rotate.

The exchange allocation holds one spare of every size per swap of a round:
`--adapt-swaps` (at most 96) times the sum of the distinct sizes. With
`--adapt-async 1` the second half of the buffers only stages copies and is
kept in the largest size alone. On IQ3_S with `--adapt-swaps 80` that is
1.06 GiB of page-locked RAM (1.26 GiB with `--adapt-async 1`), against 0.20
and 0.40 GiB for the copy path's buffers. The startup line says how many sizes
and how much:

```text
FileExpertSource: exchange buffer rotation enabled: 80 buffers in 7 block sizes (largest 2662400 bytes, 1.06 GiB page-locked); no host commit memcpy
```

With `--adapt-async 1` a rotated round also ends one verify window sooner:
there are no bytes for the background job to move, so the ownership flip runs
in the tick that sees the copies in.

`tests/core/exchange_storage_test.cpp` covers it without CUDA (three sizes,
6,144 exchanges: bytes, aliases, a spare of another size or an expert of
another layer refused, overlapping resident blocks refused).

### Measured: Swift 1.5 IQ3_S on an RTX 5090 with 64 GB (Windows 11)

Core i7-13700K, RTX 5090 32 GB, 64 GB DDR5, Windows 11, driver 617.42, CUDA
13.0.88, engine 0.1.42 built from source with this change. Swift 1.5 IQ3_S,
128K context, `--resident-experts` (31.4 GiB of experts page-locked in RAM,
about 10,800 of 24,576 in VRAM), `--adapt-every 1 --adapt-swaps 80
--adapt-decay 0.97`, `--spec 4`, `--pool-affinity p-cores`. In the first and third
rows one binary ran both arms and only `STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE` differs; in the
second the off arm is the build before this change (the third row's binary also
carried extra timers).

| Run | Rotation off | Rotation on |
|---|---|---|
| One 8K prompt, the same 1,500 forced tokens (`--spec-follow`), blocking tier, decode tok/s | 163.4, 165.1, 163.1, 161.6, 162.6 | 187.4, 188.7, 185.8, 184.9 |
| `--serve`, 23 coding-agent turns (`tools/agent_turns_bench.py`'s turns, greedy, up to 400 new tokens), blocking tier, tok/s over all turns, three interleaved rounds | 147.8, 159.2, 158.4 | 175.2, 184.9, 172.8 |
| The same turns with `--adapt-async 1`, one binary, two interleaved rounds | 166.0, 170.1 | 185.6, 182.5 |

In the first row, two runs of each arm that sized the expert cache alike (10,681
slots) wrote the same `--window-hashes` file for all 434 windows: the same
arithmetic, window by window. (`--expert-cache auto` sizes the cache from the
free VRAM at start, and a run with another slot count places experts
differently, so its hashes differ with or without rotation.) The tier swapped
about 14,000 experts in such a run, 10,100 to 10,600 of them exchanges. In the serve rows the
rotated arm was faster on 23 of 23 turns (blocking tier) and 22 of 23
(`--adapt-async 1`). On this box the tier swaps about 30 experts per verify
window all through a run (the cache holds 44% of the experts), so the copy
path moved about 50 MiB of RAM per window on the decode thread; that is the
time rotation removes. With `--adapt-async 1` the same copy ran on the
background job, and the decode thread still lost about 1 ms per window (0.4 to 2.5 by request)
while it ran; rotated, the tier's part of a window is 0.06 ms.

Not measured: Linux, AMD cards, a layer split, a pack with one block size on
this machine (the code path for it is the one above with a single size).

## Tests

The ownership test can run without CUDA:

```bash
g++ -std=c++20 -O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer \
  -pthread -Iinclude tests/core/exchange_storage_test.cpp -o /tmp/exchange_storage_test
/tmp/exchange_storage_test
```

With an existing CUDA build configured:

```bash
cmake --build build --target strata exchange_storage_test file_expert_source_test
ctest --test-dir build -R '^(exchange_storage_test|file_expert_source_test)$' --output-on-failure
./build/file_expert_source_test --rotation-gpu
compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --error-exitcode 71 ./build/file_expert_source_test --rotation-gpu
```

The CPU test checks byte preservation, pointer/alias ownership, guards, invalid
operations and concurrent residency queries across 12,304 exchanges. The CUDA
fixture performs 64 exchanges in each of three modes: copy with pinned RAM,
rotation with pinned RAM, and requested rotation with pageable RAM (fallback).
It checks exact bytes, GPU alias reads, file fallback, capacity, and close/reopen.
The GPU fixture is explicit; the ordinary CTest invocation does not run it.

On 2026-10-04, the clean patch on upstream
`6f32ec070f23ced9f50e704d854d775da52591ab` built on Linux with GCC 15.2 and CUDA
13.3 for an RTX 4090. Both CTest tests, the ASan/UBSan ownership test, and the
CUDA fixture passed. Compute Sanitizer reported **0 errors**. AMD and Windows
GPU execution were not tested for this patch.

## One native token-identical A/B

Measured on 2026-10-04 using the clean rotation build at
`18a30ad775bce86e99a54e6dc552ccb72c66d16e`, on upstream
`6f32ec070f23ced9f50e704d854d775da52591ab`. The model is the standard
GSQ-RCO **Q2_0**, with its matching IQ4_NL PLE shard. Both shards were verified
against the publisher's SHA-256 hashes at the pinned revision in the receipt.
The native pack uses the existing `tools/iq_pack.py`; no compatibility conversion
or Q8 PLE reader extension is needed.

Both arms used the same Release binary (GCC 13.3, CUDA 13.2), RTX PRO 6000
Blackwell 96GB, Ryzen 9 7950X and 128GB installed RAM. A fresh engine per arm
generated exactly 1,024 tokens after the same 1,024-token counting prompt.
The context allocation was 40,960, with 12,000 GPU expert slots, a 16.19 GiB
pinned/mapped resident complement, FP16 KV, greedy target-only decoding and
zero offered drafts, reused prompt tokens or file-tier blob reads during
generation. Only `STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE` changed. Transfer completion is
awaited before admission.

The GPU cache was deliberately capped at 12,000 slots (15.45 GiB) to exercise
resident RAM exchanges. Q2 can fit entirely on this 96GB GPU; this is a storage
path comparison, not the fastest full-GPU configuration. It does not change
the project's presets or enable resident mode for existing users.

| Rotation | Decode tokens/s | Resident exchanges | Avoided host-copy payload | Output IDs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `0` | 104.90 | 3,802 | 0 bytes | 1,024, identical |
| `1` | 113.44 | 3,802 | 5,255,884,800 bytes | 1,024, identical |

Decode rates exclude startup and prefill. The observed throughput change was
+8.1% in this one pair; repeated timing or a general speedup is not established.
The out-of-vocabulary EOS sentinel `2147483647` forces the exact output length,
so this is not a model-quality evaluation. Speculative-path token parity,
AMD and Windows GPU execution remain untested.

The same Blackwell binary passed both CTest checks and the three-mode CUDA
fixture; Compute Sanitizer reported 0 errors. The
[receipt](../bench/results/exchange-rotation-ab.json) contains source, binary,
model, pack and profile hashes, arguments, timings and diagnostics. The
[raw IDs](../bench/results/exchange-rotation-token-ids.json) retain the input
and both outputs. To check the token comparison without a model:

```bash
python - <<'PY'
import hashlib, json
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('bench/results')
r = json.loads((p / 'exchange-rotation-ab.json').read_text())
raw = (p / r['token_ids_file']).read_bytes()
assert hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest() == r['token_ids_file_sha256']
d = json.loads(raw)
assert len(d['input']) == len(d['off']) == len(d['on']) == 1024
assert d['off'] == d['on']
for name, arm in zip(('off', 'on'), r['arms']):
    sha = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(d[name], separators=(',', ':')).encode()).hexdigest()
    assert sha == arm['output_token_ids_sha256']
print('1,024 identical output token IDs')
PY
```


## docs/EXPERTDEC.md

# EXPDEC: the verify window's routed experts with the group's activations in shared memory (`STRATA_EXPDEC=1`, opt-in)

Opt-in: `STRATA_EXPDEC=1`. Unset (or `0`) the engine launches exactly the kernels it launched before. CUDA only; the
output is bitwise the default kernels' (see "Bit for bit" below; `expdec_bench` checks it).

## What it changes

`native_expert_grouped` (`src/kernels/cuda/iq_kernels.cu`) computes a verify window's routed experts that are resident
in VRAM: group g is one expert's blob, its entries are the window's rows that picked it (1 to T, T = the window's
tokens). The default gate/up kernel (`native_gu_multi_kernel`) already decodes each weight part once per block and
applies it to the group's entries (`row_dot_80_sub16<NC>`), but the apply re-reads each entry's q8_1 block from
global memory with 9 scattered 4-byte loads (36-byte blocks: a warp's load touches 16-32 sectors). On an RTX 2080 Ti
at a 131k decode that makes an extra entry cost about 60% of a whole expert (~1.6 us against ~2.6 us per expert and
layer) although it reads nothing from DRAM.

`expdec_gu_kernel` (gate/up: IQ2_XXS, IQ2_XS, IQ3_XXS, IQ3_S, IQ2_S at n_embd 2560) and `expdec_down_kernel` (down:
Q2_0 at n_ff 640; IQ4_NL with `STRATA_EXPDEC_D20=1`) instead:

- stage the group's entries (4 at a time, as the default) in shared memory in a layout where a call's 8 words are two
  16-byte loads with no bank conflicts (the block's two halves in separate planes), the fp16 block scale already a
  float (`__low2float(ds)`, the value `apply` computes); for IQ4_NL the words stay together and a call reads two
  8-byte loads;
- compute R rows per lane (`STRATA_EXPDEC_R`, 1 or 2 for gate/up, default 1; `STRATA_EXPDEC_DR` 1/2/4 for down,
  default 4): the activation words are loaded once per R rows;
- take `rb` rows per block instead of 16 (`STRATA_EXPDEC_RB` / `_DRB`; 0 = the most that keep `STRATA_EXPDEC_MINBLK`,
  default 800, blocks in the launch), so the staging is amortised over 35-140 KB of weights;
- stage the IQ3_XXS and IQ3_S codebooks in shared memory too (the IQ2 ones already were);
- gate/up `__launch_bounds__(256, STRATA_EXPDEC_MINB)`, default 4 (up to 64 registers, 4 blocks per SM like the
  default kernels; `2` allows 128).

Formats outside the list keep the default kernel for that role; `STRATA_OLD_IQ_MMVQ=1` turns EXPDEC off as it turns
the multi kernels off. The down is behind `STRATA_EXPDEC_DOWN=1`: in the engine the Q2_0 down with EXPDEC was about
10% slower than the default kernel although the micro-bench alone had it at 0.78x (the default down already keeps the
group's h rows in shared memory), so by default EXPDEC takes the gate/up only.

The first time `STRATA_EXPDEC=1` meets a (role, format) the engine writes one line, e.g.
`strata expdec: CUDA1 gate/up type 21: expdec_gu_kernel R 1 MINB 4, 16 rows per block, grid 80 x 10 (cap 10 groups), captured into a graph`
(or `... not covered: the default kernel runs`).

API (`include/strata/kernels/iq_kernels.hpp`): `native_expert_set_expdec`, `native_expert_set_expdec_params` /
`native_expert_expdec_params` (`NativeExpertExpdecParams`), `native_expert_expdec_takes`. The knobs are read from the
environment at startup; captured graphs keep the kernels they captured.

## Bit for bit

For every (row, entry) the sum is the default kernel's tree - `row_dot_80_sub16` for gate/up (lane t of a 16-lane
sub-warp: calls t, t+32, t+64 into `s`, t+16, t+48 into `s16`, `s = __fadd_rn(s, s16)`, butterfly xor 8-4-2-1),
`row_dot_40_sub8` for IQ4_NL, `row_dot_20_sub16` for Q2_0: the same lane does the same calls in the same order, and
`apply_u` is `apply` with the same integer and float operations in the same order on the same words (the q8_1 block
read from shared memory instead of global). The group's entries are independent of each other, so how many are staged
per pass does not matter; R rows per lane and `rb` rows per block only change which lane computes what. The FMA
contraction of `s += d * sumi` is the same compiler decision on the same expression in both kernels. The bench
confirms it: `identical` on every cell (10 format pairs x T 1-4 x 2 window shapes x every variant x 2 cards).

## Micro-bench: `expdec_bench`

Not in the default build: `cmake --build <dir> --target expdec_bench`.

```
expdec_bench [reps=300] [device=-1] [groups=20] [pairs=all] [choices=def,dec,dec:r2,dec:b4,dec:r2:b4] [shape=real]
```

Pairs: the model's 5 gate/up x 2 down formats or `21/20,16/42`. Choices: `def` (the reference) and
`dec[:r<1|2>][:d<1|2|4>][:b<2|4>][:w<0|1>][:x<0|1>][:g<n>][:h<n>][:m<n>]` (rows per lane for gate/up and down, min blocks
per SM, EXPDEC for the down too, also IQ4_NL, rows per block, min blocks; a missing field takes the engine's value).
Shapes: `real` = every token picks 10 experts out of `groups` distinct ones (T=1: 10 groups x 1 entry; T=2: 20 x 1;
T=4: 20 groups, 40 entries); `single` = 10 T groups of one entry; `both` also prints the per-expert / per-entry
decomposition. One line per cell: `dev T shape gu/d choice all_us gu_us down_us GB/s pct identical|DIFFERENT` (the
whole call, then the gate/up and down phases alone; memcmp of the output against `def`; exit 1 if anything differs).
The blobs rotate over >= 96 MB so every call reads its weights cold from DRAM, as the decode does each layer.

Gate/up phase, us per call, synthetic blobs, 20 distinct experts (shape `real`); `dec` = the defaults above:

| card | format | T=1 def / dec | T=2 | T=3 | T=4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RTX 2080 Ti | IQ3_S | 72 / 0.73x | 112 / 0.79x | 124 / 0.75x | 138 / 0.74x |
| RTX 2080 Ti | IQ3_XXS | 61 / 0.79x | 95 / 0.84x | 107 / 0.79x | 119 / 0.77x |
| RTX 2080 Ti | IQ2_XXS | 42 / 0.98x | 74 / 0.92x | 86 / 0.86x | 97 / 0.84x |
| RTX 2080 Ti | IQ2_XS | 60 / 0.75x | 80 / 0.92x | 92 / 0.87x | 104 / 0.84x |
| RTX 2080 Ti | IQ2_S | 62 / 0.75x | 83 / 0.92x | 96 / 0.86x | 109 / 0.84x |
| RTX 3060 | IQ3_S | 74 / 1.09x | 144 / 0.99x | 154 / 0.89x | 174 / 0.87x |
| RTX 3060 | IQ3_XXS | 78 / 0.89x | 132 / 0.92x | 143 / 0.90x | 162 / 0.82x |
| RTX 3060 | IQ2_XXS / XS / S | 60-68 / 0.90-1.04x | 112-118 / 0.89-1.00x | 119-136 / 0.89-0.95x | 132-149 / 0.87-0.91x |

Per-expert / per-entry cost (us per layer call, RTX 2080 Ti, IQ3_S gate/up): 5.20 / 1.26 default, 3.73 / 0.64 with
EXPDEC. Down Q2_0 with `w1` (EXPDEC for the down): 0.65-0.85x in the bench on both cards; down IQ4_NL 0.95-1.07x
(no gain, hence the default kernel).

## In the engine

nsys of a 131k decode (layer split: RTX 3060 layers 0-15, RTX 2080 Ti layers 16-47 and the head, `--pipeline-windows
2`, Windows, 96 verify windows), median kernel time per window, T = 1 / 2 / 3 / 4:

| | default | EXPDEC |
|---|---|---|
| RTX 2080 Ti, gate/up kernel | 1.60 / 2.58 / 3.51 / 4.16 ms | 1.42 / 2.07 / 2.75 / 3.20 ms (-11 / -20 / -22 / -23%) |
| RTX 2080 Ti, gate/up slope per row | +0.86 ms | +0.60 ms |
| RTX 3060, gate/up kernel | 0.77 / 1.43 / 1.97 / 2.23 ms | 0.80 / 1.21 / 1.83 / 1.84 ms |
| RTX 2080 Ti, down Q2_0 with `STRATA_EXPDEC_DOWN=1` | - | ~10% slower than the default (hence off by default) |

End to end, same machine, a deterministic 131k bench (forced tokens and window sizes, 1024 tokens, B-A-B with the
lever on / off / on): **+1.1%** decode tokens/s (+0.0 and +2.1 in the two B arms, no B below A), the text identical.
The expert kernels are about 20% of the critical stage's time and EXPDEC takes about 20% of that, so the end-to-end
figure is small by construction; the lever is cheap, bitwise and off by default.

Not done here: the weight side (the 8-9 two-byte loads per call and row of `Split<TG>::load`; a weight tile staged in
shared memory with 16-byte loads would be the next step), and the T=1 flat cost.


## docs/GYRO.md

# Gyro (agentionai rotor quants) on Strata

Gyro-S and Gyro-M are Qwen3.8-Flash-Next quantizations by agentionai
([agentionai/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/agentionai/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-GGUF)): the routed
experts are stored as trellis-coded blocks (ggml types TQ2_T, TQK6, TQK7) in a Hadamard-rotated basis. Strata reads the
published files unchanged. **Setup lists them as a model family of their own** ("Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Gyro)"); neither
is anybody's default.

| | Gyro-S | Gyro-M |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File | `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-S-TQ1_0.gguf` | `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-M-TQ2_0.gguf` |
| **Download** (the n-gram table is inside the file) | **58.5 GB** | **92.0 GB** |
| **Memory it needs** (VRAM + RAM together) | **27.6 GB** | **35 GB** |
| Experts (trellis) | TQK6 gate/up, TQK7 down | TQ2_T |
| In plain words | the smallest option, for PCs with little memory; lower quality than the 2-3-bit sizes | about IQ3_XXS quality with about 20% less GPU memory; decodes about 16% slower than Q2_0 on a 12 GB RTX 3060 (24% slower before engine 0.2.2) |

About half of each file is the n-gram (PLE) table: it stays on the SSD and is read row by row for every token, so keep
the file on a fast local drive. The memory figure is what the weights take once loaded.

Not defaults, by measurement (our evaluation, 2026-10): against Q2_0 at the same GPU bytes Gyro-M halves the KL
divergence (0.159 against 0.312 on 128 chunks) and is level with IQ3_XXS (0.157), but decodes 16-21% slower on a 12 GB
card (RTX 3060, measured before engine 0.2.2: 16% since) and an R9700, and its reasoning set scored lower than Q2_0's (49/60 against 57/60). Gyro-S is 13% worse
in KL than IQ2_XS (0.268 against 0.236) with 24% fewer bytes. So: pick Gyro-S where nothing bigger fits, Gyro-M when
the 20% memory saving over IQ3_XXS matters. Setup and the MCP server mention them only where the other sizes do not
fit the PC; they warn, never refuse. Gyro-L (agentionai's 50 GiB file, 2026-10-12) is not supported: it uses another
trellis family (types 147-149) that the engine does not have.

## Install

```sh
./setup.sh --setup --family gyro --model Gyro-S      # or Gyro-M;  Windows: START-HERE.bat --setup ...
```

Setup downloads the pinned revision of the file (size and SHA-256 checked), prepares the pack (`tools/iq_pack.py
--compat-bf16`: the Hadamard table and the dense weights, 1.5 GB), the draft head (Strata's own MTP head, prepared from
the original model as for every Qwen3.8-Flash-Next file) and the start script. Needs engine 0.1.45.1 or newer: the pack is native_experts.txt v5 (Hadamard-folded), which the engine reads since the
APR port, and the released 0.1.45 stops at v4. A ready-made engine that is older is replaced by one compiled from this source
(setup), or the app says the model needs a newer engine and offers Update engine.

**Supported:** NVIDIA (CUDA, Linux and Windows) and AMD (HIP, experimental: the authors validated gfx1151; we ran
gfx1201 with identical output to rc2). **Intel Arc** (SYCL, Linux, built from source) runs both files: see [Intel Arc](#intel-arc-sycl). **Apple Silicon Macs** (Metal) run both files from
0.2.2: see [On a Mac](#on-a-mac).

**Pictures.** Gyro reads pictures with the original model's picture reader file (the same one every Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
model uses; setup downloads it with the model). The reader opens only the vocabulary and the header of the Gyro file, so
the trellis tensors do not matter to it. Pictures are on by default, with the CPU reader under 24 GB of graphics memory and
the card's reader from 24 GB. This needs engine 0.1.45.1 or newer, like the Gyro files themselves.

**RTX 50 cards (sm_120).** Gyro gives correct output on them with engine 0.1.45.3. The fused gate/up SwiGLU kernel, which
is the default on compute capability 12.0 cards, handles only rows of 80 dot products; Gyro's trellis rows have 160, and
before the fix they went through it anyway. Gyro-S then answered with loops, garbage or nothing: on an RTX PRO 5000, 0 of
8 test questions were answered right before the fix and 8 of 8 after it (greedy and with the app's sampling). Now those
rows use the full-warp kernel, and the identity gate (10 prompts, 4K and 20K prompts) is identical to the run with the fused
kernel off. If Gyro misbehaves on an RTX 50 card, update the engine.

**Prompt speed and the ggml build.** The trellis prompt kernels (MMQ) are agentionai's, from their llama.cpp fork (MIT).
Strata builds against upstream ggml, which does not have them, so it adds them itself at configure time:
`cmake/strata_ggml_tq_overlay.cmake` writes a copy of the pinned ggml-cuda headers into the build folder with the three
trellis types routed like IQ2_XS (the tile loader is the fork's, `third_party/ggml-tq/`); only Strata's own MMQ library sees
the copy, every other type is compiled from the untouched files (identity gate below). The ready-made engines read Gyro
prompts through it as fast as rc2 does, and bit for bit the same. If the pinned ggml changes and an anchor of the script
no longer matches, the overlay switches itself off with a message and prompts take the slower FP16 path. A build against the
fork (`-DSTRATA_GGML_DIR=<agentionai/llama.cpp>`, as rc2 does) uses the fork's own instances instead.

## Intel Arc (SYCL)

Gyro-S and Gyro-M run on Intel Arc cards on Linux, with the SYCL engine that setup builds from this source ([INTEL.md](INTEL.md)).
Setup lists them for an Arc like for any card and warns, never refuses, when VRAM and RAM together are short. Tested on one
card: an Arc A750 (8 GB, i915 driver) in a PC with a Ryzen 5 5600X (6 cores, AVX2) and 62 GB of RAM, on the first-release files of Gyro-S and
Gyro-M (the same size as the pinned ones, a different SHA-256). The pinned Gyro-S passes the same parity run (16 cases, 0 failures) and
answers correctly through the server; it was not compared with CUDA.
Not tested by us: a B-series card (supported since 2026-10-22; `strata launch` says it is new and how to report a problem), two Arc cards (the second-card expert helper refuses a Gyro pack and says so), an Arc on the xe driver. The Battlemage AOT build
(`bmg-g31`) compiles with the trellis kernels; it was not run.

The trellis decode kernels do the same integer and float operations in the same order as the CUDA ones (int8 codebook, q8_1 activations),
the Hadamard rotation of the expert input and of the SwiGLU output runs on the card, and the prompt takes the grouped XMX path,
which now decodes the trellis types into its tiles. Experts in the card's cache run on the card; the other misses go to the CPU pool or
over the PCIe link, as with every pack.

**Checks.** `tq_sycl_parity <pack> <model.gguf> [layer ...]` (also `--synthetic [--hadamard] GU/DOWN` and `--bench GU/DOWN`) takes real
experts of the file (layers 0-3, 10, 20, 30 and 47, two experts each) and compares the card with a float reference and with the CPU path:

- the decode kernels equal a host replay of their own arithmetic **in every bit** (0 of 3,840 gate/up values and 0 of 7,680 down values
  differ, Gyro-S and Gyro-M, all 16 cases each); the prompt dequantizers equal the fp16 codebook in every bit (0 of 4.9 million values);
  the card's Hadamard rotation equals the CPU's bit for bit (the fp16 form within 3e-4);
- against the float reference the card is within 1.7-2.0e-2 relative L1 error (the int8 codebook; 3e-2 is the bound every expert type
  gets), the CPU path within 0.9e-2. The card and the CPU path therefore agree within tolerance, not bit for bit: the CPU path uses an
  int16 codebook and Q8_0 activations, the card the int8 codebook and q8_1, as on CUDA.

**Against CUDA.** The same Gyro-S file on an RTX 3060 (the f-022-int engine) and on the A750, both with 64 cached experts, no PCIe share and
no CPU prompt share, ten prompts of 26-100 tokens, 48 greedy tokens with the MTP draft: 7 of the 10 prompts give the same 48 tokens. The other three (prompts 5, 7 and 8) agree for 9, 9 and 6 tokens and then differ at a near-tie. The first-token KL is 1.3e-4 to 1.1e-2 and the top token is always the same. The two SYCL prompt paths (oneMKL and XMX) also flip prompt 7 against each other, so the prompt-path rounding alone moves it. A 1,406-token prompt gives the same 16 tokens on both.

**Measured** (A750, setup's config: 32K context, 300 MiB VRAM reserve, MTP draft of 4, PCIe probe 10.4 GB/s, median of 5 interleaved pairs):

| | before | now |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Gyro-S prompt, 1,406 tokens | 40.2 tok/s | **82.0 tok/s** (5/5 pairs) |
| Gyro-S prompt, 2,377 tokens | | 101.9 tok/s |
| Gyro-S prompt, 20,000 tokens | | 195 tok/s |
| Gyro-S decode | 13.7 tok/s | **15.8 tok/s** (5/5 pairs) |
| Gyro-M decode (8K context) | | 14.2 tok/s (12.6-14.4), prompt 62 tok/s at 1,406 tokens |

The decode speed is the CPU's and the link's: with 8 GB the card holds 410 of the 24,576 experts (the dense weights, the draft layer,
the KV cache and the prompt buffers take the rest), so about 15 experts per layer and token come from the CPU pool
(5 workers, AVX2, 8 GB/s: the trellis decode is compute bound, 48 cycles a block) and about 5 over the link. Both move about 10 experts a
millisecond, so the link takes a bigger share than for the i-quants: for packs with trellis experts the engine scales the share with a 12 GB/s
reference instead of 20 (0.48 instead of 0.29 here; fixed 0.45 and 0.60 measured the same; 0.40 gained only 7%). The card's kernels are not the
limit: 20 microseconds an expert (53-68 GB/s of weights) against 18 for IQ3_S, 15 experts take 0.3 ms.

Smaller prompt chunks leave room for more cached experts and cost prompt speed: `--prefill 1024` gives 1,090 slots and +13% decode on a
1,406-token prompt but -24% prompt speed, `--prefill 512` 1,429 slots, -36%. The default stays `--prefill auto`.

**Gyro-M on 8 GB.** Its dense weights are bigger (2.9 GiB of native projections against 1.9): with setup's 32K context the card is 750 MiB
short of one cache slot and the engine stops with that sentence. It starts with `--max-context 8192 --vram-reserve-mib 100 --prefill 1024`
(412 slots). A card with 12 GB or more does not need that.

**Memory.** Gyro-S needs about 27.6 GB of VRAM and RAM together; the n-gram table (28 GB) stays on the SSD, so on an Arc setup does not
put `--ple-io ram` in the config for Gyro (it does for the other packs on an i915 card). One run used about 24 GB of RAM for the
expert arena. Keep the file on a fast SSD.

## Decode speed on NVIDIA (engine 0.2.2)

The trellis decode kernels read the codebook (2048 two-byte entries, 8 random lookups for every 16 weights) from the global
table. On an RTX 3060 that made the gate/up and down kernels wait on the L1 cache, not on memory: 18 L1 sectors for every
lookup request, the card's L1 at 64% busy while the DRAM was 27% busy. The kernels now keep the 4 KB codebook in shared memory
(`STRATA_IQ_STAGE_GRID=0` reads it in place again) and take four rows per warp, 32 rows per thread block, so the copy is shared
and no lane idles in the 160-dot gate/up rows or the 40-dot down rows. The sums are added in the same order as before, so the
answers are bit for bit the old ones: the identity gate (10 prompts, 4096 and 20000 token prompts) is identical on Gyro-S,
Gyro-M, Q2_0 and IQ3_XXS, and the Q2_0 and IQ3_XXS kernels did not change. A Tesla P100 (compute capability 6.0) runs its own variant of the same idea, STRATA_TQ_STAGE (Gyro-S +30% there, 5 pairs).

RTX 3060 12 GB, Core Ultra 7, Ubuntu, CUDA 13.4, default flags (MTP draft 4, auto cache), 5 interleaved pairs of whole engine
starts, medians of the story, code and facts prompts (200 tokens each), the pinned Gyro files, engine 0.2.1 against 0.2.2.

| | decode before, tok/s | after | gain | pairs faster | 4K / 20K prompt |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| Gyro-S | 54.3 | 62.5 | +15.2% | 5 of 5 (10 of 10 requests per prompt) | unchanged (0.996, 1.000) |
| Gyro-M | 50.2 | 54.8 | +9.1% | 5 of 5 (10 of 10) | unchanged (1.004, 0.999) |
| Q2_0 (not changed) | 66.4 | 67.1 | 1.010 (noise) | 3 of 5 | unchanged (1.003, 0.999) |

Against Q2_0 on the same card, before: Gyro-S 54.2 against 64.4 tok/s (16% slower), Gyro-M 50.5 against 65.6 (23% slower).
After: Gyro-S 61.1 against 65.5 (7% slower), Gyro-M 54.1 against 64.5 (16% slower). What is left of Gyro-M's gap is mostly its dense weights: in a
decode profile its Q8_0 matrix-vector kernels take 26% of the GPU time, and they read as many bytes as the card's memory
delivers. The trellis kernels themselves are limited by the shared-memory bank conflicts of the random codebook lookups now. Prompt speed is not changed by this: Gyro prompts stay 7-8% (Gyro-S) and 8-9% (Gyro-M) slower than Q2_0's.

## How it runs (by hand)

The rest of this page is the authors' own guide for a manual install and their measurements on their machines (RTX 5090,
3090, 4090 and a Strix Halo, with Strata rc2). The numbers are theirs; ours are in the next section.

## 1. Build

Setup does these steps for you; by hand, from this checkout. For the fast prompt path Strata's GGML dependency is the agentionai llama.cpp fork, which has the trellis types:

```sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/agentionai/llama.cpp ../agention-llama.cpp
# NVIDIA. RTX 50 series: use CUDA 13 (CUDA 12.8 crashes the prompt path on sm_120: issues #220, #224)
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=ON \
  -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DSTRATA_GGML_DIR=$PWD/../agention-llama.cpp
# AMD (experimental: kernel parity and an end-to-end run validated on gfx1151; in a non-root container add
# --group-add $(getent group render | cut -d: -f3), otherwise HIP finds no device)
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSTRATA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DSTRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON \
  -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1201 -DSTRATA_GGML_DIR=$PWD/../agention-llama.cpp
cmake --build build -j
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## 2. Download and pack

```sh
.venv/bin/pip install huggingface_hub hf_transfer
HF_HUB_ENABLE_HF_TRANSFER=1 .venv/bin/hf download agentionai/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-GGUF \
  Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-S-TQ1_0.gguf --local-dir models
.venv/bin/python tools/iq_pack.py \
  --gguf models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-S-TQ1_0.gguf --out packs/gyro-s --compat-bf16
build/native_expert_parity --load-check packs/gyro-s models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-S-TQ1_0.gguf
```

The pack is 1.5 GB (dense weights, tokenizer, the Hadamard and expert tables); the experts are read from the
GGUF. Keep the GGUF on a fast local SSD: the n-gram table is read from it for every token.
`--load-check` must end with `0 failures`.

## 3. Draft head

```sh
.venv/bin/python tools/mtp_fetch.py fetch --out mtp
.venv/bin/python tools/mtp_pack.py --src mtp --experts q2_0 --out mtp/mtp-q2_0.gguf
.venv/bin/python tools/mtp_rt.py --gguf mtp/mtp-q2_0.gguf --out mtp/rt
cp data/draft_vocab.bin mtp/rt/draft_vocab.bin
```

## 4. Serve

Save as `strata-gyro-s.json` at the repository root:

```json
{
  "exe": "build/strata",
  "args": [
    "--pack", "packs/gyro-s",
    "--native", "models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Gyro-S-TQ1_0.gguf",
    "--expert-profile", "data/expert-profile.bin", "--expert-cache", "auto",
    "--prefill", "auto", "--spec", "4", "--spec-min-p", "0.5",
    "--mtp", "mtp/rt", "--max-context", "131072", "--kv", "int8"
  ],
  "cwd": ".",
  "tokenizer": "packs/gyro-s/tokenizer",
  "model_name": "gyro-s-strata",
  "log": "strata-gyro-s.log",
  "host": "127.0.0.1",
  "port": 8080
}
```

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m serve.server --engine strata --config strata-gyro-s.json --port 8080
```

The web interface is at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`; API clients use `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1` (OpenAI) or
`/v1/messages` (Anthropic). `--expert-cache auto` sizes the expert cache to the free VRAM: on a 32 GB card at
128k context it holds 23,464 of 24,576 experts (22.9 GiB). On smaller cards it holds fewer and streams the rest
from RAM; nothing else changes.

## Measured here (the port, 2026-10-15/16)

One AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, ROCm 7), one card of four, exclusive box lock, `--prefill auto --spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5
--mtp --kv int8`, 22K context, interleaved pairs (the arm that goes first alternates), medians, the files of the first
Gyro release (2026-10-07). A = agentionai/Strata rc2 9ff02c9, B = this port.

| B, ggml of | file | decode tok/s A / B (B/A) | pairs B faster | prompt 4K ms A / B | prompt 20K ms A / B |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| agentionai fork | Gyro-S | 85.4 / 89.7 (1.051) | 5/5 | 5418 / 5313 (0.98) | 14358 / 13859 (0.97) |
| agentionai fork | Gyro-M | 72.7 / 82.7 (1.136) | 5/5 | 5183 / 5520 (1.07) | 13421 / 14164 (1.06) |
| upstream + overlay (the ready-made engine) | Gyro-S | 85.3 / 89.6 (1.050) | 5/5 | 5413 / 5298 (0.98) | 14372 / 13854 (0.96) |
| upstream + overlay | Gyro-M | 72.6 / 82.6 (1.138) | 5/5 | 5682 / 5524 (0.97) | 15005 / 14160 (0.94) |
| upstream, no overlay (FP16 prompt path) | Gyro-S | 85.3 / 89.6 (1.050) | 5/5 | 5425 / 6939 (1.28) | 14364 / 21677 (1.51) |

Decode is faster than rc2's because the port sits on the newer Strata (0.1.45); the same engine change makes IQ3_XXS 7% faster
(rc2 86.9, port 93.1 tok/s, 2 pairs). Prompts of the ISTA files gained 11-16% from it too (IQ3_XXS 4K 6184 to 5480 ms, 20K
16587 to 13864 ms). Gyro-M's first run against rc2 showed its prompts 5-7% slower; in the second rc2's own Gyro-M prompts
took 15.0 s instead of 13.4 s (the 92 GB file's page-cache state), the port's stayed at 14.2 s, and Gyro-M's prompts are 3-6%
faster than rc2's: that difference was rc2's baseline, not a regression. Without the overlay (plain upstream ggml) the trellis
prompt kernels are missing and prompts go through the FP16 path: 28% (4K) to 51% (20K) slower than rc2, and a different
rounding. Decode is unaffected either way.

Identity (the fixed gate flags, 10 prompts, exact_pp 4096 and 20000 tokens, same card for both arms):

- Q2_0 and IQ3_XXS, f-split against the port (upstream ggml): 10/10 identical, residual dumps and outputs IDENTICAL.
- Gyro-S and Gyro-M, rc2 against the port with the fork's ggml and with upstream + overlay: 10/10 identical; exact_pp 4096 /
  20000 residual dumps and outputs IDENTICAL (run alone; a run beside other engines on the box once showed a different dump).
- Q2_0 and IQ3_XXS, f-split against the port with the overlay on, on AMD gfx1201 and on NVIDIA sm_86: IDENTICAL.
- The pack step (`tools/iq_pack.py --compat-bf16`) writes byte-identical files to rc2's tools for Gyro-S.

## Measured (the authors', rc2)

All runs: greedy or the stated sampling, same prompt tokens as llama.cpp, MTP draft `--spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5`,
int8 KV. "llama.cpp" is the agentionai fork with the CUDA trellis fixes (in its `main` since 2026-10-04).

### RTX 5090 (32 GB), Gyro-S, all experts on the GPU (2026-10-03)

Decode tokens/s, single prompts of 34-177 tokens, 384 new tokens, `--max-context 16384` (all 24,576 experts cached):

| | prose | JSON | code |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Strata | 139.9 | 221.3 | 209.0 |

Server, rc2's `gyro_setup.sh` config (128k context, 23,463 experts cached), thinking off, temperature 0.7,
top-k 20, top-p 0.95, min-p 0.05, 512 new tokens, 3 repetitions:

| | prose | JSON | code | copy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Strata | 131.7 | 200.1 | 195.2 | 201.8 |
| llama.cpp, MTP draft | 116.8 | 213.0 | 179.0 | 220.7 |
| llama.cpp, no draft | 121.8 | 123.2 | 122.5 | 121.2 |

Long real-text prompts, prefill tokens/s: 4k tokens 3,456 (llama.cpp 2,520), 16k tokens 4,883 (llama.cpp 2,471).

### RTX 5090, Gyro-M (2026-10-03)

The experts (29.9 GiB) do not all fit next to the KV cache; `auto` caches 18,007 of 24,576. Same server protocol:
prose 113.8, JSON 170.8, code 153.0, copy 175.7 tokens/s; prefill 4k 3,369, 16k 4,854 tokens/s. llama.cpp needs
`-ncmoe 8` for this file on a 32 GB card and decodes at 70.8 tokens/s without a draft.

### RTX 3090 (24 GB), 2026-10-03

Same server protocol, 128k context, `auto` cache:

| | experts cached | prose | JSON | code | copy | prefill 4k | prefill 16k |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Gyro-S | 15,756 | 31.8 | 45.2 | 42.2 | 45.1 | 1,402 | 1,863 |
| Gyro-M | 11,811 | 27.8 | 39.4 | 34.4 | 37.7 | 1,363 | 1,910 |
| llama.cpp, Gyro-S, `-ncmoe 10`, 32k context, no draft | (10 layers on the CPU) | 16.0 | 16.2 | 16.2 | 16.5 | 468 (`-ncmoe 11`) | 479 |

On a 24 GB card, cache misses run on the CPU, so the CPU matters: this box had a Zen 2 EPYC (AVX2, no AVX-512).
The llama.cpp row is the build before the CUDA trellis fixes; those added about 3 % at 24 GB, where the CPU layers
dominate.

The Strata rows predate Strata's own CPU kernels for the trellis types (`src/kernels/cpu/tq_*.cpp`, AVX2 and
AVX-512, picked at run time). Before them a cache miss ran ggml-cpu's `vec_dot`, one token at a time; the new kernels
take about 45 % of its time per expert on AVX2 and decode a block once for all the tokens of a verify window
(`build/tq_cpu_parity --bench` measures them on your CPU). `STRATA_NO_TQ_KERNELS=1` goes back to ggml-cpu;
`STRATA_TQ_ISA=avx2` or `scalar` caps the instruction set (for comparisons).

### Smaller caches (RTX 5090, 2026-10-02, before the int8 decode kernels)

| Expert cache | prose | JSON | code |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 24,576 slots (all experts) | 116.4 | 194.3 | 173.5 |
| 22,000 slots | 111.4 | 175.7 | 166.1 |
| 9,000 slots (about a 16 GB card's room) | 81.4 | 74.0 | 96.8 |
| 3,000 slots (about an 8 GB card's room) | 48.0 | 52.4 | 57.9 |

The smaller caches were emulated on the 5090 (fast GPU, PCIe 5.0 x16 at ~51 GB/s). A real 8 or 16 GB card is a
slower GPU, often on a slower link: read those rows as "it stays usable", not as a prediction for a specific card.
The decoded output was read and is fluent and correct; token-level parity against llama.cpp has not been
checked. A real chat at 128k context worked through the web interface.

### Two GPUs (2026-10-04, 2× RTX 4090, no NVLink/P2P)

- **Layer split** (Strata splits the layers across both cards automatically) works with Gyro, including the
  idle-card prompt helper (`STRATA_PREFILL_HELP=1`). Repeated runs give identical output.
- **Decode with a second card** (`--peer-device 1` or `--expert-cache-device1 auto`) works and matches single-GPU output.
- **Prompt processing on the peer card** needs GPU-to-GPU access (NVLink or data-centre GPUs); without it Strata keeps
  the prompt on the first GPU and logs `no P2P`.

Single RTX 4090 smoke run (Gyro-S, MTP draft, greedy): code 107.5, prose 84.3, JSON 76.3 tokens/s.

## Numerics

- **Decode** (Strata's own expert kernels) reads the trellis weights through an int8 copy of the codebook with one
  global scale (`tq_lut_i8`, relative RMS error 0.85 % of the codebook's standard deviation, far below the
  quantization error itself), against q8_1 activations.
- **Prompt processing** decodes them otherwise: the FP16 path through the fp16 codebook (`tq_lut_f16`, what GGML's
  own dequantizer reads); the MMQ path through the llama.cpp fork's kernels, which read the int8 codebook as well
  on the fork's current `main`.
- So decode and prompt results agree within tolerance, not bit for bit. `native_expert_parity` checks one expert
  on the decode kernels against GGML's float dequantizer and a float SwiGLU: relative L1 error below 3e-2, the
  bound every expert type gets there. Its "bitwise equal" lines compare Strata's decode-once and per-entry decode
  kernels with each other, not with a float reference.

## Known limits

- **Not in this port** (rc2 has them; see the list at the end of this page): the prompt helper on a second GPU for a Gyro
  pack. Setup of two cards still runs the layer split and the decode peer; the prompt peer says it is not used for a
  Hadamard-folded pack and the prompt stays on the first card. Gyro-L is not supported.
- **Source builds:** the SYCL tree has the trellis kernels (Intel Arc, above), and so has the Metal engine (On a Mac, below).

- **Not measured yet:** token parity against llama.cpp.
- **Benchmark mode only:** `strata --tokens-file ... --max-new N` decodes N tokens past the end of the answer;
  compare speeds only up to the answer's end.
- **AMD:** the trellis kernels pass parity on gfx1151 (ROCm 7.2.1) and a short end-to-end run there generated
  correctly (~28-31 tokens/s); no speed tuning or RDNA4 run yet.
- **Gyro-M:** 29.9 GiB of experts do not all fit a 32 GB card next to the KV cache; `auto` streams the rest.
- **Not validated end to end yet** (Strata runs them and logs a warning): an AMD GPU other than gfx1151, and
  prompt processing on a peer GPU over P2P.

## On a Mac

Apple Silicon Macs run Gyro-S and Gyro-M from 0.2.2 (Metal kernels in `metal/kernels`, the same published files, the same
Hadamard-folded pack). What a Mac needs, the measured speeds on a 32 GB Mac mini and what was checked are in
[MAC.md](MAC.md#gyro-s-and-gyro-m-agentionais-trellis-experts). Setup: `./setup.sh --family gyro --model Gyro-S` (the app and
`strata launch` list it under Gyro models).


## docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md

# How does Strata work?

Models like Qwen3.8-Flash-Next normally run on servers with hundreds of gigabytes of graphics memory. Your graphics
card has 12-24 GB. Strata makes it fit by **sharing the work across your whole PC** - the same idea as a kitchen, where
the things you use all the time stay on the counter and the rest waits in the pantry. Back to the
[README](../README.md#how-does-it-work).

## Who does what

<p align="center"><img src="media/how-it-works.svg" width="860" alt="The model's 24,576 experts: the busiest on the graphics card, all of them in RAM, a lookup table on the SSD"></p>

- **The model is a team of 24,576 small specialists ("experts"),** and each word it writes needs only 10 of them.
  So it doesn't have to have all of them on the graphics card at once.
- **Your graphics card** does the part of the work needed for every word, and keeps the few thousand experts that
  are asked most often. It keeps learning which ones those are while you use it.
- **Your RAM** holds every expert. When a word needs one the card doesn't have, **your processor** works on it -
  at the same time as the graphics card, so neither waits for the other.
- **Your SSD** holds a big lookup table; the model only reads a few small rows of it per word.

The same in technical terms:

- **GPU (VRAM):** attention and DeltaNet mixers, the gated-residual weights, routers, shared experts, output head, the
  MTP draft layer, the KV cache (from 64K: only its most-read part, the rest streams from RAM), and an **expert
  cache** that fills the rest of VRAM with the most-used experts (it adapts to the conversation while you chat).
  More VRAM matters more than a faster GPU: every extra GB holds ~700 more experts, and every expert on the GPU is one
  the CPU does not have to compute.
- **RAM:** all 24,576 experts, pinned. The CPU computes the experts that are not on the GPU **in place**, at the same
  time as the GPU works on the cached ones (AVX-512 / AVX2 kernels, ggml's for the i-quants). On a PC with little RAM
  and a big card, the [low-RAM mode](MODELS.md#a-big-graphics-card-and-little-ram) keeps in RAM only what the GPU does
  not hold.
- **SSD:** the 28.8 GB n-gram table, read a few rows per token through the OS cache.

This works the same on NVIDIA (CUDA) and AMD (HIP) cards: the same engine, compiled for each.

## Guess, then check

<p align="center"><img src="media/guess-and-check.svg" width="860" alt="A small helper guesses the next words; the big model checks them all at once and keeps the right ones"></p>

- **Guess, then check.** A small, fast helper built into the model guesses the next few words, and the big model
  checks all the guesses in one go. It keeps the ones it agrees with and writes the next word itself - so one step
  often produces several words. The helper only guesses - the big model decides every word - so you get the same
  quality answer, 1.6-1.8x sooner.
- In technical terms: the model's own MTP layer drafts up to 3 tokens; one pass over all 48 layers checks them, 2.4-3.2
  tokens per pass on average. When the reply repeats the context (code edits, quoted text), **prompt lookup** drafts
  up to 5 tokens from the earlier copy, but only where its measured acceptance and cost say it pays: code edits 6-11%
  faster, other text unchanged. The drafts are checked like the MTP's, so the output is the same.

## Reading long texts

**Long texts are read in big pieces** (up to 8,192 tokens - pieces of words - at a time), which is why a long
document or code base is read at over 1,000 tokens per second. The experts of the next layer stream to the GPU over
PCIe while the current layer's attention runs. After the first message, Strata keeps the conversation and reads only
what is new, so follow-ups start in seconds.

## More

The [details](DETAILS.md#how-it-works) explain every part and its numbers, and the
[paper](paper/Strata-Paper.pdf) tells the whole story, with the measurements behind it.

## docs/IMAGES.md

# Image generation (Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo)

Strata's server can also make images: `POST /v1/images/generations`, OpenAI's images API. The model is
[Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo) (8 steps, CFG 1) in
[Unsloth's GGUF quants](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo-GGUF), run by
[stable-diffusion.cpp](https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp) (`sd-cli`), which setup compiles for your GPU.
It is optional and off unless you ask for it.

The model is under the **Qwen Research License**, not Apache 2.0: read
[its license](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo/blob/main/LICENSE) before you use the images
commercially.

## Set it up

    ./setup.sh --setup --images qwen-image          (Linux)
    START-HERE.bat --setup --images qwen-image      (Windows)

or, for an install that is already set up, without running the whole setup again:

    .venv/bin/python tools/image/install.py --config strata-<model>.json

Setup compiles `sd-cli` (stable-diffusion.cpp at a pinned commit) into `engine-image/`, downloads three files into
the data folder's `models/qwen-image-2.1-turbo/` and checks each against its SHA-256, and writes an `"images"` section
into the model's run config.

| piece | file | size |
|---|---|---|
| denoiser (by GPU memory) | `qwen-image-2.1-turbo-Q4_K_M.gguf` up to 8 GB, `Q6_K` up to 12 GB, `Q8_0` above | 4.2 / 6.3 / 7.6 GB |
| text encoder | `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` | 5.1 GB |
| VAE | `qwen_image_2.1_vae_bf16.safetensors` | 0.7 GB |

Options: `--image-quant Q4_K_M|Q6_K|Q8_0` (a bigger one than recommended is kept, with a warning),
`--image-backend cuda|hip|vulkan|cpu`, `--image-gpu-policy auto|keep|shrink|unload`, `--images no` (takes the section
out of the config).

Backends: CUDA on NVIDIA (needs the CUDA Toolkit), HIP on AMD cards with their own memory (Linux, the same ROCm as the
engine), Vulkan on AMD APUs/iGPUs (Radeon 780M, Strix Point/Halo), Intel Arc and AMD under Windows. A Linux PC without
the Vulkan development files gets the LunarG Vulkan SDK unpacked into `third_party/` (no sudo); on Windows install the
Vulkan SDK first. On Vulkan setup adds `--vae-tiling --vae-tile-overlap 0.25`: an untiled 1024x1024 VAE decode on a Radeon 780M is one
GPU job long enough to trip the kernel driver's job timeout (no image), and a quarter's overlap decodes in half the
time of sd.cpp's default half overlap.

## Use it

    curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/images/generations -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"prompt": "a cartoon sloth mascot waving, flat vector illustration", "size": "1024x1024", "seed": 42}'

| field | |
|---|---|
| `prompt` | the description (required) |
| `size` | `WIDTHxHEIGHT`, each side a multiple of 32 from 256 to 2048 (`max_side`); default and `auto`: `1024x1024` |
| `n` | images, 1 to 4 (`max_n`); image *i* uses seed + *i* |
