## docs/INTEL_INT8_EXPERTS.md

# Fused int8 DPAS expert products on Battlemage (branch f-151-b70)

Behaviour note, written before the kernel (2026-10-18) and kept in step with `sycl/src/prefill/esimd_moe.dp.cpp`. The measured numbers
are at the end.

## What it replaces

The prompt path computes a routed expert as dequantize (gate/up and down to FP16, 9.8 MB written) then oneMKL GEMMs and SwiGLU. On
the Arc Pro B70 (IQ3_S pack, 4K prompt) that chain is ~38 us of GPU time per expert (dequant 25.6 us, GEMMs and SwiGLU ~12 us) and
23% of the prompt. The fused path decodes the quantized weights in registers straight into the DPAS B operand, so the FP16 copy
never exists and the weights are read once, compressed (2.1 MB per expert instead of 9.8 MB written and read back).

## Switches

* `STRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=1` (alias `STRATA_PF_I8=1`): every group of experts whose formats are supported takes the int8 chain.
* `STRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=0`: the FP16 path everywhere. The name is MMQ's because the other backends' int8
  prompt-expert path is MMQ; here it is this kernel.
* `STRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=auto` (the Battlemage default): per group, int8 while the group's mean rows per expert are under the crossover measured on this GPU.
  At the first layer of each expert format the engine times both chains on synthetic experts (random blobs of the layer's format and
  shape, uneven row counts like a real group) at 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256 mean rows per expert, interpolates where the FP16 chain
  becomes the faster one, flags the result "clear" when the cost ratio falls steadily and the bracketing samples are 5% away from
  1, and keeps it in `~/.cache/strata/i8-crossover.txt` (`STRATA_CACHE_DIR` moves it) keyed by device name, driver version, the two
  ggml types and the shape. A matching key is read back instead of measured. The measurement costs ~1.2 s once, during the first
  prompt. A measurement that fails (no VRAM) falls back to 64 rows.
* `STRATA_I8_FORCE=0` hides the device from the kernels, `STRATA_I8_MT=2|4|8` forces the tile height, `STRATA_I8_WG=0` the
  non-work-group kernels, `STRATA_I8_GRF=128` the 128-register mode, `STRATA_I8_DBG` bring-up switches (skip decode / loads / stores).
* Default (unset): `auto` on a Battlemage GPU (bmg-g21 or bmg-g31 by the SYCL architecture id, not by name; the kernels must be in the binary and pass `available()`), the FP16 path on every other GPU. The engine prints one line at load ("int8 prompt experts are on ... STRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=0 turns them off"). If the kernels are not in the binary for the device (an AOT build for other devices) or a launch throws, the group and the rest of the process take the FP16 chain with one log line. The activations are quantized, so the bits differ from the FP16 path (see "Quality").

## Tiles and thresholds

* One hardware thread (ESIMD, sub-group 16, 256 GRF) owns 16 output rows of one expert, all of K, and `MT x 8` activation rows.
  `MT` = 2, 4 or 8 from the group's mean number of 8-row tiles per expert (<=2 -> 2, <=4 -> 4, else 8). A thread's accumulators are
  MT tiles of 512 bytes in an 8 KB register file (256 GRF of 32 bytes), so MT 12 or two output tiles per thread spilled 3-15 KB and ran
  2-5x slower. An expert with more rows than 8 MT is split over row-block threads, each decoding the weights again.
* A work group is 8 such threads on 8 consecutive output tiles (128 outputs) of one row block: the activation tiles of the row block
  are read from global memory once per group, in chunks of 4 steps of 32 (128 of K), into double-buffered local memory (one barrier per
  chunk), and every thread reads them from there; the group also copies the codebook the decoders gather from into local memory.
  IQ2_S gate/up keeps the plain kernel: its 8 KB codebook costs more to copy per group than the gathers save (35 against 16 us).
* K step 32 (one s8 DPAS 8x16x32): decode the 16 rows' 32 values (lanes = rows, one weight decode per tile, applied to all MT row
  tiles), one DPAS into a zeroed int32 tile, float epilogue. Group of up to 16 experts per launch (the same group the FP16 grouped path
  holds in the prompt walk), 4 launches per group (quantize, gate/up, SwiGLU + quantize, down) against 4 per expert.
* The kernels need the s8 8x16x32 matrix combination (Xe2: Battlemage, Lunar Lake). Large GRF: `grf_size<256>` is requested for
  every kernel; a device that cannot build it keeps its default and the spills show in the build log. DP4a fallback: none; without the
  DPAS combination `available()` is false and the FP16 path runs (the build without ESIMD for an Alchemist / Xe-HPC AOT device
  compiles stubs, `STRATA_I8_NO_ESIMD`).

## Scales

* Activations: llama.cpp's q8_1 grid. Per row and 32 of K, `d = amax / 127`, `q = round(x / d)` half away from zero, int8 stored in
  DPAS A-operand order (`[8-row tile][K/32][8 rows x 32 bytes]`, experts padded to 8 rows with zeros), the 8 row scales of a tile
  contiguous.
* Weights: IQ3_S `d (1 + 2 s)` per 32, IQ3_XXS `d (2 s + 1) / 4`, IQ2_S `d (2 s + 1) / 8` per 16 (two DPAS per 32, the other half
  zeroed), IQ4_NL `d` per 32, Q2_0 `d` per 64; the int8 values are the codebook entries with their signs (IQ3_S/IQ3_XXS/IQ2_S: 1..62,
  IQ4_NL: -127..113, Q2_0: -1..2), never rounded.
* Each 32-block's int32 dot product (<= 32 * 127 * 127) is exact and exactly convertible to float; it is scaled by the weight scale of the
  column and the activation scale of the row and added to a float accumulator, K ascending (the float multiply and add are the only
  roundings besides the activation quantization). After gate/up, `silu(gate) * up` (the FP16 path's formula, in float, not rounded
  to FP16) is quantized per 32 of the 640 FF values into the down input.

## Edge cases and fallback rules

* A row count is padded to a tile of 8 with zero rows (stores are masked to the real rows); an expert with no rows is not in the group.
* IQ3_S rows are 110-byte blocks (IQ3_XXS 98, IQ2_S 82, IQ4_NL / Q2_0 18): 2-byte aligned only, so every field is read as dwords, two
  gathers and a funnel shift when not dword aligned. The down matrix ends the expert blob, so its reads clamp the second dword of an unaligned read to the
  matrix's last dword (`ld32c`); the gate/up reads stay inside the blob (the down matrix follows them). The first version read up to 3 bytes
  past the end of a test allocation and faulted the GPU (an xe CAT error and an engine reset; nothing else was affected).
* Supported: gate/up IQ3_S (21), IQ3_XXS (18), IQ2_S (22) with K a multiple of 256; down IQ4_NL (20) with K a multiple of 32 and Q2_0
  (42) with K a multiple of 64; 640 FF x 2560 embedding; output rows a multiple of 16; a held group of at most 16 experts. Any other type or
  shape makes the layer take the FP16 path (IQ4_XS gate/up, 1 of 48 layers of the IQ3_S pack). A group the kernels cannot run (no VRAM for
  the int8 scratch, a format they refuse) takes the FP16 chain for that group.
* Multi-GPU: the codebooks, the scratch and the availability are kept per device.

## ESIMD on this compiler (oneAPI 2026.1, bmg-g31) - what went wrong while writing it

* A dynamic index into a kernel-argument array gave a garbage value (the first weight read faulted the GPU, the xe driver logged
  hundreds of page faults and reset the engine, the box recovered each time): the kernels read the arrays at constant indices
  (`pick_expert`, the unrolled expert lookup in the quantize kernels).
* `t % n` and `t / n` with a run-time `n` gave `t % n == t`: the kernels use 2-D grids.
* `gather<T, N, VS>` with VS > 1 is not available on Battlemage; a lambda capturing a simd by reference puts it in private memory.

## Quality

The int8 path is near-lossless against the FP16 path. 28 prompts (code, reasoning, chat, multi-turn, long up to 3.2K tokens), 6002
positions teacher-forced on the FP16 path's greedy continuations (`cuda_kl.py` with `STRATA_FOLLOW`), fixed flags: reference against
itself KL exactly 0; int8 against reference KL mean 0.0002 nats (p99 0.006, max 0.04), top-1 99.7%, perplexity ratio 1.0004, first-token
KL 0.0005. For comparison a chunk-size change (`--prefill 8192` against 4096) moves the first-token distribution by 0.01-0.03 nats.
The kernel arithmetic itself matches an exact host reference on the same int8 activations to 3e-7 relative; against FP64 with the
unquantized activations each product carries ~1% rms (the q8_1 grid; synthetic data with 1% outliers), the chain 1.7% against
dequantize + oneMKL. `esimd_moe_parity` runs all six gate/up x down type pairs.


## docs/KV_PREFETCH.md

# Overlap streamed KV uploads with prefill computation

## Why this helps

When long-context KV lives partly in system RAM, prefill uploads each attention
layer's cached prefix. Waiting for every upload on the compute stream leaves
the GPU idle.

This opt-in change starts the next attention layer's upload on a separate stream
while the current layer continues computing. It reuses the existing staging
pool; it does not allocate another KV buffer.

## Use and ordering

Set `STRATA_KV_PREFETCH=1` before starting the engine. It is off by default.
A release event protects the staging pool's last reader; a ready event orders
the next attention consumer. Early returns drain pending copies before the caller
can refill borrowed expert slots. Relayout and destruction also drain the stream.

## Validation environment

- Two modified RTX 3080 20 GB cards; CUDA SM86, CUDA 13.1, Linux.
- Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 (18 cores / 36 threads), about 94 GiB usable RAM.
- PCIe 3.0, no GPU peer-to-peer access; 17 expert-pool workers.
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_S, 131,072-token context, INT8 KV,
  32,768 resident KV cells.
- Medium thinking: 2,048-token reasoning cap, 8,192-token output cap.
- Physical GPU power limits stayed at 250 W and 280 W. No power increase.
- Historical performance tests used an isolated engine based on official
  v0.1.38 plus reviewed architectds/Strata changes (best, 05c0f36).
  This PR contains only our change, ported to official main (99f3dbd).
  The historical timings are NOT a measured speedup of this pure-upstream port.

## Historical benefit

ABBA comparison, two observations per arm, all 20 complete JSON checks passed:

| Cold input | Serial prefill | Overlapped prefill | Serial request | Overlapped request |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8K | 5.013 s | 5.025 s | 6.727 s | 6.726 s |
| 32K | 16.989 s | 16.082 s | 18.468 s | 17.559 s |
| 64K | 32.604 s | 31.259 s | 34.354 s | 32.775 s |

Prefill time fell by 5.3% at 32K and 4.1% at 64K.
There was no useful 8K improvement and no decode speedup.
Profiling showed roughly 939 ms / 1,553 ms of serial KV-stage wait moving off
the critical path. The copies still execute; they are not eliminated.

## Validation and remaining work

- Linux compile/link against pure official main (99f3dbd) passed. No engine
  was started and no production settings were changed.
- No claim of a pure-upstream GPU speedup or bitwise numerical parity yet.
- The standalone historical prototype did not run the full vision/120K/cancel
  safety suite. Later combined builds did, but they do not validate this port.
- Keep draft until pure-upstream long-context, cancellation, and image-history
  tests pass. HIP and other GPUs are unvalidated.


## docs/LLAMA_SWAP.md

# Running Strata behind llama-swap

[llama-swap](https://github.com/mostlygeek/llama-swap) puts several model servers behind one address and starts the one a
request names, stopping the others to free the GPU. Strata works as one of its models. This page is what we needed to
get it running; it was tested with llama-swap's default stop behaviour, Strata 0.1.39 (Coder IQ1_M on a Tesla V100) and
clients reaching the machine by its host name.

## The entry

Set Strata up as usual first (`./setup.sh --no-start ...`), then point llama-swap at the server directly. The start script
setup writes (`run-<model>.sh`) fixes the port at 8080, so call `serve/server.py` with llama-swap's port instead:

```yaml
healthCheckTimeout: 300            # Strata takes ~1.5-2 min to load; give it room

models:
  strata:
    cmd: >-
      sh -c 'cd /path/to/Strata && exec .venv/bin/python serve/server.py
      --engine strata --config strata-coder-iq1_m.json --port ${PORT}'
    env: ["STRATA_ALLOWED_HOSTS=my-server"]     # the host name your clients use -- see below
    checkEndpoint: /health
    ttl: 1800
```

- `exec` makes the Python server the process llama-swap stops. On llama-swap's stop (SIGTERM) the server stops its engine:
  in our test the engine was gone and the V100's memory freed within 2 s.
- `checkEndpoint: /health` -- Strata's `/health` answers only once the model is loaded. Measured load time on our machine
  (model files on a SATA SSD): 80 s, 105 s while another download was using the disk.
- If other models share the GPU, put them in a llama-swap group or let swapping unload them; Strata needs the card's
  memory to itself.

## The trap: "Host ... is not allowed"

The first request through llama-swap failed at once with:

```text
403 Host 'my-server:8040' is not allowed (DNS rebinding protection)
```

Strata only answers to the host names it knows, so a web page cannot reach it by pointing a DNS name at 127.0.0.1.
llama-swap passes the client's Host header through, so a client that reaches the proxy by name (`http://my-server:8040`)
is refused. Requests by IP address and to `localhost` always pass, which is why it can work in a quick test and fail
from another machine. Any one of these fixes it:

- `STRATA_ALLOWED_HOSTS=my-server` in the entry's `env` (comma-separated names; ports are ignored), or
- `"allowed_hosts": ["my-server"]` in `strata-<model>.json`, or
- an `"api_key"`, which turns the check off -- then every client must send the key.

## Strata's own pages through llama-swap

llama-swap forwards `/upstream/<model>/...` unchanged, so Strata's status and health pages stay reachable, and calling one
also loads the model without sending a chat request:

```bash
curl http://my-server:8040/upstream/strata/health
curl http://my-server:8040/upstream/strata/v1/status
```

## Claude Code and other Anthropic-API clients: the thinking level

Claude Code (and the Claude Agent SDK) send `"output_config": {"effort": "high"}` with every request unless told
otherwise, so Strata thinks at its highest level (seen by logging the requests). `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL=medium` (or
`low`) in the client's environment changes it. One measurement, for scale only: on one real coding task in our setup,
`medium` finished in 6.5 min against 9.7 min at `high`, both correct; `low` took 10.1 min (more trial-and-fix steps).
One run each -- not a general result.


## docs/LOGIT_BIAS.md

# Per-request token biases

`POST /v1/chat/completions` accepts `logit_bias` with a supporting CUDA or HIP
engine, without continuous batching. The same bias applies to every generated
token in the request, including tokens checked together during speculative
decoding. It does not force single-token verification windows.

## Example: Hello becomes Hi

We use `Hello` because it is a familiar word, it is exactly one token in the
tested tokenizer, and the unbiased model naturally chooses it for this prompt.
The tokenizer maps `Hello` to **token ID 9419**. That number identifies the token;
it is not its logit or probability. The value **-100** is the requested bias,
which this implementation treats as a hard exclusion.

Before: send this request without a bias. The measured response was **Hello**.

```json
{
  "model": "bias-validation",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with one English greeting, one word only."}],
  "max_tokens": 8,
  "temperature": 0,
  "reasoning_effort": "none"
}
```

After: add only `logit_bias`. The measured response was **Hi** (token 12675).

```json
{
  "model": "bias-validation",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with one English greeting, one word only."}],
  "max_tokens": 8,
  "temperature": 0,
  "reasoning_effort": "none",
  "logit_bias": {"9419": -100}
}
```

The equivalent llama.cpp-style pair list is `"logit_bias": [[9419, false]]`;
it also produced **Hi**. Removing the field on the next request restored **Hello**.
Nothing is banned by default. This is a per-request example, not a built-in list.
The `model` value above is the test server's alias; use your server's model name.
Numeric pair values are also supported, for example `[[42, 2.5]]`.
Token IDs belong to the loaded model's tokenizer; the example ID is not portable
between arbitrary models. Leading spaces and letter case can also change token IDs.
The four English requests were measured on ISTA IQ3_XXS; a
[reproduction script](../tools/logit_bias_english_example.py) is included.

## Semantics and limits

Biases must be finite numbers in `[-100, 100]`. Negative values discourage a
token, positive values encourage it, and **-100 excludes it** (`false` in a
pair list has the same meaning). The bias is added before repetition/frequency/
presence penalties, temperature, and candidate filtering. Raw model logits
are not overwritten. Banning a token does not ban a word or language: other
token sequences may produce the same text.

Omitting the field, `null`, `{}`, or `[]` clears the previous request's bias.
Biases are request sampling state; they are not stored in a conversation cache.
They do not change the model weights or prompt KV. A fixed dense vocabulary
vector is uploaded when the bias changes and reused within the request.

Malformed entries, duplicate IDs in pair lists, IDs outside the vocabulary,
out-of-range biases, or banning the entire vocabulary return HTTP 400. Validation
on the chat route occurs before SSE streaming headers are sent. Nonempty biases
also return HTTP 400 with older engines, the current SYCL engine, or continuous
batching (`--batch`), rather than being silently ignored. The engine advertises
`logit_bias=1` in its `INFO` response when this implementation is present.

MTP target verification applies the bias; the draft model is not biased, so a
restrictive list may reduce draft acceptance. Ordinary MTP was tested. The
experimental coupled/rejection-sampling combinations and multi-GPU execution
were not validated in this campaign. There is no startup bias-file option in
this change: send the field with each request.


## docs/MAC.md

# Strata on a Mac (Apple Silicon, Metal)

Strata runs on Apple Silicon Macs through its own engine on Metal. This is the same engine as on a PC. The NVIDIA
kernels are replaced by Metal ones (`metal/`), and the host code and the server are the PC's. There are two ways in:

- **The Strata app (`.dmg`) and the Terminal (`strata launch`).** The Metal engine comes ready-made: the `.dmg` has it
  inside, and the Terminal fetches it as an engine component. Nothing is built on your Mac and you need no Command Line
  Tools ([below](#the-desktop-app-and-strata-launch-on-a-mac)). macOS 15 or newer, as for the source build. If macOS says the
  app is "damaged", see [Troubleshooting](TROUBLESHOOTING.md#the-desktop-app-and-the-terminal); how the builds are signed:
  [packaging/mac/README.md](../packaging/mac/README.md).
- **From source: `./setup.sh`.** It sets things up the way `START-HERE.bat` does on Windows and builds the engine on your Mac
  (about 1-15 minutes).

**Pictures:** on by default in the app, the Terminal and the source build. The reader (`strata-vision`) comes in the engine package
and runs on the Mac's GPU through Metal ([Limits](#limits-this-version)). The NVIDIA, AMD and Intel engines are unchanged.

**Status:** new. It is measured on three Macs: an M5 Max with 128 GB, where the model stays in memory; and an M4 Mac mini
with 32 GB and an M1 Max with 34 GB, where the experts stream from the SSD (the M1 Max: 7.9 tok/s decode, 186 tok/s on a
9,940-token prompt, Q2_0, the expert cache at 64 slots, as reported with the kernel fix #2348). Other chips are untested, and reports help
([COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md](COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md)).

## What you need

- **An Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or newer).** Intel Macs cannot run it.
- **macOS 15 or newer.** The engine keeps its buffers resident through a residency set, which macOS 15 introduced.
- **The Command Line Tools:** `xcode-select --install`. That is the compiler. Xcode itself is not needed.
- **Enough unified memory for the pack.** The GPU maps the model's main file and keeps it in memory while the model runs. Metal lets one
  program keep about 3/4 of the memory resident (107.5 GB of 128 GB, measured on the M5 Max).

| Pack | The file the GPU maps | Needs about (with the prompt buffers, KV cache, draft layer) | Recommended from |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q2_0 | 37.6 GB | 46 GB | 64 GB |
| IQ3_XXS | 47.0 GB | 55 GB | 74 GB (where IQ3_S does not fit) |
| IQ3_S (recommended; the default from 96 GB) | 54.8 GB | 63 GB | 96 GB |
| UD-Q4_K_XL (Unsloth, recommended: higher quality) | 82.6 GB | 91 GB | 128 GB |
| UD-Q5_K_XL, UD-Q6_K_XL (Unsloth) | 103.9 / 114.8 GB | stream from the SSD on 128 GB | 128 GB, streamed |
| Gyro-S (agentionai, one 58.5 GB file) | 29.7 GB (the file's other 28.8 GB is the n-gram table) | 38 GB | 48 GB; streams below that (measured on 32 GB) |
| Gyro-M (agentionai, one 92.0 GB file) | 63.2 GB (+ the 28.8 GB table) | 71 GB | 96 GB; streams below that (not measured on a Mac) |

- **The n-gram table:** each pack also has a 28.8 GB n-gram table (the model's second file). It is read from the SSD a few rows at a time and does not count against the memory above.
- **Disk:** the download is 66-84 GB, plus about 7 GB for the pack and the draft layer. A Mac that streams also needs room for the experts' copy (below): 34-40 GB.
- **A Mac whose memory cannot hold the pack (32-48 GB):** the engine streams the experts from the SSD instead. It decides this by itself when the experts are more than 60% of Metal's share.
  - It keeps the most-used experts in an arena: Metal's share, or the memory macOS reports as available less what it keeps for macOS, whichever is smaller. It keeps 7 GB, or 15% of the RAM when that is more, and it also keeps the n-gram table's share. It counts as free only what macOS can give without swapping (free and purgeable memory and the clean file cache, not other programs' idle memory). It checks again just before it takes the arena, and fills the arena in 1.5 GB steps, checking again before each one; it stops early rather than push macOS below what it keeps. On a Mac with 64 GB or more the arena, the Metal buffers and the host memory together also stay under 60% of the RAM (see "The engine's whole anonymous footprint" below).
  - It reads the rest as each token needs them, and reads ahead the experts the next layer will probably use.
  - Setup writes a second copy of the experts for such a Mac (`<model>.experts`, 40 GB for IQ3_XXS). In it each expert's three matrices sit together, so the SSD reads an expert with one request instead of three. On the 32 GB M4 that is about 17% faster decoding and 30% faster prompts, with the same tokens. Setup writes it only when the disk has room for it plus 10 GB; otherwise it warns, and the engine reads the model file as before.
  - Setup configures such a Mac without the MTP draft layer: one token per step is faster there.
  - Measured at 32 GB (below). Smaller Macs are untested.
- **Setup recommends, and never forces.** It recommends the pack by memory; a bigger pack chosen with `--model` is kept, with a warning about what it risks.

## Install

```
git clone https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata && cd Strata
./setup.sh                 # asks the size; --yes takes the recommended answers
```

What the first run does (each step is skipped when it is already done):

1. **Python.** It needs Python 3.10 or newer, but macOS ships 3.9. If that is all your Mac has, `setup.sh` downloads a standalone Python 3.12 (25 MB, pinned by SHA-256) into `.python`. No sudo, no Homebrew.
2. **Checks your Mac:** the chip, the memory, the macOS version, the Command Line Tools and the free disk.
3. **Python packages** into `.venv`. CMake and Ninja come from pip too, installed just before the build in step 4.
4. **Builds the engine** (`build-metal/strata`). It uses Apple's metal-cpp headers (pinned by SHA-256) and llama.cpp's ggml at the commit the PC build pins.
5. **Downloads the model.** The download resumes if interrupted. `--gguf-dir` uses files you already have.
6. **Prepares the model:** the pack (seconds), and the MTP draft layer (about 5 GB of the original checkpoint). On a Mac that streams: the experts' copy instead of the draft layer (about 3 minutes on the M4, checked byte for byte against the model file).
7. **Writes `strata-<model>.json` and `run-<model>.sh`, then starts the server.**

The config uses the Mac defaults: `--spec 2` and the Q8_0 hyper-connection read (below). After that, `./setup.sh` or `./run-q2_0.sh` starts the model directly. The server is the same as on a PC:
- the OpenAI-compatible API on `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`;
- the Anthropic API on `/v1/messages`;
- the chat page on `http://127.0.0.1:8080/`.

Options: `--model Q2_0|IQ3_XXS|IQ3_S|UD-Q4_K_XL|UD-Q5_K_XL|UD-Q6_K_XL` (the UD files are Unsloth's), `--vision yes|no`, `--context N`, `--port`, `--host` / `--api-key`, `--draft-vocab`, `--no-browser`,
`--data-dir`, `--models-dir`, `--gguf-dir`, `--setup` (another model or new settings), `--no-start`, `--check` (only
check the Mac), `--build` (build the engine again).

### The desktop app and `strata launch` on a Mac

The Strata app (and the Terminal's `strata launch`) do not build anything on your Mac. The Metal engine comes ready-made, as an engine component: from the update feed, or inside the app's installer. The model install is `setup.py` in its Control mode (`STRATA_CONTROL_INSTALL=1`): it downloads (or uses with `--gguf-dir`) and prepares the model files and writes a run config whose engine is `component:strata-engine`. It does not run `metal/setup_mac.py`, needs no Command Line Tools, and writes the same Metal flags (`--mmap-experts`, `--spec 2`, no draft layer when the experts stream from the SSD).

The model list and the recommendation judge a Mac by its unified memory with the rules of `strata_control/mac_fit.py`, the module `setup_mac.py` uses too: Q2_0, IQ3_XXS and IQ3_S are offered (the Unsloth many-shard files need the repack of `./setup.sh` for now); a pack that does not stay in memory is listed as "read from the SSD", and a Mac under 16 GB of unified memory is told the model does not fit.

## Measured (M5 Max, 128 GB, macOS 27.2)

**Decode**, in tokens per second over 200 generated tokens, with greedy answers. The table gives two prompts: a short question
("prompt1") and a story.

| | Q2_0 | IQ3_XXS | IQ3_S |
|---|---|---|---|
| Setup's defaults (`--spec 2` with MTP, the suffix drafter on) | **119.5 / 108.2** | **108.9 / 97.0** | - |
| `--spec 2` with MTP, suffix drafter off | 114.0 / 107.9 | 103.5 / 96.9 | 98.2 / 94.1 |
| No MTP (one token per step) | 87.4 / 87.3 | 78.7 / 78.6 | 74.5 / 74.3 |

The output with MTP is the same as without it, token for token, in every run. MTP only proposes tokens, and the
full model checks every one of them.

**Prompt reading** (time to the first token), on the needle-test prompts below:

| | 4K tokens | 32K tokens |
|---|---|---|
| Q2_0 | ~1,430 tok/s | ~1,460 tok/s |
| IQ3_XXS | ~1,260 tok/s | ~1,240 tok/s |
| IQ3_S | ~1,320 tok/s | ~1,140-1,190 tok/s |

The first prompt after the Mac starts is slower, while macOS reads the model file (IQ3_S: 413 tok/s on the first 4K
prompt, cold).

**For comparison**, llama.cpp on the same Mac with Q2_0: 56.6 tok/s decode on the story, and 887 / 809 tok/s on 4K / 32K prompts.

### Unsloth's UD-Q4/Q5/Q6_K_XL on the M5 Max

IQ3_S and UD-Q4_K_XL are the recommended sizes. Setup offers IQ3_S as the default and names UD-Q4_K_XL as the
higher-quality choice where it fits. Decode is tokens per second over 200 tokens (greedy, MTP); prompts are the warm rate
of the second request on (the first request after the start pays a few seconds of first-use cost).

| | IQ3_S | UD-Q4_K_XL | UD-Q5_K_XL (streamed) | UD-Q6_K_XL (streamed) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quality against Q8_0 (top-1 / KL) | 87.9% / 0.142 | 92.8% / 0.055 | not measured | not measured |
| Decode, short question, no MTP / MTP | 75.4 / 101.9 | 60.7 / 94.0 | - | - |
| Decode, story, no MTP / MTP | 74.8 / 94.7 | 59.7 / 73.7 | 28 / 46-51 (`--spec 3`) | not measured / 47-51 (`--spec 3`) |
| Prompt 4K / 32K | ~1,180 / ~1,290 | ~1,150 / ~1,290 | ~1,070 / ~1,110 | ~1,020 / ~1,020 |
| llama.cpp Metal, decode (story / code) | 51.1 / 44.1 | 48.4 / 47.3 | 45.1 / 43.2 | does not run (Insufficient Memory) |
| llama.cpp Metal, prompt 4K / 32K | 791 / 730 | 821 / 739 | 729 / 693 | - |

- **UD-Q5 and UD-Q6 cannot stay resident:** their repacked file (103.9 and 114.8 GB) is bigger than the largest buffer Metal gives (86.6 GB), so the experts stream from the SSD into an arena of about 65-67 GB on the 128 GB M5 Max (about 68% of Q5's experts, 62% of Q6's; it was 80-86 GB before the footprint cap below, and the decode and prompt speeds did not change: Q6 story 51 tok/s, 15K prompt 1,020 tok/s at both sizes).
- **The cost is a fixed hand-shake per layer** (the engine reads the router's choice and makes sure the experts are in the arena), not the SSD. A window of 2 tokens costs 38 ms against ~17 resident, so a longer window pays: Q5 story 28 tok/s without MTP, 41.8 with `--spec 2`, 50.6 with `--spec 3`, 46 with `--spec 4`. Setup writes `--spec 3` and keeps the MTP draft layer for a streaming Mac with 96 GB or more.
- **The engine's whole anonymous footprint is limited to 60% of the RAM on a Mac with 64 GB or more (82.4 GB of the M5 Max's 137.4 GB): the arena, every Metal buffer and the host memory the process holds, not only the Metal buffers.** macOS keeps a floor of file cache (`vm.vm_page_filecache_min`: 37.2 GB here) and compresses anonymous memory instead of dropping cache below it. The arena is anonymous, and the GPU wires it only while a command buffer runs, so while it is filled it is ordinary pageable memory. Two kernel panics on the M5 Max (the watchdog daemon starved for 92 s) had the engine at 95 and 90 GiB resident and the compressor at 2-4 million pages. Measured again with a memory watchdog every second: an old-build arena of 100 GB compressed 19 GB of itself in 7 seconds and swapped 24,000 pages; the old automatic arena (69 GB) with a 40 GB file write and a 16 GB program beside it took the compressor from 21,000 to 4.07 million pages in 10 seconds (pressure "warn"). With 30% left (footprint 94.5 GB) and the file write alone, 12,000 pages were swapped out; with 35% left, 316; with 40% left and the write and the 16 GB program, none and the compressor at 0.3 million pages. The old rule (arena + Metal buffers under 67%) counted 7.5 GB of buffers where the process held 11-15 GB, so its real total was about 100 GB. A resident pack is different (clean file pages that macOS drops, never compresses): UD-Q4_K_XL resident (wired 91.7 GB) took the same 40 GB write and 16 GB program with no swap-out and nothing compressed, so resident packs are limited to 70% of the RAM as before. The arena is also wired (`mlock`) once it is filled: unwired it is ordinary pageable memory whenever the GPU is idle (the GPU's own wiring ends a few seconds after its last command buffer; a Metal residency set did not hold it), and a 20 GB file written beside the idle engine took the arena into the compressor and froze the Mac (a third watchdog panic, in a control run of this work). Wired, the same write at full speed raised the compressor by 0.7 million pages (the engine's non-arena memory), swapped out 408 pages and changed nothing else. `STRATA_METAL_WIRE_ARENA=0` turns it off; it is on for Macs with 64 GB or more. The engine prints the planned total (`planned resident footprint ... cap ...`) and the footprint after the fill. `STRATA_METAL_ARENA_GB` still sets the arena as you say, with a warning when it is over the cap.
- **The experts' copy** (`<model>.experts`, 98 GB for Q5) did not pay on the M5 Max: decode 50.3 against 50.2 tok/s without it, 4K prompt 741 against 685 (noisy). Setup does not write it on a Mac with 96 GB or more.
- **Prompts stream in chunks of 4096** on a streaming Mac with 96 GB or more (the engine's own default there; 1024 on a smaller one): every chunk makes one pass over the experts that are not in the arena, so a longer chunk reads them fewer times. UD-Q5, warm, 2 interleaved rounds: chunks of 1024 gave 700 tok/s on the 4K prompt, 2048 gave 920 and 4096 gave 1,100 (32K: 710, 970, 1,100); the decode did not change. `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT_CHUNK=N` sets it. On a resident model 4096 instead of 2048 gained only 2-4% (Q2_0), so that default stays.

### M4 Mac mini, 32 GB, experts streamed from the SSD

The arena was 11.5-14.7 GB. Tokens per second, one token per step (no MTP), medians of 5 interleaved runs:

| | Q2_0 | IQ3_XXS | llama.cpp, CPU only (Q2_0 / IQ3_XXS) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Decode, short question (200 tokens) | **14.1** | **10.0** | 6.3 / 4.1 |
| Decode, story (200 tokens) | **13.5** | **9.2** | 6.3 / 4.1 |
| Decode after a 6K-token document | **13.1** | **7.7** | 5.1 / 2.8 |
| Prompt, 4K tokens | **93.6** | **65.8** | 21.2 / 8.7 |

- The greedy answers equal the M5 Max's (model in memory) on 10 of 10 test prompts, for both packs.
- No memory was swapped out during the runs; the least memory left to macOS was 7.1 GB.
- MTP was slower here (Q2_0 story 12.1-12.3 with it against 12.3-12.8 without). The draft layer's 1.2 GB do more as expert cache.

**The experts' copy** (`<model>.experts`, one SSD request per expert): IQ3_XXS after the 6K-token document, the arena held at 12 GB, medians of 5 interleaved runs each:

| | Decode | The 6K prompt | SSD wait per token |
|---|---|---|---|
| The model file (three reads per expert) | 7.37 tok/s | 64.7 tok/s | 46.6 ms |
| The experts' copy (one read per expert) | **8.62 tok/s** | **84.1 tok/s** | 31.5 ms |

- The tokens are identical in all 10 runs.
- The 4K-token prompt (3 interleaved runs each, default arena): 72.9 tok/s with the copy against 62.5 with the model file (+17%), the same tokens.
- 32K-token prompts through the server, with the copy: 29,768 tokens at 89.2 tok/s (5.6 minutes to the first token), 33,803 tokens at 84.4 tok/s. The code word was found both times.
- A 34-minute server run with the copy (47 requests: 32K and 6K needles, short questions, a story, code; context 34,816) got every answer right and did not slow down over time. Decode was 7.2-7.7 tok/s on short answers and 9.9-10.4 on the story; the 6K prompts ran at 80-90 tok/s. macOS's memory pressure was never critical: one 2-second "warn" sample while the arena filled at the start. About 90 MB were swapped out in those same 2 seconds and nothing after; three restarts afterwards (smaller arenas, less memory free) swapped nothing.
- The SSD alone measures the same: 2.97 GB/s for one 1.75 MB read per expert against 2.30 GB/s for three 0.58 MB reads (6 threads, uncached).
- The arena's size matters most. With the model file, a 7.5 GB arena gave 5.5 tok/s, 10.5 GB gave 6.7 and 12 GB gave 7.5. The read-ahead depth, the I/O threads and the eviction order each moved decode by less than 3%.
- The Q2_0 copy is not measured yet. The numbers in the table above are with the model file.
- **Measured again on the release build, with less memory free:** the M4 had 13-17 GB available when the engine started (another user's programs held the rest), so the arena was 5.7 GB (Q2_0) and 9.3 GB (IQ3_XXS, with the experts' copy). One token per step, medians of 3: Q2_0 story 8.3 tok/s, 4K prompt 80; IQ3_XXS story 8.3, 4K prompt 89. That is the arena's size effect above, not a regression: with a 6.6 GB arena the engine used to stop at the first prompt ("no free slot"); a small arena now gives the prompt's 1.6 GB of buffers their own allocation, also when no chunk of the arena is big enough for them (on a 24 GB M2 whose arena shrank below the prompt's needs, every prompt stopped with "no arena region for the prompt buffers"), and a 26-minute server run with a 5.4 GB arena (29 requests, 6K and 31K needles found) was clean.
- With the default arena (12.1-12.2 GB here), the experts' copy gives 8.35-8.48 tok/s decode and 82.5-82.8 tok/s on the prompt. Nothing was swapped out. macOS's memory pressure stayed "normal", except for one 2-second "warn" sample while the arena fills; keeping 7 GB for macOS shows the same sample.
- Those runs and the server run below kept 5 GB for macOS. The default is now 7 GB with the stepped fill: after the 6K document, 7.3 and 6.7 tok/s decode (arenas 9.3 and 7.6 GB, as much as was free), the same tokens, the memory pressure "normal" throughout and nothing swapped out.

**Why `--spec 2`:** measured with MTP on the same two prompts.

| Window | Q2_0 (prompt1 / story) | IQ3_XXS (prompt1 / story) |
|---|---|---|
| `--spec 2` | 111 / 106 | 102 / 95 |
| `--spec 3` | 116 / 92 | 108 / 95 |
| `--spec 4` | 111 / 81 | 108 / 83 |
| `--spec 5-6` | slower | slower |

`--spec 2` is the best default on mixed text. An explicit `--spec N` in the config's `args` is kept.

### Gyro-S and Gyro-M (agentionai's trellis experts)

From 0.2.2 the Mac engine runs [Gyro](GYRO.md): the routed experts are trellis-coded blocks (ggml types TQ2_T, TQK6, TQK7) in a
Hadamard-rotated basis, read from the published file unchanged. The kernels are ours (`metal/kernels/quant.metal`, `moe.metal`,
`moe_mm.metal`); the codebook and the decoder are the CPU engine's, the rotation is applied to the gate/up and down inputs as on CUDA.
Setup offers Gyro-S and Gyro-M next to the other sizes (`./setup.sh --family gyro --model Gyro-S`), never as the default, and says
what the choice risks on your Mac's memory. The 28.8 GB n-gram table is inside the file and is read from the SSD like every other
pack's, so Gyro-S needs 58.5 GB of disk and about 38 GB of memory to stay resident (29.7 GB of weights).

**Measured on the M4 Mac mini, 32 GB** (the experts stream from the SSD; no experts' copy, because the copy would need 26 GB more
disk than this Mac had; one token per step, no draft layer; the arena was 11-12 GB of the 25.8 GB of experts):

| | Gyro-S |
|---|---|
| Decode, story, 120 tokens (5 interleaved pairs, medians) | **9.14 tok/s** (9.07-9.15) |
| Decode, with the dense-weight tiles turned off (`STRATA_METAL_GYRO_TILES=0`) | 8.70 tok/s (8.69-8.73); same tokens in all 10 runs |
| Prompt, 4,065 tokens (3 runs) | **109 tok/s** (108-110) |
| Memory the engine held | 18.6 GB of the 32 GB |

Where the time goes: a decode window of two tokens takes 111 ms. The routed experts are about 40 ms of it, the dense weights
(Gyro keeps its attention, state-space and shared-expert matrices in Q5_K and Q6_K: 3.6 GB read a token)
about 66 ms before the tile change (a run with those kernels skipped). The kernel for one expert layer (ten experts, one token) takes
278 us on the M4, 37.5 GB/s; IQ3_XXS takes 333 us and Q2_0 166 us. The trellis decode is limited by latency and ALU, not by memory:
32-bit funnel shifts for the stream bits, fetching the next unit while decoding the current one, one lane a row with the unit index
folded away and the codebook in constant memory were all tried and none beat the plain kernel, so it is the plain kernel with the
tile that measured fastest. The prompt kernels (fp16 matrix units) are on par with IQ3_XXS: 68 ms against 62 ms a layer for
1,024 tokens.

**Checked against the CPU engine's decoder, on the real file:** the decoder equals the format's definition written out bit by bit
(614,400 sampled blocks a layer, none differ); the Hadamard rotation equals the CPU's bit for bit (f32 and f16); the expert
kernels reproduce a double-precision reference to 1e-7 relative on real experts of layers 0 and 47 of Gyro-S and of layers 0, 23
and 47 of Gyro-M (the 92 GB file was read by range requests, 16 experts a layer: it does not fit this Mac's disk). Run it with
`metal/tests/gyro_parity.sh`.

**Against the CUDA engine, same file** (the pinned Gyro-S; `tools/quant_quality.py`, teacher-forced over the 5 text segments of
`data/quant_quality/v1`, 4,995 positions; CUDA = an RTX 3060 with the engine of this release, run twice: experts on the GPU, experts on the CPU):

| Reference -> run | top-1 agreement | mean KL | KL p99 | perplexity of the text |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CUDA GPU experts -> CUDA CPU experts (the noise floor: two numerics of one engine) | 95.80 % | 0.0186 | 0.195 | 4.462 / 4.477 |
| CUDA GPU experts -> Mac | 95.46 % | 0.0207 | 0.241 | 4.486 / 4.477 |
| CUDA CPU experts -> Mac | 95.38 % | 0.0187 | 0.272 | 4.486 / 4.462 |

The Mac is as far from either CUDA run as the two CUDA runs are from each other (the CUDA GPU path quantizes the activations to q8_1 and
reads an int8 copy of the codebook, the CPU path an int16 one; the Mac multiplies fp16 codebook values with the float activations).

### Quality

- **The Q8_0 hyper-connection read is the default on Mac.** It keeps a Q8_0 copy of the hyper-connection matrices instead of BF16. `STRATA_HC_Q8=0` in the config's `env` gives the exact BF16 read.
- **How the KL was measured:** teacher-forced over 28 prompts (code, reasoning, chat, six languages, documents), about 6,000 positions per set. The reference is BF16.
  - On the model's own text: mean KL 0.0007, top-1 agreement 98.9%.
  - On another model's text: mean KL 0.0007, top-1 agreement 99.1%.
  - Perplexity of the text is unchanged (×0.9995 and ×1.0006).
  - For scale, IQ3_XXS against Q2_0 is a KL of 0.094.
  - The Mac engine is deterministic: two runs give identical numbers.
- **The fast prompt path** (the prompt kernels) against reading the prompt through decode windows: mean KL 0.0004, top-1 99.4-99.6%.
- **Needles:** a code word hidden in 8K, 16K and 32K tokens of text, at 10/50/90% depth. Found 9 of 9 with Q2_0 and with IQ3_XXS, both with Q8_0 and with BF16. With the fast prompt path (4K-32K) the answers are the same.
- **Same answers as on a PC:**
  - against the CUDA engine on a Tesla P100 (IQ3_XXS and IQ3_S), the first 200 tokens of a reply are identical on the short question;
  - on the story, the first IQ3_S tokens differ at token 1, a near-tie (margin 0.12). Following the CUDA engine's tokens, 4 of 200 picks differ, all at margins 0.06-0.21;
  - against the HIP engine on a Radeon AI PRO R9700 (Q2_0), 36 of 39 first tokens are identical.
  - The differences are near-ties between the two best tokens, from a different floating-point order.

## Limits (this version)

- **Images (vision):** on by default. The app and the Terminal use the `strata-vision` that sits beside `strata` in the engine package;
  `./setup.sh` builds it itself and asks "Should the model also read images?" (default yes). One program does both jobs: with `--gpu` it
  reads on the Mac's GPU (ggml's Metal backend, the shaders are built into the program), without it on the CPU. A Mac always gets the GPU
  reader, whatever its memory. The 24 GB rule of the PC cards does not apply: the Mac has no separate card memory to keep free, and the
  reader's footprint is about the same on either side (1.18 GB on the GPU, 1.05 GB on the CPU, mostly the 0.9 GB projector file).
  Measured on a Mac mini M4 (32 GB), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's BF16 projector:

  | Picture | GPU reader | CPU reader |
  |---|---|---|
  | 260 tokens (640x400) | 0.45 s | 50.7 s |
  | 972 tokens (1600x1200) | 2.4 s | 194 s |

  `--vision cpu` is still allowed and prints that note. The CPU reader is slow because ggml has no vector kernel for BF16 on ARM (a build
  for newer chips, with the BF16 and int8 instructions, took the same 50.7 s). If the GPU reader cannot start, the server prints one line
  and starts the same program on the CPU. With Q2_0 streaming from the SSD on that M4, the STRATA 42 test picture (red circle, blue square,
  green triangle, the text "STRATA 42") was described correctly with both readers. Checked on one Mac only; the M5 Max is untested for pictures.
- **Context:** measured up to 32K (needles, KL). Setup recommends 32K below 96 GB and 64K from 96 GB. Up to the model's 262K can be set, but it is not measured.
- **One request at a time.** `--parallel` (batch slots) is not ported. Several clients queue.
- **Not ported:** the control vector (`--control-vector-scaled`) and the PC tuning (`--calibrate`).
- **Streaming:** measured at 32 GB only. The model's file must be on the internal SSD; an external disk is untested and likely much slower.
- **Families:** the original Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Unsloth's UD-Q4/Q5/Q6_K_XL and agentionai's Gyro-S are measured (above). Setup repacks Unsloth's shards into one file for the GPU; a Gyro file is used as it is. Gyro-M runs on the same kernels (checked tensor by tensor) but no Mac here could hold it. The Swift and Coder releases are not set up on Mac yet, and Qwen3.6 does not run on the Mac engine.
- **The ready-made Mac engine is in the app and in the Terminal's engine component, not in the release zips.** The zips
  (for `START-HERE.bat` and `setup.sh`) have no Mac engine: `./setup.sh` builds it.

## Switches (for testing; all off unless set, the defaults are above)

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `STRATA_HC_Q8=0` | The BF16 hyper-connection read (exact) instead of Q8_0 |
| `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT=window` | Read the prompt through decode windows (the slow, exact fallback; ~190 tok/s) |
| `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT_CHUNK=N` | Prompt chunk size (default 2048) |
| `STRATA_METAL_MTP_Q8=0` | The draft layer's matrices in BF16 instead of Q8_0 |
| `STRATA_METAL_MTP_CHAIN=0` | One GPU submission per draft step instead of one per round |
| `STRATA_METAL_FUSE=0`, `STRATA_METAL_LAZY_FOLD=0` | Turn off two decode fusions (same tokens, slower) |
| `STRATA_METAL_PARTIAL=1`, `STRATA_METAL_ROUTE=1` | Two decode variants that measured no faster here (same tokens) |
| `STRATA_METAL_STREAM=1` / `=0` | Stream the experts from the SSD even when the pack fits / never (the default decides by size) |
| `STRATA_METAL_CONTIG=0` | Streaming: read the model file even when the experts' copy is there |
| `STRATA_METAL_ARENA_GB=N`, `STRATA_METAL_KEEP_FREE_GB=N` | Streaming: the arena's size, or the memory left to macOS when the arena is sized |
| `STRATA_METAL_LEAVE_SHARE=0.4` | Streaming, Macs with 64 GB or more: the share of the RAM left to macOS and its file cache when the footprint cap is set (for measuring) |
| `STRATA_METAL_WIRE_ARENA=0` | Streaming, Macs with 64 GB or more: leave the filled arena pageable (default: wired with mlock) |
| `STRATA_METAL_IGNORE_REPACK=1` | Start the engine although a model repack or setup's preparation is running beside it (the engine refuses by default: it froze this Mac) |
| `STRATA_METAL_KEEP_HOST_WEIGHTS=1` | Streaming: keep the host code's own copies of the weights (2-3 GB) instead of giving them back to macOS |
| `STRATA_METAL_TRACE=1`, `STRATA_METAL_PROFILE=1`, `STRATA_METAL_KPROF=T` | Per-window traces, a time breakdown, per-kernel GPU times |

**Two opt-ins an M1 Max cannot run (measured on an M1 Max, macOS 26.6.2, Q2_0):** `STRATA_METAL_PROMPT_EXPERTS=v3` - the
prompt's expert GEMMs with the M5's layout, `mm_gu3` - loses the threadgroup once a prompt spreads over more than 40
threadgroups of it (35 pass, 40 fail; 190 tiles and the engine's tile both fail, one tile passes), so it is off there (the
default is v2). `STRATA_METAL_ROUTE=1` - the router GEMV and `moe_route` fused into one dispatch - routes with stale
logits and gives a different top-10 per run (two identical runs differ in ids, weights and plan; the logits themselves
stay bitwise): the fusion hands the routing to the last threadgroup of the GEMV through a device counter, and this
Metal's device atomics are relaxed-only, with no acquire to pair with the writers' fence. Both are off by default. The
`no faster` measurement in the table is from the Macs above; on an M1 Max `ROUTE` is also wrong.

## How it works

The code is in `metal/` (the engine's side in `metal/src/engine`, the kernels in `metal/kernels`). In short:
- **Host code:** the PC host code compiles unchanged for macOS. `metal/include/metal_compat` maps the CUDA runtime calls it makes onto a small Metal runtime (`metal/src/gpu`).
- **The decode and prompt work** run in Metal kernels (`metal/kernels`, `metal/src/engine`):
  - one command buffer per verify window;
  - the experts are read in place from the mapped model file;
  - the hyper-connections, the GDN state and the QSA attention stay on the GPU;
  - a whole MTP draft round runs in one command buffer.
- **The PC builds are byte-identical** with this code present. Every shared file's change is behind `STRATA_GPU_METAL` or `__APPLE__`, and the CUDA and HIP objects are compared after each change.


## docs/MANAGEMENT_PROTOCOL.md

# Owner-local management bridge, version 1

The Strata CLI and a local Desktop host use the same saved-profile store and `strata_control.management.runtime_action()` for runtime operations. A trusted Desktop host can invoke the one-shot `python -m strata_control.management` process for runtime actions, component/model inspection, reviewed benchmark runs and saved evidence, reviewed calibration and profile edits. Send one UTF-8 JSON object on stdin, close stdin, and read one JSON object on stdout. The command exits with the response's `exit_code` on failure; ordinary success exits 0. Diagnostics go to stderr. The input limit is 64 KiB.

This is **owner-local process IPC**. It has no HTTP listener and does not accept an inference or monitor API key. The imported Node host has limited, opt-in loopback HTTP seams for one host-configured saved profile: `/api/native/runtime` for Serving, `/api/native/telemetry` for Monitor, `/api/native/components` for component inspection, `/api/native/models` for installed run configs, `/api/native/models/inspect?id=MODEL_ID` for details, `/api/native/models/import-plan` for an explicit read-only GGUF preflight, `/api/native/profile` for saved settings, `/api/native/bench/review`, `/execute` and `/job?id=JOB_ID` for reviewed benchmark launch, `/api/native/bench/report` and `/compare` for saved evidence, plus `/api/native/calibration/review`, `/execute`, `/job?id=JOB_ID` and `/cancel` for reviewed calibration, bounded progress and exact active-measurement stop requests. Serving, Profile, Benchmarks and Calibration use short-lived, single-use server-side reviews before mutations. The Node routes check local Host/Origin and a custom JSON action header for action POSTs; Python rechecks reviewed preconditions. This local preview is not audited Desktop authentication or a general browser management API. The other UI screens still use prototype data; native mode refuses prototype mutations and `/v1` inference. The shared Desktop journal and full operation API remain integration work.

## Request and response

```json
{"schema_version":1,"action":"runtime.start.plan","profile":"four-gpu","params":{"shutdown_timeout_s":30}}
```

`schema_version` must be the integer `1`. `action` and `params` must match one row below exactly. `profile` is a saved lowercase profile ID. Unknown fields, duplicate JSON keys, nonfinite numbers, booleans in numeric fields and unexpected actions are rejected before an operation starts. Runtime errors return `{"schema_version":1,"ok":false,"error":"...","exit_code":N}`. Successful results include `schema_version:1` and the owner runtime's result. Journaled actions also return an `operation_id` that both UI and CLI can inspect with `strata ops result`.

| Action | Exact `params` keys | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bench.run.plan` | `path`, `suite`, `concurrency`, `repeat`, `request_timeout`, `condition` | Check a new absolute output directory, bounded workload, loaded model and matching managed profile/owner/telemetry instance. Return the planned request count, phase list and pinned identities. No inference request or output directory is created. |
| `bench.job.create` | `job_id` plus all `bench.run` review and identity keys | Create an owner-only journal receipt for a reviewed Desktop job before launching its worker. The 32-character job ID is generated by the host. A receipt without an active lease or final report does not prove that the worker started. |
| `bench.job` | `job_id` | Read the durable receipt, exact-run lease, private progress and matching report. A saved final report can finish a receipt left running by a crash after report write. An unfinished receipt without an active lease becomes `completion_unknown` after a short launch window. |
| `bench.run` | all `bench.run.plan` keys plus `if_profile_revision`, `if_source_sha256`, `if_owner_id`, `if_instance_id`; Desktop also sends `job_id` | Recheck the reviewed source, owner and instance, then use the CLI benchmark runner with managed matching before and after. Create a private `results.json` when measured phases fail. With a job ID, the worker verifies the receipt matches the reviewed request and finishes it with a bounded outcome. |
| `bench.progress` | `path` | Read the owner-only `progress.json` in an absolute output directory (or next to its `results.json`). It reports completed phases and the current phase without prompts, answers or credentials. For saved-profile runs, the response also checks the exact output path against the owner-local lease: `active`, `ended`, `other_active` or `untracked`. A `running` record alone does not prove process liveness. |
| `bench.cancel` | `path` | Request a stop for the exact active saved-profile run. The owner-local lease and private output directory are checked before writing an owner-only `cancel.request` marker. Returns `cancel_requested` until the runner writes final evidence; it does not claim that the engine has already stopped. CLI: `strata bench cancel --profile NAME --path /absolute/run/results.json`. |
| `bench.report` | `path` | Read an absolute local `bench run` output directory or `results.json`, summarize its phases and produce a privacy-safe Markdown export. No workload, mutation or journal entry. |
| `bench.compare` | `baseline`, `candidate` | Read two absolute local saved reports, apply the CLI's workload and available-environment match checks, and produce a provisional comparison and privacy-safe Markdown export. No workload, mutation or journal entry. |
| `calibration.plan` | none | Read-only decode-sweep preflight, including saved-profile revision, source digest, selected devices and component status. No engine launch or journal entry. |
| `calibration.job.create` | `job_id`, `action`, `path`, `exclusive_ack`, `if_profile_revision`, `if_source_sha256`, `if_report_sha256` | Create an owner-only receipt for a reviewed Desktop measure/apply/rollback action before launching its worker. `if_report_sha256` is `null` for measure. The receipt alone does not prove the worker started. |
| `calibration.job` | `job_id` | Read a bounded receipt after a Desktop host restart. A measurement report bearing the exact job ID and reviewed profile/source identity can finish a receipt left running after report write. An exact worker lease proves active work; without it or a final journal result or matching report, the receipt becomes `completion_unknown` after a short launch window. The response also carries bounded stage progress and stop-request state. |
| `calibration.cancel` | `job_id` | Request a stop only for the exact active measurement worker. The owner-only marker is polled by that worker and passed into engine generation; the request acknowledges intent, while the final receipt says whether cancellation occurred. Apply and rollback cannot be cancelled in flight. |
| `calibration.measure` | `path`, `exclusive_ack`, `if_profile_revision`, `if_source_sha256`; Desktop also sends `job_id` | Require explicit exclusive-access acknowledgement, reject a stale saved profile or source, then measure into a new absolute local report path and journal the result. Recheck source under the calibration lock. With a job ID, every preflight and execution failure finishes the matching receipt. |
| `calibration.apply.plan` | `path` | Review one saved report for freshness and applicability, pin report body digest, profile revision and source digest. No write or journal entry. |
| `calibration.apply` | `path`, `exclusive_ack`, `if_profile_revision`, `if_source_sha256`, `if_report_sha256`; Desktop also sends `job_id` | Recheck reviewed profile, source and report, then smoke-test and apply the candidate with private rollback evidence; journal the outcome. |
| `calibration.rollback.plan` | `path` | Review the exact applied state and saved backups for rollback; pin report, profile and current source. No write or journal entry. |
| `calibration.rollback` | `path`, `exclusive_ack`, `if_profile_revision`, `if_source_sha256`, `if_report_sha256`; Desktop also sends `job_id` | Recheck the reviewed state, smoke-test the previous config and restore config/settings; journal the outcome. |
| `components.inspect` | `live` | Read the saved profile's installed component report. `live: true` also runs the bounded host GPU probe. An inspection can succeed (`ok: true`) while `report.ok` is false because required files or selected cards are missing. No operation journal entry is created. |
| `models.installed` | none | List at most 128 setup-written local run configs for model selection; presence and execution compatibility remain separate. Requires the configured saved profile to exist. |
| `models.inspect` | `model_id` | Inspect one installed run config and its component report. Model-file integrity and engine compatibility remain unverified. No journal entry. |
| `models.import.plan` | `path` | Check an absolute local GGUF file or shard folder using the CLI's bounded preflight. It never copies, adopts or loads a model. No journal entry. |
| `profile.inspect` | none | Read the saved profile, revision, source digest and effective serving values. No mutation or journal entry. |
| `profile.change.plan` | `overrides`, `source_config`, `if_revision` | Validate typed overrides and an absolute run config against the revision loaded in the editor; show before/after, effective values, current profile revision and proposed source digest. No file write or restart. |
| `profile.change` | `overrides`, `source_config`, `if_revision`, `if_source_sha256` | Save the reviewed candidate through the same versioned profile store as CLI. Reject changed profile revision or source digest. The running instance is unchanged; the operator reviews Restart separately. Profile history records the old revision, but this save is not a runtime journal operation. |
| `runtime.status` | none | Read the owner's current instance state. |
| `runtime.start.plan` | `shutdown_timeout_s` | Validate the saved profile and show effective launch arguments, `launch.profile_revision` and `source_sha256`; no launch or journal entry. |
| `runtime.start` | `wait_s`, `shutdown_timeout_s`, `if_profile_revision`, `if_source_sha256` | Start through the owner host with both reviewed preconditions and journal the outcome. Both preconditions are required by the Desktop bridge. |
| `runtime.restart.plan` | `allow_source_switch`, `allow_source_migration` | Compare the current owned launch with the saved profile and report source, owner and instance preconditions. |
| `runtime.restart` | `wait_s`, `startup_wait_s`, `if_profile_revision`, `if_owner_id`, `if_instance_id`, `allow_source_switch`, `allow_source_migration`, `if_source_sha256` | Drain and restart through the owner host, with reviewed profile, source, owner and instance preconditions and a journal record. All four preconditions are required by the Desktop bridge. |
| `runtime.verify.plan` | `load` | Read the ready owner and instance IDs, model load state and whether this check would load the model. It performs no probe and creates no journal entry. |
| `runtime.verify` | `wait_s`, `load`, `if_owner_id`, `if_instance_id` | Recheck the reviewed owner and instance inside the owner host before checking API identity, launch attestation and generation when loaded. It may explicitly load a model and is journaled. Both IDs are required by the Desktop bridge; direct CLI verification may omit them. |
| `runtime.stop.plan` | none | Read the current owner ID and, when available, engine instance ID; no drain or journal entry. |
| `runtime.stop` | `wait_s`, `if_owner_id`, `if_instance_id` | Drain and stop only the reviewed owner and instance; journal the outcome. `if_owner_id` is required by the Desktop bridge. |

Desktop benchmark review bounds the total phase count and per-request timeout against its 1,900-second bridge deadline; longer workloads remain available through `strata bench run`. Saved-profile CLI runs and Desktop runs share a local per-profile benchmark lease that refuses overlapping launches; a raw `--url` run has no saved-profile lease. `STRATA_API_KEY` and optional `STRATA_TELEMETRY_KEY` are read only by the host process. Desktop now creates a private journal receipt before launch and recovers a job by ID after a host restart. The phase progress file and final report persist in the private output directory. Reports retain the planned and completed phase counts; success requires every planned phase to pass. A caught phase exception saves partial evidence and is labelled incomplete in the Desktop and Markdown export; an abrupt process kill can leave only the last progress record. Operator cancellation closes active benchmark-owned response streams and saves `cancelled: true`, `successful: false`, and a `cancelled` final progress state. It can take up to the configured request timeout if a connection has not received response headers yet. The request marker is an acknowledgement, not the final outcome. A malformed postflight telemetry response is saved as failed evidence with unavailable after-state. The exact-run lease check distinguishes a process still holding that path from one that released it. `other_active` and `untracked` do not prove that the saved run is alive. A held lease does not prove that inference is making progress. A crash before the benchmark creates an output directory can leave only the receipt; after the launch window it is labelled `completion_unknown`. Windows lease and receipt recovery still need target qualification.

Times are seconds. `if_profile_revision` is a 16-character lowercase profile revision; `if_source_sha256` is a 64-character lowercase digest. For start, take them from `runtime.start.plan` as `plan.launch.profile_revision` and `plan.source_sha256`. For restart, take `candidate_profile_revision`, `candidate_source_sha256`, `current_owner_id` and `current_instance_id` from `runtime.restart.plan`. For stop, take `plan.owner_id` and `plan.instance_id` from `runtime.stop.plan`; the instance ID may be `null` while the engine is starting or has failed. Owner and instance IDs are 32-character lowercase values when present. Restart plans require a ready instance, so both identities are present. The bridge rejects stale restart and stop reviews before journaling; the owner host checks again before draining. A stale start plan is rejected before the journal begins when possible; the owner host checks the same preconditions again immediately before launching the engine. A plan does not reserve the profile, source file or instance. An interrupted or timed-out mutating call may have an uncertain outcome. Inspect the operation journal and runtime status before retrying; never assume the process exit reversed a side effect.

## Desktop adapter requirements

The Desktop host now maps one configured profile's Start, Stop, Restart and Verify controls to these typed actions and displays the returned operation ID and owner state. A changed source config causes the first Restart review to refuse the action and show an explicit source-change review; the second plan sets only the operator-selected source-switch/migration allowances and displays the candidate path, digest and rollback requirement before drain. Its Components screen reads the same `doctor.inspect` report as the CLI; the optional live card probe runs only after the operator requests it. Profile presents typed override fields and installed model config choices, stores a reviewed candidate server-side for 90 seconds and saves through the shared profile store. Models lists the same setup-written run configs as CLI, inspects one config and its component report on request, and offers an explicit read-only GGUF file or folder preflight. Benchmarks reads saved local results through the shared CLI parser, shows selected bounded phase fields and compares only workload-compatible runs; its Markdown download omits addresses, credentials, prompts and answers. It launches reviewed managed workloads and can request cancellation for the exact active run. Calibration reviews a decode sweep and saved apply/rollback candidates through the same Python calibration module as CLI. The browser receives only bounded selected settings and findings; argv and raw measurement reports stay on the host. One host job can run at a time. The browser polls an owner-journal job ID for launching, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled or uncertain status, while the Python action writes bounded progress and the final shared operation record. Benchmark jobs are queryable by the same ID after a Desktop host restart through the owner journal and saved evidence. Calibration jobs have owner-only journal receipts recoverable by ID after a Desktop host restart. An exact saved measurement report can reconcile a receipt left running after report write. Measurement writes bounded stage/sample progress; a live exact worker lease distinguishes active work from an orphaned receipt. An operator can request cancellation for an active measurement, and its engine generation receives the stop event. The final receipt records `cancelled` only after the worker exits; inspect `strata ops runs` and the report path before retrying an uncertain operation. The browser receives only selected, bounded inspection fields; a plausible model file set still needs engine, model-pack, integrity and hardware checks. The host filters and bounds every report before sending it to the browser. Verify uses a single-use 90-second review and pins owner and instance IDs; an explicit Load + Verify choice is shown when the model is unloaded. A successful one-token probe does not establish answer quality or sustained throughput. It must preserve the plan/execute review step, keep only one lifecycle authority for a profile, and never build shell command strings from browser content. The harness screen still needs its shared typed mapping. Calibration progress, exact-worker liveness and measurement cancellation are implemented locally; long-run GPU behavior, cleanup after abrupt worker death, and unmanaged/Windows engine exclusion need target qualification. The current one-shot bridge does not provide a general write lease, streaming progress or recovery for an ambiguous start/stop/restart result.

Before production use, qualify this bridge and its owner transport on Windows/Linux, test an actual engine launch, and run UI/CLI parity scenarios against the same profile and journal. The source-run macOS fake-engine test checks that a bridge-started instance is visible and stoppable from CLI, that stale start, stop and restart reviews do not affect a different launch, and that malformed requests create no journal entry.


## docs/MCP_SERVER.md

# Strata's MCP server: let your AI assistant install and run Strata

`tools/strata_mcp.py` is an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server for the AI assistant you already use
(Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Codex ...). Add it once, then ask in plain words:

- "Install Strata for this PC."
- "Start Strata." / "Stop Strata."
- "Is Strata running? How much VRAM does it use?"
- "Which Strata model fits my PC?"
- "Strata didn't start - what does the log say?"
- "How fast is Strata on this PC?" (a short speed test)
- "How do I connect Open WebUI / the OpenAI SDK / Claude Code to Strata?"

The assistant calls the server's tools. The tools run Strata's own setup and start the model the way the start
scripts do. It is one Python file that uses only the standard library, so it works before setup has created
`.venv`. It needs Python 3.10 or newer, 64-bit on Windows.

It is not the same thing as [Tools from MCP servers](DETAILS.md#tools-from-mcp-servers). That feature
(`serve/mcp.py`) lets the *Strata model* call tools from your MCP servers in its chat page. This page is the other
direction: *your assistant* manages Strata.

## Add it

You need a copy of Strata: the zip from GitHub, or `git clone https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata`. Below,
`C:\Users\you\Strata` (Windows) and `/home/you/Strata` (Linux) stand for that folder. Use `python3` on Linux. On
Windows, use `py` if `python` is not on your PATH.

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add strata -- python C:\Users\you\Strata\tools\strata_mcp.py         # Windows
claude mcp add strata -- python3 /home/you/Strata/tools/strata_mcp.py           # Linux
```

Add `--scope user` to have it in every project. `/mcp` in Claude Code shows that it is connected.

### Claude Desktop

Open Settings > Developer > Edit Config (`claude_desktop_config.json`) and add:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "strata": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["C:\\Users\\you\\Strata\\tools\\strata_mcp.py"]
    }
  }
}
```

On Linux, use `"command": "python3"` and `"args": ["/home/you/Strata/tools/strata_mcp.py"]`. Restart Claude
Desktop after the change.

### Cursor

Use `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project, or `.cursor/mcp.json` in one project. The format is the same as
Claude Desktop's:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "strata": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["C:\\Users\\you\\Strata\\tools\\strata_mcp.py"]
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code (GitHub Copilot agent mode)

Use `.vscode/mcp.json` in a workspace, or run "MCP: Open User Configuration" from the command palette:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "strata": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["C:\\Users\\you\\Strata\\tools\\strata_mcp.py"]
    }
  }
}
```

On Linux, use `"command": "python3"` and `"args": ["/home/you/Strata/tools/strata_mcp.py"]`.

### Codex CLI

In `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.strata]
command = "python"
args = ['C:\Users\you\Strata\tools\strata_mcp.py']    # Linux: command = "python3", args = ["/home/you/Strata/tools/strata_mcp.py"]
tool_timeout_sec = 180                                # strata_stop / strata_benchmark can take longer than 60 s
```

### Any other MCP client

The command is `python <Strata folder>/tools/strata_mcp.py`. The transport is stdio. It speaks MCP revision
2025-06-18, and also 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05.

`--root <folder>` manages a Strata folder other than the one the file is in. For example:
`python D:\tools\strata_mcp.py --root D:\Strata`.

## The tools

| Tool | What it does | Arguments (all optional) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `strata_status` | Whether a model is running: the model, engine version, context, busy or idle, VRAM and RAM in use. What is installed: models, start scripts, engine version, data folder, downloads. An install in progress. This PC's hardware: OS, CPU, RAM, GPUs, page file, free disk. The model and context setup recommends for this PC. | `port`, `hardware` (true/false) |
| `strata_models` | Every family and size setup offers, with download size, RAM needed, whether it fits this PC, and whether it is installed. Also the context lengths and the recommendation. | - |
| `strata_install` | Runs setup without questions, in the background (see below). Without `confirm: true` it only returns the plan. A second call shows the progress. `cancel: true` stops the install. | `family` (qwen, swift, coder, unsloth), `model` (Q2_0, IQ2_XS, IQ3_XXS, IQ3_S, IQ1_M, UD-IQ4_XS, UD-Q4_K_XL), `context` (8192 ... 524288), `vision` (no, yes, gpu, cpu), `kv` (int8, q4_0, k8v4), `gpu` (a number) or `gpus` ("0,2", "all"), `backend` (auto, cuda, hip), `low_ram`, `port`, `data_dir`, `confirm`, `cancel` |
| `strata_start` | Starts an installed model in the background and waits until it answers. If it is not ready after `wait_seconds` (default 50), it returns "loading". | `model` (an id from `strata_status`, e.g. `q2_0`, `coder-iq1_m`; default: the most recently used), `port`, `gpu`, `wait_seconds` (0-600) |
| `strata_stop` | Unloads the model through the server's own API, then ends the server it started. | `port`, `force` |
| `strata_logs` | The last lines of the server log, the engine log or the setup log. | `source` (server, engine, setup), `model`, `lines` (1-500) |
| `strata_benchmark` | Sends a short fixed request (greedy, thinking off) and reports output and prompt tokens/s. | `port`, `max_tokens` (16-512) |
| `strata_connect_info` | The OpenAI and Anthropic base URLs, the model id, whether a key is needed, and settings for Claude Code, Codex, the OpenAI SDK, curl, Cursor, Continue and Open WebUI. | `port` |

Every result is JSON with a one-line `summary`. It is sent both as text and as MCP structured content.

## How it works

**Install.** `strata_install` uses setup's own logic and tables (it imports `setup.py`'s `MODELS`, `FAMILIES`,
`CONTEXTS` and RAM checks) to fill in what you left out:

- the size setup itself would pick: IQ3_XXS from 60 GB of RAM, Q2_0 from about 44 GB, the Coder from about 28 GB,
  and the Coder in the low-RAM mode below that when the GPU makes up for the RAM;
- the context setup recommends for the GPU's VRAM;
- pictures on where the model can read them (the reader runs on the CPU under 24 GB of VRAM and on the GPU from 24 GB, on NVIDIA and AMD cards; a Mac reads on its GPU).

The first call returns the plan: the download size (58-111 GB), the free disk space, the RAM check, and the exact
setup command. The assistant should show you the plan and call again with `confirm: true` once you agree.

It then runs the same steps `START-HERE.bat` / `setup.sh` run:

1. It creates `.venv` with the Python it runs on, if `.venv` is missing.
2. It runs `setup.py --yes --no-start --family ... --model ... --context ... --vision ...` as a background process.
   The output goes to `.strata-mcp/setup.log` in the Strata folder.

The tool returns at once. Call it again to see the step (1-7), the download percentage, or setup's error message.
Everything setup has finished is skipped on the next run, and downloads resume. If the AI app closes, the install
keeps running. The install is refused while a model this server started is running, because setup may replace the
engine files that model uses.

**Start.** `strata_start` runs the same command as the `run-<model>` script, `serve/server.py --engine strata
--config strata-<model>.json --port N`, with the venv's Python, without `--open` (no browser) and without a console
window. The server's output goes to `.strata-mcp/server.log`. The tool then polls `GET /health` until the model
answers. Loading takes 1-3 minutes. If the server ends while loading, the tool returns the end of its log. The model
keeps running after the AI app closes, until `strata_stop`. If the AI app runs its tools inside a Windows job that
does not allow processes to leave it, the model ends together with the app.

Two cases are refused:

- a model is already running: the tool returns it and starts nothing;
- another program uses the port: the tool says so.

**Stop.** `strata_stop` first sends `POST /unload`. The server sends the engine `QUIT`, and the engine frees its
VRAM and pinned RAM itself, as when you close the window. Then the server ends:

- Linux: SIGTERM, which runs the server's own Ctrl+C path.
- Windows: the process ends. Its job object ends the vision encoder and the MCP servers it started.

While a request is running, the tool refuses unless you pass `force: true`.

**Status.** The tool reads `GET /health`, `/v1/status`, `/status` and, on older servers, `/metrics` on 127.0.0.1.
If a config of the folder sets an `api_key`, the tool sends that key with its own requests. It never shows the key.

## Safety

- **No shell, no free paths.** Every argument is checked against a fixed schema and against setup's own choices. An
  unknown argument, a model or family setup does not offer, or a `gpus` value other than digits and commas is
  refused before anything runs. Commands are passed as argument lists; nothing goes through a shell.
- **Paths.** The only path argument is `data_dir`. It must be one of:
  - the current Strata data folder;
  - a folder inside the Strata folder;
  - a new absolute folder whose name starts with `Strata` (e.g. `D:\Strata-data`), whose parent exists, and which is
    not in a system folder.

  `..`, relative paths and network (UNC) paths are refused. Logs are read only from `.strata-mcp/` and from the
  engine log a config names, if that log is inside the Strata folder or the data folder.
- **Only its own processes.** The server records the process id *and start time* of every process it starts, in
  `.strata-mcp/*.json`. It only ends a process when both match, so a process id the OS has given to another program
  is never touched. A Strata started some other way (its window, a run script, a service) is only asked over its
  API to unload the model. To end that server, close its window.
- **Big downloads need a yes.** `strata_install` does nothing until it is called with `confirm: true`. The plan
  shows the download size and the free space first, and the install is refused if the disk is too small.
- **Local only.** The server checks `127.0.0.1` and never changes the network settings: it does not install with
  `--host 0.0.0.0` or an API key. To share Strata on your network, run setup yourself (see
  [Using it](DETAILS.md#using-it)). Experimental options are left off too: the speed projection, rope scaling past
  262K and `--build`. Run setup by hand for those.

## Troubleshooting

- **The assistant does not see the tools.** Run the command by hand:
  `python C:\Users\you\Strata\tools\strata_mcp.py`. It should print `[strata-mcp] ready (Strata folder ...)` to
  stderr and wait for input (Ctrl+C ends it). If it reports `not a Strata folder`, the path is wrong or `--root` is
  needed. Python older than 3.10 is refused.
- **The install failed.** Ask the assistant for the setup log (`strata_logs` with `source: setup`), or open
  `.strata-mcp/setup.log`. Setup's `[X]` line says what to fix. Then install again: every finished step is skipped.
- **The model does not start.** Get the server log with `strata_logs`, and the engine log with `source: engine`.
  [Troubleshooting](DETAILS.md#troubleshooting) has the usual causes.
- **Tests.** `python -m unittest tools/test_strata_mcp.py` runs the tests with a fake setup and server. They do not
  download anything or use the GPU.


## docs/MESSAGE_BOUNDARY_CACHE.md

# Reuse long chat history when the last user message is edited

## Why this helps

An agent can keep the same long history but replace the final user message.
The final cached state no longer matches, and the nearest periodic checkpoint
may be far behind. The engine then rereads history it already processed.

This opt-in change saves one checkpoint at the previous turn boundary, before
the final short message. It uses the existing bounded cache and leaves normal
token and image-prefix validation in charge of reuse.

## Use and limits

Set `STRATA_CACHE_MESSAGE_BOUNDARY=1` before starting the engine.
It is off by default, requires prompt caching and a valid turn token, and
only selects prefixes of at least 8,192 tokens with a tail of at most 1,024.
Layer-split execution is excluded (`multi_gpu`); helper-expert GPUs still work.
It can split prefill chunks and add snapshot cost to a fresh request.

## Validation environment
