engine's own q8_1 kernels, which decode UE4M3/E2M1 in software. The engine was built for sm_75/86/89 as PTX and run
on the RTX 5090 with the host answering as that generation. On those builds `mmq_nvfp4_parity` and
`nvfp4_expert_gpu_parity` gave results identical to sm_120.

HIP: the decode kernels use no CUDA-only intrinsics. The NVFP4 MMQ instance and the W4A8 unit are CUDA-only and
guarded (`GGML_USE_HIP`). Neither was built for HIP here.

## Tests

- `nvfp4_expert_gpu_parity`: the decode kernels against ggml's reference.
- `nvfp4_avx512_parity`: the CPU rows against ggml-cpu (with `--expert`: one whole expert).
- `mmq_nvfp4_parity`: the prompt path's products against FP64 (with `--real`: rows dumped by `STRATA_DUMP_MOE_INPUT`).
- `tools/nvfp4_verify.py` and `tools/nvfp4_verify_gguf.py`: the conversion, bit for bit.

## NVIDIA's FP4-Local checkpoint

`nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` (setup size **NVFP4-QAD**) is NVIDIA's own retrained 4-bit model: ModelOpt 0.47
safetensors, experts retrained by quantization-aware distillation. Strata reads it by converting it on the user's PC;
nothing of NVIDIA's weights is redistributed (licenses: NVIDIA Open Model Agreement and Qwen Community License 1.0).

What the checkpoint holds, and what `tools/nvfp4_local_pack.py` does with it:

| In the checkpoint | Becomes |
| --- | --- |
| routed experts: NVFP4 (E2M1, E4M3 scale per 16, F32 scale per tensor); the scales stored in NVIDIA's "CSF" form (`.nvfp4_csf_fixed` U8 + `.nvfp4_csf_exceptions` U32) | the scales are decoded to the plain E4M3 matrix (byte-exact; the format is the one vLLM's loader documents), then repacked exactly like every other NVFP4 pack: `experts.bin` with the same 36-byte super-blocks and the 16-byte scale tail. Checked: 304 complete experts and the whole `experts.bin` (SHA-256) equal the route through a full GGUF |
| attention, GDN projections, shared experts, indexer: MXFP8 (E4M3 values, E8M0 scale per 32) | dequantized exactly, then Q8_0 (same 32-value blocks; +0.6% RMS on top of MXFP8's own ~3%), or BF16 for the small projections the BF16 kernels read |
| n-gram (PLE) table, 26.8 GiB: NVFP4 rows of 160 values | a one-tensor GGUF of 90-byte rows (80 B codes + 10 E4M3 scales, one F32 for the table), read by the new PLE format `NVFP4` (`strata.ple.format = nvfp4x16`) in `ngram.cpp`; same row size as IQ4_NL |
| MTP head: NVFP4 experts, BF16 rest | a Q2_0 draft layer built with `mtp_pack.py` / `mtp_rt.py` (88.7% of drafts accepted over 225 test requests) |
| vision tower | not converted. Pictures are read by the original model's picture reader (the shared `mmproj` file that setup downloads, as for the other NVFP4 versions); the dense GGUF supplies the vocabulary |

`python tools/nvfp4_local_pack.py prepare --model <checkpoint> --out <dir>` runs every step (setup does this): the n-gram
table, the dense GGUF (no experts), the pack (experts written straight from the checkpoint) and the draft layer. It needs
about 110 GB of free disk beside the 102 GB download, which can be deleted afterwards. On a Threadripper PRO with the files
on NVMe it took about 12 minutes.

Measured on an RTX PRO 5000 72 GB (Blackwell), 128K context, int8 KV, every expert in VRAM (`tools/strata_bench.py`):
decode 159 tokens/s (median of chat answers, 137-216), 4K prompt 3,981 tokens/s, 16K 4,813, 32K 4,916 (first token 6.6 s),
agent session 151 tokens/s; the engine holds 69 GB of RAM beside 72 GB of VRAM. Quality is in the table below
(`tools/quant_quality.py`, set v1, against Unsloth's Q8_0): top-1 90.5%, mean KL 0.085, perplexity 3.95 (Q8_0: 4.05).
This is a retrained model, so its distance to the original's Q8_0 includes real weight changes, not only rounding.


## docs/NVIDIA_V100.md

# NVIDIA Tesla V100 / Titan V (Volta, sm_70): the community build

Strata's ready-made engine and the support matrix start at compute capability 7.5 (RTX 20). A V100 (7.0) runs the same
engine compiled for it, through the experimental build that issue #236 added. It is **community-tested, not part of the
supported cards**: no ready-made engine is published for it and the numbers below come from one machine.

## Build

CUDA 13 dropped Volta, so the build needs a **CUDA 12.x** toolkit (12.8 was used) and a host GCC that toolkit accepts.

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF \
      -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=70 -DSTRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=ON
cmake --build build --target strata -j
```

Setup does the same by itself for a model on a V100 (the experimental CUDA 12 engine, in `engine-cuda12/`: ready-made
on Windows, compiled with a CUDA 12.x toolkit on Linux; [OLDER_GPUS.md](OLDER_GPUS.md)). For a PC with a V100 and a newer card, a build for both architectures (`-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="70;86"`) is the
natural choice (a community report in issue #509 ran an RTX 3080 beside a V100 that way; it was not repeated here). On the
measuring PC a Quadro RTX 4000 (sm_75) sits beside the V100s and was hidden with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` because the sm_70-only
build has no code for it.

## What runs on Volta

The flag only lowers the floor (CMake and the runtime device check) and replaces two intrinsics Volta lacks. It does not
select "old" kernels everywhere: which kernel runs is decided per architecture when the engine is built.

| Part of the prompt path | On sm_70 |
| --- | --- |
| MoE experts | opt-in (`STRATA_PF_WMMA=1`, only when every visible card is compute capability 7+; MMQ otherwise): `gemm_iq_f16_grouped`: a group of experts per launch on the FP16 tensor cores, the weights dequantized in shared memory (+10% prompt speed against MMQ's `dp4a` kernels, [bench](../bench/results/2026-10-07-v100-prompt-experts/README.md); FP16 activations instead of MMQ's q8_1, so the answers differ) |
| Dense projections (dequantized weights) | FP16 tensor-core GEMMs (cuBLAS / CUTLASS `s884`) |
| BF16 projections (hyper-connection, router, indexer, ...) | converted to FP16 and run on the FP16 tensor cores (#655, #540; `STRATA_BF16_TC=0`: cuBLAS BF16, an FP32 SIMT kernel on Volta) |
| QSA attention for decode and verify windows (and prompts with `STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_OLD=1`) | #540's kernel (fewer shuffles, bit-exact; `STRATA_ATTN_PRE75=0`: the one other cards run) |
| QSA prompt attention, int8 / FP16 / K8V4 KV | `prompt_attn_v70_kernel` on `mma.m8n8k4` (`STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_OLD=1`: the decode kernel, one query at a time) |
| QSA prompt attention, Q4_0 KV | the decode kernel |
| QSA block scores | the warp kernel (the tensor-core scorer needs sm_80) |

| Part of a decode / verify window | On sm_70 |
| --- | --- |
| Routed experts in VRAM | gfx906's expert mode 8: the codebook grid and the group's activations in shared memory, SwiGLU fused (`STRATA_EXP_MODE=0`: the CUDA layout other cards run) |
| Dense 2-4 column GEMVs and the head | the interleaved `native_mmvq_il` with a Volta rows table (`STRATA_MMVQ_IL=0`: `native_mmvq`) |
| Hyper-connection read, up projection | gfx906's latency-hidden up kernel (`STRATA_GR_FAST=0`: the plain one) |

All three are bitwise the kernels they replace; on a V100-SXM2 they take a verify window's GPU work from 22.8 to 21.2 ms
([bench/results/2026-10-07-v100-decode-kernels](../bench/results/2026-10-07-v100-decode-kernels/README.md)).

## Measured

One V100-PCIE-32GB, i9-7960X, Unsloth `UD-IQ4_XS` (not a setup model), int8 KV, MTP `--spec 2`; prompt read speed of random-word prompts, tokens/s,
with and without the Volta attention kernel (`STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_OLD=1`):

| Prompt tokens | old attention path | `prompt_attn_v70_kernel` |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 7,194 | 1,010 | 1,164 |
| 28,650 | 1,063 | 1,251 |
| 114,338 | 973 | 1,123 |

Decode was 38-51 tok/s in every run and is not affected. The profile, the parity numbers, the needle test and the limits are in
[bench/results/2026-10-03-v100-prompt-attn](../bench/results/2026-10-03-v100-prompt-attn/README.md).

What the kernel does and does not guarantee: against an FP64 reference its error is about 2-3e-6 (output scale 3.6; the FP32 kernel it replaces: 2e-6; 5e-6 before the hi and lo halves got separate accumulator chains); 15 of 15
needles were found; greedy output was identical on the 28,650- and 114,338-token prompts and differed late in the answer on the 7,194-token one (another
summation order).

## Checking and benchmarking the Volta kernels

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DSTRATA_PARITY_PROMPT_ATTN=ON ... && cmake --build build --target qsa_prompt_attn_parity
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 ./build/qsa_prompt_attn_parity 32768 2048 5     # synthetic, no model; exit 0 = PASS
```

It compares the tensor-core attention with the FP32 kernel and an FP64 host reference and times both. The Q4_0 cases are skipped below
sm_80.

## Limits

- A layer split over two V100 was not measured with this kernel. The cards work in turn on a single request, so a split adds expert-cache room, not prompt speed.
- sm_60 (Pascal) is covered by the same flag, and community runs exist: two Tesla P40 with a layer split (#1028, bench
  [2026-10-05-community-2x-p40](../bench/results/2026-10-05-community-2x-p40/README.md)), a Tesla P100 alone and with an RTX 2070 SUPER as
  the expert-helper card (#1069: 30.5 tok/s alone, 35.8-38.4 with the helper), and a V100 + P100 pair (#1079: +6-11% decode from 0.1.39 to
  0.1.40 with the P100 as helper cache). One reporter's numbers each; this page's own kernel measurements are V100 only.
- Volta's tensor cores take FP16 only: a model's BF16 weights are converted, and a weight outside FP16's range would saturate (none did in
  the check above).

## The decode kernels measured on a V100 (opt-in: `STRATA_SM70_TABLE=1`)

The interleaved 2-4 column matvec with a Volta rows table, expert mode 8 and the latency-hidden norm/up (bitwise the default
kernels' output, GPU work per verify window 22.8 -> 21.2 ms on a V100-SXM2 in the contributor's measurement) are used on
sm_70 only when `STRATA_SM70_TABLE=1` is set. They become the default once the contributor has confirmed them on a V100 with
the 0.1.41 code. Without the variable sm_70 runs what 0.1.40.3 ran. The single switches (`STRATA_EXP_MODE`, `STRATA_MMVQ_IL`,
`STRATA_GR_FAST`) still apply on top.

## More opt-in switches (CUDA 12 experimental build)

None of these is on by default. Each was measured by its contributor on a V100, not by the maintainers.

| Switch | What it does | Contributor's number |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `STRATA_FUSE_DECODE=1` | the decode GEMV / MoE operator fusions of #1097 (gate/up + SwiGLU in one kernel, SwiGLU + quantizer in one kernel, all activation images of a vector in one pass, two BF16 projections in one kernel); bitwise the unfused kernels | 4-16 us per token saved, not visible end to end |
| `STRATA_PF_WMMA=1` | the FP16 tensor-core prompt experts (above); also takes IQ4_NL down projections (K=640, #1771) | +10% prompt speed (#1401) |
| `STRATA_PF_WMMA2=1` | a second prompt-expert kernel for IQ2_S gate/up and IQ4_NL down (#2356) | +2.5-4.3% prompt speed |
| `STRATA_ARGMAX_ROWS_SM70=1` | the multi-block greedy pick on sm_7x (#2357), bitwise the one-block pick | +0.7-0.8% decode |
| `STRATA_GR_NORM_FAST=1` | the register-split hyper-connection norm on CUDA (#2358) | +0.5-0.6% decode |
| `STRATA_Q8_GATHER_WIDE=0` | turns off the 8-wide int8 KV gather (#1095) that the experimental build uses below compute capability 7.5 | +11% on the gather kernel |
| `STRATA_GDN_REC_WARP=2` | the chain-split DeltaNet recurrence of the prompt on a V100 (#1098); changes the summation order (FP32 level), so the default stays the pipelined kernel; `1` is the bit-exact sync-free variant, `STRATA_GDN_CHUNK=1` the chunked path | +6-9% on the recurrence |


## docs/OLDER_GPUS.md

# Older GPUs (experimental)

Strata's supported cards are NVIDIA RTX 20 / 30 / 40 / 50 and the AMD cards in [AMD_HIP.md](AMD_HIP.md). The cards
below run through **opt-in, experimental** paths that community members wrote and measured on their own machines. The
maintainers have one of these cards, a Tesla P100, and test on it; they have none of the others: each path is
compile-checked and unit-tested here, and the ready-made engines and their output stay exactly as they were. Numbers are
the reporters' own, on one machine each, unless the text says the maintainers measured them.

## Support matrix

### NVIDIA

| Cards | Compute capability | How it runs | What is different on it | Reported |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tesla P100 | 6.0 | the CUDA 12 engine | `__dp4a` emulated (bit-exact); BF16 projections through fp32; opt-in: `STRATA_Q8_SM60=1` runs the Q8_0 dense projections and head on a GP100 kernel ([below](#pascal-gp100-a-q8_0-decode-kernel-opt-in)) | 2x P100, IQ3_S, engine 0.1.39: prompt 526-532 tok/s, decode 28-32 tok/s at 128K prompt tokens, 3 of 3 needle checks at 122K ([report](../bench/results/2026-10-06-community-2x-p100/README.md), #1157); PH402 (4 GP100 dies), IQ3_XXS: decode 28.3 -> 38.9 tok/s with `STRATA_Q8_SM60=1` and a Q8_0 dense shard |
| Tesla P40 / P4, GTX 10 series | 6.1 | the CUDA 12 engine | BF16 projections through fp32 (cuBLAS has no BF16 GEMM there, #395); the dense weights dequantized by a wide kernel, expert mode 8 and its own interleaved-matvec table; opt-in `STRATA_DENSE_F32=1`: the large dense GEMMs as `cublasSgemm` ([below](#tesla-p40-sm_61-what-was-measured-and-changed)) | P40, IQ3_S, engine 0.1.30: prompt 217-374 tok/s, decode 30-33 tok/s (#395); 0.1.43.1 with the sm_61 changes: prompt 255 tok/s at 565 tokens (was 205), decode 37-38 tok/s (was 34-35); with `STRATA_DENSE_F32=1` 464-474 tok/s at 7K tokens (was 360-432) |
| Tesla V100, Titan V | 7.0 | the CUDA 12 engine | BF16 projections on the FP16 tensor cores (#655, #540); the prompt attention on `mma.m8n8k4` (#600); a leaner attention kernel (#540) | V100-PCIE-32GB, UD-IQ4_XS: prompt 1,123-1,251 tok/s (#600); V100 32GB, IQ2_XS: prompt +22% from #540 |
| RTX 20 (Turing) | 7.5 | **supported**, the ready-made engine | opt-in: `STRATA_BF16_TC=1` runs the BF16 projections on the FP16 tensor cores | RTX 2080 Ti, Q2_0: prompt +15-18% (#655) |

A card needs enough VRAM to be useful: 12 GB or more is recommended, as for every card (a 2 GB GT 1030 is compute
capability 6.1 too, and cannot hold any of the model).

### AMD

| Cards | Architecture | How it runs | Reported |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RX 6800 / 6900 series | gfx1030 | setup (`--backend hip`), unvalidated; #540's attention kernel is the default there, with 8 cells per step and DPP lane exchanges (bit-exact; `STRATA_ATTN_PRE75=0` runs the standard kernel) | [AMD_HIP.md](AMD_HIP.md#rdna2-gfx1030); RX 6900 XT, IQ3_S: prompts +4-6% alone, +7-12% with #835 ([bench/results/2026-10-04-rdna2-pre75-attention](../bench/results/2026-10-04-rdna2-pre75-attention/README.md)) |
| RX 6700 XT | gfx1031 | setup (`--backend hip`), unvalidated (#524) | used daily by its reporter, one card |
| RX 5500 XT (RDNA1) | gfx1012 | built by hand: `-DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1012` (HIP 5.7 or 7) | 8 GB card, IQ3_S, 8K prompt: 15.3 tok/s decode (#442) |
| RX 5700 XT (RDNA1) | gfx1010 | built by hand: `-DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1010`, on ROCm 7.14's `gfx101X-dgpu` wheels; needs `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` in a PC that also has an AMD iGPU | 8 GB card, Coder IQ1_M, 32K context: prompt 115 / 144 / 149 tok/s and decode 18.0 / 20.3 / 23.3 tok/s at 4K / 16K / 30K prompt tokens, 6 of 6 needle checks at 8K and 30K, 61 of 61 ctest on the card, 607 of 12,288 experts in VRAM |
| RX 5700 and the 6 GB RX 5600 (RDNA1) | gfx1010 | as above | the same Navi 10 silicon as the RX 5700 XT, so the same build; a 6 GB card leaves ~50 expert slots, expect the RX 5500 XT's range, not this one's |
| Radeon PRO V520 / Pro 5600M (RDNA1) | gfx1011 | built by hand: `-DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1011` | untested on hardware: it is the same RDNA1 ISA as gfx1010 (Navi 12), and the engine builds for it with 0 errors on the same wheels |
| Instinct MI50 / MI60, Radeon VII | gfx906 (wave64) | built by hand: `-DSTRATA_HIP_GFX906=ON` | 2x MI50, Coder IQ1_M, 128K context: decode 50.1 / 47.8 / 45.7 tok/s at 4K / 32K / 128K prompt tokens, prompt ~520 tok/s (#677) |

## NVIDIA: the CUDA 12 engine

CUDA 13 dropped Pascal and Volta: it cannot compile for them. Setup therefore keeps a **second engine**, built with
CUDA 12.9 and `-DSTRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=ON`, in its own folder (`engine-cuda12\`, beside `engine\`). One engine runs
per model, so the choice is made per model, by the oldest card that model runs on:

- **Every card the model uses is RTX 20 or newer:** the ready-made CUDA 13 engine, as always.
- **A card is Pascal or Volta:** the CUDA 12 engine. Setup says so (`CUDA 12: sm_70 is older than CUDA 13 supports
  ...`). On Windows it downloads `strata-windows-x64-cuda12.zip` with NVIDIA's CUDA 12 libraries (from pip, like the
  CUDA 13 ones); on Linux, or with `--build`, it compiles the engine with a CUDA 12.x toolkit.

### Opting in

An older card is used only when you choose it; a PC with a newer card keeps recommending the newer one.

| You | Setup |
| --- | --- |
| have only Pascal / Volta NVIDIA cards (and no AMD card it can use) | uses them, with the CUDA 12 engine |
| name the card: `START-HERE.bat --setup --gpu 1`, or `--gpus 0,1` with a newer card | uses it; the model gets the CUDA 12 engine |
| `--cuda 12` (or `STRATA_CUDA=12`) | the CUDA 12 engine for this model, on any card |
| `--cuda 13` | the CUDA 13 engine even with an older card (a warning: it has no code for that card) |
| `STRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=1` | the older cards are listed as usable (the setting from #295 still works) |

The choice is kept in the model's config (`"cuda": 12`): its starts and `UPDATE.bat` keep it, and other models keep
their own engine. Setting the model up again chooses again (by its cards; add `--cuda 12` to keep a forced choice). A Pascal / Volta card added to a model at a start (`--gpus`) moves that model to the
CUDA 12 engine.

`--cuda 12` is also the way to run Strata with an NVIDIA driver older than 580: CUDA 12 needs 528 or newer on Windows
(527.41, NVIDIA's minor-version compatibility) and 525 on Linux; setup's "driver too old" stop says so. Such old
drivers were not tested here.

### Mixed cards

A model that shares a V100 with an RTX 30 / 40 card runs both on the CUDA 12 engine (it has code for sm_60 to sm_89,
plus PTX). An RTX 50 card (sm_120) in a CUDA 12 engine is a warning, not a stop: CUDA 12.8 and newer compile for it,
but engines built with 12.8 crashed on long prompts there (#220, #224). Keep the RTX 50 card on its own model (`--gpu
N`), where it runs the CUDA 13 engine.

### Building it yourself

```sh
# Linux (Windows: the same with the toolkit's nvcc.exe)
cmake -S . -B build-cuda12 -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DSTRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=ON \
      -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="61;70" -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=/usr/local/cuda-12.9/bin/nvcc
cmake --build build-cuda12 --target strata -j
```

Setup does the same when it compiles: it looks for the newest CUDA 12.x toolkit (`STRATA_NVCC=<path to nvcc>` picks
one, #601; on glibc 2.43 use 12.8, see [TROUBLESHOOTING.md](TROUBLESHOOTING.md)).

On GCC 12.3 with nvcc (openEuler 24.03, CUDA 12.8, 2x V100) the build needed `-D_BITS_OPT_RANDOM_H` added to the host flags (#1074; one
report, not reproduced here). The `size_t` error in `vmm.hpp` that the same report hit is fixed in 0.1.40.2.

### What the flag changes, and what it does not

`-DSTRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=ON` lowers the runtime floor to compute capability 6.0 and compiles the older cards' code
paths into that build only: the Volta prompt attention (#600), #540's attention kernel (used below sm_75), and the
Pascal BF16 path. The ready-made CUDA 13 engine has none of them, so its kernels and its output are unchanged. The
FP16 path for BF16 projections is in every build but runs by default only below sm_75; RTX 20 owners can try it with
`STRATA_BF16_TC=1` (`=0` turns it off on a V100). It is not bitwise the same as cuBLAS's BF16 kernel (FP16 tensor-core
sums round differently): #540 measured a mean KL of 8.4e-3 on the next-token distribution of 24 code prompts on a V100
(the same top-1 in 23), the size of other summation-order changes; #655 a worst relative difference of 3.5e-5 per
product on an RTX 2080 Ti.

### Tesla P100 (sm_60): seven decode switches on by default (engine 0.1.45.3)

On a Tesla P100 the engine now turns on a set of seven switches that change only how the work is scheduled, so the answers
stay bit for bit the same: `STRATA_ADAPT_NOWAIT=1`, `STRATA_ADAPT_LAG=2`, `STRATA_SIDE_MIXER=2`, `STRATA_FUSE_WAIT=2`,
`STRATA_B6_MMVQ_ROWS=1`, `STRATA_FUSE_DECODE=1` and `STRATA_GR_UP75=1`. `STRATA_SM60_PERF=0` turns the whole set off, and a
switch you set yourself, to any value, is kept. The set is used when every visible card has compute capability 6.0.
Measured by the maintainers on a Tesla P100 16 GB, IQ3_XXS, default flags, 8 interleaved pairs of fresh engines: decode 36.56
-> 41.76 tokens/s (+14.2%, faster in 8 of 8 pairs; a run against itself gave 0.975), with the same number of expert-cache
slots; the identity gate (10 prompts and 4K/20K prompt dumps) is identical with the set on. The full list, the RTX 30 set
and the per-switch results: [DETAILS.md](DETAILS.md#rtx-30-series-sm_86-and-tesla-p100-sm_60-bitwise-decode-switches-on-by-default).

### Pascal GP100: a Q8_0 decode kernel (opt-in)

GP100 (P100, PH402) is the one Pascal chip without `__dp4a`, and the decode kernels are written for the cards that have
it: on a GP100 die the dense projections of a verify window read their weights at 40-80 GB/s of its ~730, decoding K-
and i-quant blocks (Q6_K, IQ4_XS, Q4_K, IQ3_S, ...) one int at a time. Two changes, both measured on a PH402 only:

- **`STRATA_Q8_SM60=1`** packs every Q8_0 dense matrix and the head into the planes of `STRATA_Q8_PACKED` (any shape)
  and runs them on `src/kernels/cuda/q8_sm60.cuh`: a warp (half or quarter warp for narrow rows) per row, 16-byte
  weight loads, the window's q8_1 activations copied once per workgroup into shared memory as an int8 plane, the dot
  on `STRATA_DP4A` (vmad), a shuffle sum - no barrier per row. Shapes it declines (a 6144-wide row with 7-8 columns)
  keep the usual kernel. Not bitwise the exact kernels (the per-32 products are added in another order). The packed
  copies cost their size in VRAM beside the GGUF layout the prompt path reads (Flash-Next: 2.9 GiB of dense
  projections over the stages and 0.6 GiB for the head).
- The GSQ-RCO packs have no Q8_0 dense matrices, so the kernel needs a copy of the model whose dense projections and head are
  Q8_0: `python tools/q8_dense_gguf.py <model>-00001-of-00002.gguf <new folder>` writes one: every shard that holds
  such matrices is converted (Swift 1.5 keeps them in both of its shards) and the rest are hard-linked beside them
  (+3.5 GiB; the experts keep their offsets, so the native pack is reused). Point `--native` and
  `--ple-gguf` at the new folder. Requantizing costs at most 0.4% of a tensor's |w|max (Q8_0 is finer than the
  sources).
- **Opt-in `STRATA_IQ_STAGE_TABLES=1`**: IQ3_XXS's and IQ3_S's codebooks and sign-mask tables are staged in shared memory by
  the grouped expert kernels (IQ3_XXS's ported from shinbunbun/llama-cpp-p100-patches 29 and 30, IQ3_S's the same for its
  sign bytes; bitwise the same output). IQ3_S was the one gate/up format whose codebook those kernels still read from
  global memory: the contributor measured a verify window's layer of IQ3_S experts (20 experts, 24 entries) 24% faster on a
  GP100 die (517 -> 393 us with a Q2_0 down projection, 492 -> 369 us with IQ4_NL), and Swift 1.5 IQ3_XXS (13 of its 48
  layers are IQ3_S) 3.2% faster at 1M context (39.3 -> 40.5 tok/s); IQ3_XXS's tables alone were within noise (+0-4%). The
  maintainers' interleaved A/Bs on a Tesla P100 (PCIe, IQ3_XXS pack and IQ3_S pack, 5-6 pairs each) showed no end-to-end
  change (decode 0.97-1.03x, inside the noise of that box), so it is off by default (the contributor's version had it on
  for compute capability 6.0). On an RTX 3090 Ti, forced on, the same IQ3_S layers took 3-13% longer (those kernels already
  read at 490-665 GB/s there).
- Neither change is measured on compute capability 6.1 (P40, P4, GTX 10 series), which has `__dp4a`. Both build for
  sm_61, and on a card with `__dp4a` the Q8_0 kernel's dot is the hardware instruction (`tools/q8_sm60_check.cu`
  passes on an RTX 3090 Ti); numbers from a 6.1 card with `STRATA_Q8_SM60=1` or `STRATA_IQ_STAGE_TABLES=1` would
  show whether either helps there.

Measured on a PH402 SKU 200 (two boards, four GP100 dies of 48 SMs and 32 GB HBM2), application clocks locked at
1050 MHz, Windows 11, driver 581.80 (TCC), CUDA 12.9, engine 0.1.40.2; Flash-Next IQ3_XXS, 32K, `--layer-split 12,24,36
--prefill 2048`; greedy, 256 tokens, medians of 2-3 interleaved starts, decode tok/s:

| | ~10.7K-token document | the same, cached | short reasoning | code | mean |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| GSQ-RCO shard, exact kernels | 28.8 | 29.4 | 28.4 | 26.8 | 28.3 |
| Q8_0 dense shard, `STRATA_Q8_PACKED=1` | 27.5 | 31.0 | 34.4 | 31.8 | 31.1 |
| Q8_0 dense shard, `STRATA_Q8_SM60=1` | 37.5 | 38.4 | 41.2 | 38.5 | 38.9 |

GPU time per verify window (`STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE`): dense projections 19.2 -> 11.2 ms, head 4.25 -> 2.1 ms; the
draft policy then picks longer windows (2.10 -> 2.31 tokens per window). Prompt reads are unchanged (437-438 tok/s at
10.7K). `tools/q8_sm60_check.cu` checks the kernel against a CPU reference on these shapes (1-8 columns) and times it.

Two things that mattered as much on this card: its default application clock is 759 MHz, and a layer split leaves
each die idle most of a window, so the dies decode below 1050 MHz unless the clocks are locked
(`nvidia-smi -i <dies> -ac 715,1050` as administrator; 25.0 -> 29.1 tok/s at 10.7K context). And a second engine on
the same PC that pins its threads to the same logical CPUs halves this one's decode while it runs (the host thread
is time-sliced); keeping the two on different logical CPUs (SMT siblings) avoided it.

A/B switches: `STRATA_DEQUANT_WIDE=0`, `STRATA_SM61_TABLE=0` (sm_61: the kernels 0.1.43.1 ran), `STRATA_DENSE_F32=1` (Pascal, opt-in),
`STRATA_Q8_SM60=0|1` (Pascal GP100, opt-in), `STRATA_BF16_TC=0|1`, `STRATA_PROMPT_ATTN_OLD=1` (the decode kernel for prompts), `STRATA_ATTN_PRE75=0`
(#540's kernel off; on gfx103x with HIP that kernel is the default, see the AMD table above, and `=1` turns it on for
another wave32 AMD card). [NVIDIA_V100.md](NVIDIA_V100.md) has the V100 build, its measurements and the parity test.

### Tesla P40 (sm_61): what was measured and changed

One Tesla P40 24 GB in a 20-vCPU VM (Xeon E5-2695 v4, 98 GB RAM), CUDA 12.4 (cuBLAS 12.4.5.8), IQ3_S with MTP
(`--spec 4`), int8 KV, `--max-context 262144`, engine 0.1.43.1; the numbers and every run are in
[bench/results/2026-10-12-p40-sm61-kernels](../bench/results/2026-10-12-p40-sm61-kernels/README.md).
`STRATA_PREFILL_TIMING=1`, `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` and `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1` show a card that is the bottleneck
everywhere: the prompt's GPU timeline equals its wall time (waiting for expert copies 0.2%, host grouping 0.2% of a
7K-token prompt) and a decode window is 49 ms of GPU stages with 1-3 ms of CPU experts. Of a 7K-token prompt, 36% is
the dense projections' GEMMs, 28% the experts (ggml's MMQ, which has its own Pascal dp4a configuration), 13% the
hyper-connection read and 12% the attention.

Three things run differently on compute capability 6.1 by default and a fourth is opt-in. Each gives the same bits as
what it replaces:

| Change | What it replaces | Measured on the P40 | Switch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wide dequantization (a thread per 8 values, 16-bit loads, 16-byte stores) for Q4_K / Q5_K / Q6_K / IQ4_XS | a thread per 32 values with byte loads: 0.5 s of every prompt chunk, whatever its length | Q6_K 10240 x 2560: 7.2 -> 0.33 ms (10 -> 227 GB/s); Q4_K 5.2x, Q5_K 3.8x, IQ4_XS 3.6x; `dequant_wide_parity` 360 cases bitwise | on; `STRATA_DEQUANT_WIDE=0` |
| Expert mode 8 for the experts in VRAM (decode and verify windows) | the CUDA layout | an 18-expert call at 2 tokens: IQ3_S 390 -> 255 us, IQ3_XXS 345 -> 252, IQ2_S 290 -> 238, IQ4_XS 328 -> 261; `native_expert_bench` bitwise | on; `STRATA_SM61_TABLE=0` (or `STRATA_EXP_MODE=0`) |
| The interleaved small-batch matvec with a table measured on the P40 (`kIlRows_61`) | `native_mmvq` | IQ4_XS 2560 x 10240 at 2 columns 112 -> 65 us, Q6_K 12288 x 2560 at 4 columns 189 -> 127 us, the Q5_K head at 3 columns 2,545 -> 1,766 us; `mmvq_il_parity` bitwise | on; `STRATA_SM61_TABLE=0` (or `STRATA_MMVQ_IL=0`) |
| The large dense GEMMs (qkv, query, gate, output projections) as `cublasSgemm` on FP32 copies of the FP16 operands | cuBLAS's FP16-operand kernels, which run at 4.3 TFLOPS instead of 7.6 for most chunk sizes (a 7K-token prompt reads in 16.3 or 19.5 s by its exact token count) | 8.4-9.8 TFLOPS at every size from 512 tokens; qkv at 7,041 tokens 85 -> 45 ms; `gemm_f32_parity` 5,201 chunk sizes bitwise | **opt-in**, `STRATA_DENSE_F32=1` |

The GEMM route is opt-in because its equality is a property of the cuBLAS build, not of the code: it was measured with
cuBLAS 12.4.5.8 only. Run `gemm_f32_parity` (a build with `-DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON`; exit 0 = every size bitwise) with
your toolkit's library before you set it.

Through the server, medians of 3 requests per run, two runs per build alternated, each run started with the card at
65 C (see below). By default: a 565-token prompt 203 / 205 -> 256 / 255 tok/s, decode after it 35.0 / 34.2 -> 38.2 /
37.2 tok/s, a 7,047-token prompt 1-3% faster at the same token count. With `STRATA_DENSE_F32=1` as well: the
7,047-token prompt 430 / 364 -> 474 / 473 tok/s (the old build reads it at ~361 or ~431 tok/s depending on whether the
chunk has more than 7,040 tokens; with the route every request read at 464-474), decode after it 32.1 / 33.4 -> 35.9 /
34.0. With `STRATA_DEQUANT_WIDE=0 STRATA_SM61_TABLE=0` and the route off the new build measures as the old one (210 /
365 tok/s, 33.3 tok/s).

Measured and **not** changed: the latency-hidden hyper-connection read (`STRATA_GR_FAST=1`) is slower on the P40 below
5 tokens (82 -> 88 us at one); `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE=auto` and `STRATA_ADAPT_OVERLAP=1` gave nothing.

Two things to know when measuring on such a card:

- **Temperature.** A P40 has no fan of its own. This one reaches 87-89 C in a few minutes of work; at 89 C the driver
  reports `SW Thermal Slowdown: Active` and the clock falls from 1,531 to ~1,300 MHz (`nvidia-smi -q -d PERFORMANCE`,
  `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,clocks.gr --format=csv -l 2`). Start every arm of an A/B at the same
  temperature, or the later arm loses.
- **Greedy answers are not identical run to run on a CPU without AVX-512**, even with `--prompt-cache 0
  --adapt-swaps 0 --pcie-frac 0`: an expert computed on the CPU rounds differently for a lone token than in a window
  of several (`native_gu_mt_min`), and how many drafts a window holds depends on timing. Add `STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN=1`
  (and `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE=0`, `STRATA_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP=0`) to compare two builds' answers byte for byte.

### Quadro RTX 8000: measurements of existing switches

The Quadro RTX 8000 is Turing (sm_75): it has FP16 tensor cores, but no native BF16 or TF32 tensor cores. Two
**existing, opt-in** CUDA switches are worth comparing on your own workload:

- `STRATA_BF16_TC=1` converts BF16 projection operands to FP16 and uses FP16 tensor cores with FP32 accumulation.
  The default on sm_75 is off; `=0` restores the cuBLAS BF16 path. The switch applies to 7.x cards, not the native
  BF16 path on sm_80 and newer. Conversion clamps finite values outside FP16's range to ±65504; small values and
  differently ordered sums can round differently.
- `STRATA_SELECT_SIMT=1` uses the tiled FP32 QSA block scorer on the pre-sm_80 CUDA path instead of the default
  warp scorer. `=0` keeps the warp scorer. It does not enable TF32 on Turing, and its summation order differs.

The existing paths are in [gemm.cu](../src/prefill/gemm.cu) and [qsa_select.cu](../src/kernels/cuda/qsa_select.cu).

Set the environment before starting the engine, or set the switches in the model config's `env` object, then
restart. For example, this config fragment opts into both (keep the config's other settings):

```json
"env": {
  "STRATA_BF16_TC": "1",
  "STRATA_SELECT_SIMT": "1"
}
```

This section records an investigation, **not a new kernel or a change to defaults**. Measurements on 2026-10-07
used one 48 GiB Quadro RTX 8000 (physical GPU 3), a 260 W power limit, a Xeon W-2295, CUDA 12.4 and GCC 13.
The source-built engine was based on v0.1.40.3 with other local changes integrated; unrelated opt-in changes
were disabled in these arms. These are not measurements of an otherwise clean documentation-only checkout,
not results at the launcher's 200 W setting, and not a speed promise for every sm_75 card.

The model was IQ3_S with MTP (`--spec 4`), `--max-context 262144`, INT8 KV with `--kv-resident 32768`,
`--pcie-frac 0.20`, a fixed `--expert-cache 19000` request and `--prefill auto` (8,192-token ceiling).
The engine reported 21,189 cache slots including the prompt loan. Prompt caching and adaptive swaps were off
(`--prompt-cache 0 --adapt-swaps 0`). Each size used three fresh, seeded synthetic prompts and 128 output tokens
per request; the table gives median engine-reported rates, not end-to-end server latency.

| Existing switch settings | 537 tokens: prompt / decode tok/s | 4,057 tokens: prompt / decode tok/s | 32,057 tokens: prompt / decode tok/s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BF16_TC=0, SELECT_SIMT=0 | 493 / 86.8 | 1,055 / 79.9 | 1,135 / 70.6 |
| BF16_TC=1, SELECT_SIMT=0 | 661 / 83.7 | 1,262 / 75.4 | 1,416 / 68.4 |
| BF16_TC=1, SELECT_SIMT=1 | 679 / 87.1 | 1,290 / 78.2 | 1,501 / 71.6 |

BF16_TC improved prompt throughput by about 20–34%, but did not improve decode in these comparisons. Adding
SELECT_SIMT improved the 32K prompt rate by about 6% over BF16_TC alone; this is not a universal decode win.
BF16_TC changed replies in 3 of the 9 paired requests, so use it only if different rounding is acceptable.
All five basic arithmetic/JSON checks passed in each arm, which is a smoke check, **not a model-quality study**.
A separate synthetic QSA scorer check at 131,072 context tokens matched selected IDs for all 256 queries and
passed its FP64 accuracy gate. That check does not prove identical selections on arbitrary prompts or model quality.

Two other existing tuning options did not justify a recommendation on this machine:

- `--prefill auto:16384`, with BF16_TC on and SELECT_SIMT off, increased the prompt's cache loan from 4.38 to
  7.38 GiB for only about 0.6% more 32K prompt throughput (1,425 versus 1,416 tok/s). Just 24 MiB of VRAM remained
  at the last graph capture. Keep the 8,192 ceiling rather than spend that memory margin for this small gain.
- `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE=auto` gave no gain at the two tested sizes (537 and 4,057 tokens): prompt rates were
  647 and 1,253 tok/s versus 661 and 1,262 with BF16_TC alone; decode was also lower. Larger prompts were not
  tested for this setting.

## AMD: building gfx906 and gfx1012

Setup does not build these; build by hand and run `serve/server.py` with a config, as on any other card.

- **gfx906** (MI50 / MI60 / Radeon VII, wave64): a separate opt-in build, `-DSTRATA_HIP_GFX906=ON
  -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx906` (not `STRATA_ENABLE_HIP`). Current ROCm no longer ships gfx906 libraries; the
  reporter used a community ROCm 7.14 image. Recipe, kernels and measurements: [AMD_HIP.md](AMD_HIP.md#gfx906-instinct-mi50--mi60-radeon-vii-wave64-built-from-source).
- **gfx1012** (RX 5500 XT): the wave32 backend, `-DSTRATA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1012`. HIP 5.7
  (Ubuntu's packages) works: older hipBLAS (0.x) is used through rocBLAS, the legacy HIP names and the missing
  `__syncwarp` are version-gated, and RDNA1's missing signed dot4 uses llama.cpp's SDWA sequence
  (`-DSTRATA_GFX1012_PORTABLE_DOT=ON`: the portable one).

## Reports welcome

These paths stay experimental until more people run them. A report with the card, the driver / ROCm version, the
model and the engine log (`strata-<model>.log`) in an issue helps; [COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md](COMMUNITY_BENCHMARKS.md)
has the format for measurements.


## docs/ORCA.md

# OrcaRouter IQ3_XXS compatibility

Validated on Linux with an RTX 5090 (32 GB), Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 128 GB RAM on 2026-09-27.

The target is `orcarouter/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-GGUF`, **IQ3_XXS** (two shards, 85.20 GB total).
It has Strata's Qwen4Exp geometry, but ordinary quantization also compresses the hyperconnection,
small attention and PLE projections which Strata's kernels read as BF16.

`tools/iq_pack.py --compat-bf16` expands only those projections, rounding to BF16 using nearest-even.
This adds rounding relative to the GGUF's dequantized weights; it does not recover the original BF16
checkpoint or its quality. Expert weights, native attention weights, embeddings and the 28.8 GB PLE
lookup table remain unchanged. The latter stays on disk. The pack records its conversions in
`compat-bf16.json`.

The native loader retains this pack's converted PLE key. Its existing native Q2_0 key path remains
available to the original model. Hugging Face snapshot symlinks are supported; all split shards must
finish downloading before packing. Pass the snapshot filename, not its hash-named blob target.

## Preparation

Build Strata normally using the pinned llama.cpp dependency. Python needs numpy, regex and gguf-py
from that dependency (`STRATA_GGUF_PY` can point to its `gguf-py` directory).

```sh
.venv/bin/python tools/iq_pack.py \
  --gguf /path/to/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-IQ3_XXS-00001-of-00002.gguf \
  --out packs/orca-iq3_xxs --compat-bf16
```

Use this model's own tokenizer exported into the pack. Do not share another model's `dense.bin`,
and do not rename the Orca files to impersonate one of setup's GSQ-RCO models.

Strata's persistent server also uses the MTP runtime (optional: without `--mtp` it drafts by lookup only), prepared by
the existing tools:

```sh
.venv/bin/python tools/mtp_fetch.py fetch --out mtp
.venv/bin/python tools/mtp_pack.py --src mtp --experts q2_0 --out mtp/mtp-q2_0.gguf
.venv/bin/python tools/mtp_rt.py --gguf mtp/mtp-q2_0.gguf --out mtp/rt
cp data/draft_vocab.bin mtp/rt/draft_vocab.bin
```

This uses the original model's draft head, as setup does for Swift. The target model verifies its
proposals; draft acceptance and performance must be measured for this fine-tune.

## Local server

Save the following as `strata-orca-iq3_xxs.json` at the repository root, replacing both `/path/to/`
entries with the **same first shard**. Orca's PLE table is in shard 1. Start with a 32K context and
512-token prefill chunks; the expert cache sizes itself to available VRAM. The expert arena alone
needs about 49.8 GiB of available system RAM, plus draft/runtime buffers and other applications.

```json
{
  "exe": "build/strata",
  "args": [
    "--pack", "packs/orca-iq3_xxs",
    "--native", "/path/to/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-IQ3_XXS-00001-of-00002.gguf",
    "--ple-gguf", "/path/to/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-IQ3_XXS-00001-of-00002.gguf",
    "--expert-profile", "data/expert-profile.bin", "--expert-cache", "auto",
    "--prefill", "512", "--spec", "4", "--spec-min-p", "0.5",
    "--mtp", "mtp/rt", "--max-context", "32768", "--kv", "int8"
  ],
  "cwd": ".",
  "tokenizer": "packs/orca-iq3_xxs/tokenizer",
  "model_name": "orcarouter-qwen3.8-flash-next-uncensored-iq3_xxs",
  "log": "strata-orca-iq3_xxs.log",
  "host": "127.0.0.1",
  "port": 8080
}
```

Run from the repository root:

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m serve.server --engine strata --config strata-orca-iq3_xxs.json --port 8080
```

The web interface is at `http://127.0.0.1:8080`; API clients use `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`.
Vision is not configured in this text-only example. Performance of the original GSQ-RCO model
does not establish this fine-tune's speed or accuracy.

## Scope and validation

- IQ3_XXS is the target of this change; other Orca quantizations are not validated.
- IQ3_M additionally uses Q5_0 expert down matrices, which the native GPU expert path does not support.
- The installer model menu is unchanged. This is an explicit local packing workflow.
- Focused conversion and split-file tests: `.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tools -p test_iq_pack.py`.
- All eight packing tests, 17 server tests and the GPU gated-residual parity check passed.
- The complete model packed successfully: 460 tensors converted, 1.39 GiB of converted BF16 weights;
  1.43 GiB total packed dense weights. The 48 expert layers remain IQ3_XXS gate/up and IQ4_NL down.
- Real server checks passed: arithmetic, Python code, translation, a longer explanation, multi-turn context
  reuse (25 prompt tokens reused), streaming cancellation and a subsequent correct response. The engine
  PID stayed unchanged. These are smoke tests, not a quality benchmark or a full-context stress test.
- With the configuration above, a 111-token explanation generated at 77.7 tokens/s (engine decode timing);
  total request time was 1.77 seconds. This single short measurement is not a general throughput claim.


## docs/ORCA_Q4_K_S.md

# OrcaRouter Uncensored Q4_K_S (manual setup)

This path uses the three original `orcarouter/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-GGUF` Q4_K_S shards without rewriting their expert, embedding or PLE table bytes. It is separate from the installer model menu. Keep all three shard filenames together.

The ordinary GGUF quantizes some small projections which Strata reads as BF16. `--compat-bf16` dequantizes and rounds those projections to BF16 in the separate pack; it does not restore their original precision. The Q5_0 PLE table remains in the source GGUF and currently uses the mapped reader (`--ple-io mmap`). The Q4_K gate/up experts and Q5_0/Q5_1 down experts remain in GGUF form, including layers whose three tensors cross shard boundaries (each role is read from its own shard). The GPU expert kernels take Q4_K with Q5_1 (or Q8_0) downs; Q5_0 downs are not among them yet, and the engine refuses to start on a pack with such a layer (it names the layer).

## Build and prepare

Build Strata with CUDA, native experts, `STRATA_ORCA_Q4KS_MMQ=ON` (and `STRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON` for the two parity programs below). This opt-in compiles the Q5_0 GGML MMQ instance for CUDA or HIP (the Q4_K and Q5_1 instances come with the engine's K-quant MMQ build on CUDA); the usual Q8_0 draft-layer instance remains in both builds. HIP also needs `STRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON`. Select your card's compute capability, for example `89` on an L40S. On Windows with Ninja and CUDA 12.6, use the Visual Studio developer environment and `-DCMAKE_CUDA_RUNTIME_LIBRARY=Shared` to keep the CUDA runtime linkage consistent. The default pinned ggml checkout is supported by the project build.

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DSTRATA_NATIVE_EXPERTS=ON -DSTRATA_ORCA_Q4KS_MMQ=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89 -DCMAKE_CUDA_RUNTIME_LIBRARY=Shared -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --target strata native_expert_parity ple_q5_parity
python tools/iq_pack.py --gguf /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-Q4_K_S-00001-of-00003.gguf --out packs/orca-q4_k_s --compat-bf16
```

`iq_pack.py` needs NumPy and the `gguf-py` module from the pinned llama.cpp dependency (`STRATA_GGUF_PY` can point to that directory). It writes a roughly 1.43 GiB dense pack and a native-expert manifest. The original 112 GB of model shards are read in place; `experts.bin` is optional and is not written by this command.

Check the changed kernels against the real files before starting the service:

```sh
build/native_expert_parity /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-Q4_K_S-00001-of-00003.gguf /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-Q4_K_S-00002-of-00003.gguf /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-Q4_K_S-00003-of-00003.gguf 0 5 6 20 47
build/ple_q5_parity /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-Q4_K_S-00001-of-00003.gguf
```

## Engine flags

Pass the same first shard to `--native` and `--ple-gguf`; Strata discovers the other two shards by name. For a first text-only run, use 32K context and a modest cache. Once that passes, increase the context and cache with memory measurements on the target machine.

```sh
--pack packs/orca-q4_k_s --native /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-Q4_K_S-00001-of-00003.gguf --ple-gguf /models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored-Q4_K_S-00001-of-00003.gguf --ple-io mmap --expert-profile data/expert-profile.bin --expert-cache auto --prefill 512 --spec 4 --mtp /path/to/mtp/rt --max-context 32768 --kv int8
```

For two GPUs in persistent server mode, add `--layer-split auto --split-device 1` (with CUDA0 and CUDA1 visible). The usual Strata MTP runtime is built from the original model's draft layer; draft acceptance on the Uncensored fine-tune must be measured. Keep this model's own tokenizer from the pack. `--expert-cache-per-layer` on a native pack gives every layer the same number of slots, each the size of that layer's own blob. `--expert-cache N` is still the budget of N largest blobs.

This port does not claim that Q4_K_S beats llama.cpp on a given computer. Compare the same model bytes, prompt, context, output length and GPU load; report prefill and decode separately.


## docs/PREFILL_HEAD_ALIAS.md

# Lend the output head's VRAM to the prompt path (`--prefill-head-alias`, opt-in)

Two large VRAM users never work at the same time. The native output head (417 MiB for the Q5_K head of
IQ3_XXS) turns the last hidden state into logits, so it is needed only while tokens are generated. The batched prompt
path's buffers are needed only while a prompt is read. With `--prefill-head-alias` the engine takes turns: the head's
VRAM holds prompt buffers while a prompt is read, and the head is read back in before the first generated token.

The flag is off by default. With it off, the engine does exactly what it did before.

## Why

On an 8 GB card the prompt chunk is as large as the free VRAM allows, and prefill speed follows the chunk closely. Here
is the same 29,854-token prompt with a fresh engine per trial and one request each. The card and settings are listed
under [Measurements](#measurements).

| Prompt chunk | Trials | Prefill, median (range) | How the engine got there | Free VRAM after start |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 256 | 4 | 185.5 (177.8-195.9) tok/s | `--prefill auto`, reserve 686-745 MiB | 383-443 MiB |
| 512 | 12 | 292.5 (281.0-306.1) tok/s | `--prefill auto`, reserve 442-667 MiB (590 is our tuned value) | 137-365 MiB |
| 768 | 7 | 387.4 (375.8-397.2) tok/s | `--prefill auto`, reserve 331-405 MiB | 27-103 MiB |
| 1,024 | 4 | 442.9 (440.8-444.1) tok/s | `--prefill auto`, reserve 239-295 MiB | 0 MiB |
| 1,280 | 5 | 514.5 (512.8-517.3) tok/s | `--prefill auto`, reserve 147-221 MiB | 0 MiB |
| 1,536 | 2 | 573.6 (571.0-576.3) tok/s | `--prefill auto`, reserve 73-110 MiB | 0 MiB |
| 1,792 | 3 | 631.4 (628.7-632.9) tok/s | `--prefill auto`, reserve 0-36 MiB | 0 MiB |
| **2,048** | **6** | **667.1 (661.5-667.7) tok/s** | **`--prefill-head-alias`, reserve 590 MiB** | **289 MiB** |

Without the flag, every chunk above 768 tokens came only from lowering `--vram-reserve-mib`, and that left 0 MiB free.
Under WDDM that is the state in which Windows starts paging. With the flag, the 2,048-token chunk came with the 590 MiB
reserve unchanged.

## What it does

1. **At start**, after the MTP draft layer has copied its draft-head rows from the output head, the head is unloaded.
   The auto expert cache is then sized with the head's VRAM counted as free (on our card: 749 slots instead of 508).
   The prompt path borrows cache slots 1 to N (slot 0 stays). Whatever does not fit there is allocated by the prompt
   path itself, which makes a "hybrid" layout. The chunk is the largest of 2,048, 1,536, 1,024 and 512 tokens whose
   buffers fit in the borrowed slots plus free VRAM with 512 MiB to spare.
2. **For each request**:
   1. If the head is loaded, unload it and lay the prompt path out again (median 20 ms).
   2. Read the prompt.
   3. Refill the lent slots and free the prompt path's own buffers.
   4. Load the head again (median 255 ms) before the first decode window.
3. **Graph safety.** The verify windows' CUDA graphs are captured during the first decode and hold the head's address.
   If a later reload puts the head at a different address, the engine stops with an error, and the server starts it
   again. It does not run graphs that point at freed memory. We never saw this happen; see
   [Open questions](#open-questions).

The engine refuses the flag, with the reason, without `--serve`, with more than one GPU or a layer split, with
`--batch`, with `--pipeline-windows`, with `--short-read` above 0, with a fixed `--expert-cache` above 1, without `--mtp`,
or without the native output head.

## Costs

- **Short reads get slower.** Each request reloads the head (median 255 ms over 2,717 restores, p90 261 ms, max
  495 ms) and rebuilds the prompt path (20 ms). It also lends and then refills almost the whole cache, even for a few
  tokens. The engine's own prompt time, which includes all of this, by fresh tokens read (production, medians):

  | Fresh tokens read | Default | Head alias |
  |---:|---:|---:|
  | 1-64 | 671 ms (293 requests) | 1,311 ms (614) |
  | 65-512 | 1,703 ms (409) | 2,453 ms (955) |
  | 513-2,048 | 4,062 ms (278) | 3,331 ms (618) |
  | 2,049-8,192 | 15,206 ms (118) | 6,876 ms (277) |

  So the flag costs about 0.6-0.75 s on reads of up to 512 tokens and pays off from somewhere between 513 and 2,048
  tokens. In the agent loop, 614 of 2,717 requests read 64 fresh tokens or fewer.
- **Less free VRAM while decoding.** In the default run, the verify windows were captured with 207-287 MiB free. With
  the flag, they were captured with 0 MiB free. Over 2,717 requests (about 26 hours) we saw no paging symptoms: decode
  held about 29 tok/s from the first request to the last (table below). This is the main risk on other cards and
  drivers.
- **More slots to refill after each prompt.** The prompt path borrows almost the whole cache (748 of 749 slots instead
  of 328 of 508), so more experts are copied back after each prompt. That time is counted in the prompt time above.

## Measurements

Card and settings for every number on this page:

- NVIDIA RTX PRO 2000 Blackwell Laptop GPU, 8,151 MiB, Windows 11 Pro (WDDM, driver 597.16), CUDA 13.0, sm_120.
- Intel Core Ultra 9 285H (AVX2), 64 GiB RAM, PCIe probe 25 GB/s (`pcie_frac` 0.55 picked by auto).
- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_XXS native pack, `--max-context 262144`, `--kv q4_0`, `--kv-resident 32768`, `--spec 4`,
  `--spec-min-p 0.5`, MTP with the English draft vocabulary, `--prompt-cache 3`, `--vram-reserve-mib 590`,
  `--expert-cache auto`, `--prefill auto`.
- The engine was a local 0.1.41 build with this change. Both sides also used a local `STRATA_ARENA_REGISTER=0` switch
  that is not part of this change: it skips `cudaHostRegister` of the 40 GiB arena on this machine.

### Controlled: one prompt, one forced output

Each trial ran a fresh engine on the 29,854-token prompt. The same 3,072-token continuation was forced one verify row per
token, with no speculative drafts, so the decode numbers compare the same work. A local benchmark switch did the forcing;
it is not part of this change.

| Setting | Trials | Expert slots | Prompt chunk | Prefill | Decode | Expert-cache hits |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1-slot cache | 4 | 1 | 1,024 (own buffers) | 441.0 tok/s | 22.26 tok/s | 0.2% |
| 1-slot cache + head alias | 2 | 1 | 2,048 | 666.3 tok/s | 24.50 tok/s | 0.2% |
| auto cache + head alias | 3 | 749 | 2,048 | 667.7 tok/s | 26.21 tok/s | 24.9% |

We did not run the default (auto cache, no head alias) in this forced mode. Its free-running result on the same prompt
is the 512-token row of the first table: one trial at the 590 MiB reserve read 306.1 tok/s and decoded 27.9 tok/s, and
six head-alias trials decoded 26.6-29.0 tok/s (median 27.9). Free-running outputs differ from trial to trial, so their
decode rates are only a rough comparison.

### Production: an agent loop

The workload was OpenCode agents (worker, reviewer and retrospective) running a coding loop against `/v1/chat/completions`.
Prompts went up to about 150K tokens, with `--prompt-cache 3` prefix reuse.

- Default: 1,200 requests over 8 loop cycles.
- `--prefill-head-alias`: 2,649 requests over 20 cycles.

The flag also needs `--short-read 0`; the default run had 64. Everything else was the same. Rates come from the engine's
own lines (`reading the prompt` progress over at least 5 s, and the decode rate of requests with at least 32 output
tokens). They are compared inside 16K-token context bands, so a heavier or lighter mix of prompts on either side does not
count as a speed change. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals.

| | Default | Head alias | Change within context bands |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Prefill, median | 256 tok/s | 583 tok/s | +125% (+123% to +129%) |
| Decode, median | 24.8 tok/s | 29.2 tok/s | +19% (+17% to +23%) |
| Expert-cache hits, median | 20.8% | 25.9% | 508 -> 749 slots |

The decode difference needs care. The default runs alternated between long stretches near 27.5 tok/s and long stretches
near 19.5 tok/s. A rolling median over 51 requests showed plateaus of hundreds of requests each, and in one run the
switch from slow to fast came with no engine restart. In the head-alias run, each twelfth of the 2,649 requests had a
median decode of 28.7-29.8 tok/s. Against the default's
fast stretches only, decode was about 6% faster. We do not know what caused the slow stretches, so we do not claim that
this change removes them.

The engine binary was also rebuilt between the two runs, to add prompt-cache support to this change. The controlled
table above is the comparison that holds the binary fixed.

## Port check on 0.1.43.1

This change was moved to upstream main (0.1.43.1) and checked on the same PC. Both runs used the same build, a fresh
engine each, and `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB=auto`: without it, the full sliced arena pin on this 64 GB PC left WDDM with
0 GiB free for the cache (#243). The requests were the 29,842-token prompt cold, then a 31-token follow-up on its
prefix, two 45-token prompts, and the long prompt again. Output was capped at 768 tokens with low reasoning, and
generation was free (not forced).

| | Default | Head alias |
|---|---:|---:|
| Expert slots, prompt chunk | 507, 512 | 753, 2,048 |
| Free VRAM when the verify windows were captured | 207-245 MiB | 0 MiB |
| Cold 29,842-token prompt, two runs | 276.5, 277.1 tok/s | 643.1, 649.7 tok/s |
| Decode on those two | 35.7, 34.7 tok/s | 34.1, 31.6 tok/s |
| 31-token follow-up (29,837 reused), prompt time | 632 ms | 1,721 ms |
| 45-46-token prompts, prompt time | 871, 1,005 ms | 1,780, 1,424 ms |

All five requests completed with coherent answers. The head came back at the same address every time, so the guard
never fired. 0.1.43.1's new start-of-request warning ("below 1024 MiB free") appears with both settings, at 289 MiB
for the default and 0 MiB with the flag.

## Open questions

- **A fixed address for the head.** The head goes back with `cudaMalloc`, which does not promise the same address. The
  check above makes a moved head a clean engine restart. A cleaner design would keep the head's virtual range and swap
  its backing (CUDA VMM), or lay prompt buffers directly into the head's allocation instead of freeing it.
- **Skip the swap for short reads.** A request that reads a few dozen fresh tokens pays about 0.6 s (table above) for a
  2,048-token chunk it does not need. A threshold on fresh tokens, below which the head stays and the read goes through
  the decode windows as `--short-read` does, would remove that cost.
- **Other cards.** We measured only the 8 GB card above, on Windows. A larger card already gets a large chunk without
  the flag, so we expect the gain to be smaller there.

## Not tested

- This change on upstream main (0.1.43.1) was compiled for CUDA (13.0, sm_120, MSVC, Windows) and checked with the
  short run above. The longer measurements come from the 0.1.41 build.
- HIP (the same sources) and SYCL. On SYCL, `Prefill::init` refuses the hybrid layout; the SYCL engine has no flag
  for it.
- Linux, multi-GPU, `--batch` and `--pipeline-windows` (all refused), and models other than Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ3_XXS.


## docs/PROMPT_CACHE_TAIL.md

# Optional checkpoint near the prompt tail

`--prompt-cache-tail` saves at most one extra mid-prompt checkpoint near the end
of a request, at a boundary the batched prefill already reaches. It is off by
default and applies to single-GPU serve with positive `--prompt-cache` and
`--prompt-cache-every` values.

A branch can share most of a prompt but diverge before its final cached state.
If the periodic checkpoint before that branch is far away, the engine has to
read the gap again. The extra checkpoint can reduce that gap. It uses the
existing bounded checkpoint cache; it does not add another unbounded history.

The tail is the first chunk boundary within one chunk of the prompt's end, where the chunk is the size that chunk
really had (`--prefill auto` chunks differ from `--prefill N`). The tail checkpoint is evicted first (only one stays
alive, the root is never dropped), so it never pushes out a periodic checkpoint when `--prompt-cache` is full.

The option does not split prefill chunks or alter the periodic checkpoint
schedule. It selects the first completed batched chunk within one configured
chunk of the prompt's end, excluding the short final suffix controlled by
`--short-read`. If a periodic checkpoint already falls there, the same state is
saved once. Reread diagnostics and layer splits keep their existing behavior.

For example, with a 6144-token chunk and a 16384-token checkpoint interval,
the first periodic checkpoint is at 18432 and the next would be at 36864.
A branch sharing 32769 tokens cannot use the latter. A near-tail checkpoint
at 30720 can reuse more of that prefix,
without changing how the original prompt was computed. The benefit depends
on the request and the branch position; it is not a universal speed increase.

This is a separate conservative alternative to the Strata-2080Ti Daily's
checkpoint-grid patch. The grid changes chunk boundaries to reach exact
checkpoint intervals and failed its local paired numerical gate. This option
does not claim that the original grid patch has been fixed or validated.


## docs/QSAROWS.md

# QSA_ROWS: the decode window's QSA block scores with the queries in registers (`STRATA_QSA_ROWS=1`, opt-in)

Opt-in: `STRATA_QSA_ROWS=1` (exactly `1`). Unset the engine runs the kernels it ran before. CUDA, the verify window's
decode (calls of `qsa_block_scores` without `active_blocks` and with up to 4 queries); the prompt path and HIP are not
touched. Scores and top-k ids are bitwise the multi kernel's (`qsa_rows_bench --rows` checks it).

## Why

In a 131k decode the QSA kernel that grows most with the window's rows is `block_scores_multi_kernel`: about 20 us more
per call for every row of the window on an RTX 2080 Ti and an RTX 3060 (nsys; 8 QSA layers on the second card of a
layer split, 4 on the first). The keys are already read once for all the queries; the cost per row is in the shared
memory and shuffle pipes: per (key block, query) the kernel reads the four query slices from shared memory (4 x
`LDS.128`) and reduces each head's lane products with its own five shuffles (20 per block and query): at 32 769 blocks
that is 15-20 us of issue per query.

## What it changes

`block_scores_rows_kernel<NQ>` (`src/kernels/cuda/qsa_select.cu`, NQ = 1..4):

1. the NQ queries' slices (4 heads x 4 floats per lane) stay in registers for the whole kernel (44 / 63 / 78 / 94
   registers, no stack, `cuobjdump -res-usage`);
2. the lane products of the 4 heads are reduced with a scatter that keeps `warp_sum`'s pairings: xor 16 and 8 leave
   one head per lane, then 4, 2, 1 - six shuffles for the four heads instead of twenty - and gathered on lane 0 in head
   order (three shuffles).

Every addition adds the same two operands of the same `warp_sum` level (float addition commutes), the product
expression is the same text in the same file, the relus are summed in head order: the same bits as the multi kernel
and the per-query kernel. Tail block and the `+1e9` as before. Beyond 4 queries, with `active_blocks`, or without the
variable, the multi kernel runs.

## Micro-bench: `qsa_rows_bench`

Not in the default build: `cmake --build <dir> --target qsa_rows_bench`. Synthetic data at the real geometry (24 query
heads x 256, 2 KV heads, indexer 4 x 128, blocks of 4 cells, top-k 2048), int8 pools, no model.

```
qsa_rows_bench [--device N] [--iters 100] [--ctx 131072] [--max-context 262144] [--rows] [--no-dense]
```

Without `--rows` it measures what the T rows of a verification window cost in a QSA layer's decode kernels (block
scores, top-k, attention over each row's selection, indexer append; `--no-dense` skips the drafter's 32768-cell window).
`--rows` runs `block_scores_rows_kernel` against the multi kernel - scores and top-k ids bit for bit (memcmp) at T =
1..4 at 131k and at a short context (cells 100-103, a full tail block), 16 cases per card - and prints both kernels'
microseconds. Exit 0 (77: no GPU; 1: a parity failure).

`qsa_block_scores`, us per call, 131k context (both kernels read the same pooled keys):

| | T=1 | T=2 | T=3 | T=4 | per row |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RTX 2080 Ti, multi (reference) | 47.2 | 56.9 | 78.2 | 101.2 | +18.0 |
| RTX 2080 Ti, `STRATA_QSA_ROWS=1` | 36.2 | 38.0 | 49.2 | 54.6 | +6.1 |
| RTX 3060, multi | 73.4 | 109.4 | 151.9 | 193.5 | +40.0 |
| RTX 3060, `STRATA_QSA_ROWS=1` | 63.3 | 75.5 | 98.0 | 130.2 | +22.3 |

Parity: 8 cases per card, 0 differ. On the RTX 3060 at T=4 the
kernel is at 94 registers (2 CTAs per SM); a two-pass version of 2 queries would stay at 63 if that card matters.

## In the engine

Layer split RTX 3060 (layers 0-15) + RTX 2080 Ti (layers 16-47, head), Windows, `--pipeline-windows 2`, 131k context:
per window the second card saves -0.09 ms at T=1 and -0.37 ms at T=4 (8 QSA layers), the first -0.04 / -0.25 (4
layers). End to end on a deterministic 131k bench (forced tokens and window sizes, 1024 tokens, B-A-B): **+3.2% and
+0.1%** decode tokens/s in the two B arms, the text identical.

## Not done

A multi-row attention kernel (K/V of a cell read once for all the rows that selected it) is possible bit for bit only
if every row keeps its own chunk partition; at the decode window's sizes (cap 2051 cells, T <= 4) the blocks of all rows
fit in one wave and the kernel is bound by its block's latency chain, so the gain is bounded by ~0.1-0.2 ms per row on
8 layers: not worth it here. `STRATA_QSA_ROWS` turns on the scores kernel only.


## docs/QUANTS.md

# Unsloth's K-quants and Q8_0: formats, kernels and quality

This page covers Unsloth's files of the model ([unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF),
revision `38bb39e`; the repository's head `766911a` has the same files, byte for byte): what each file stores in
each layer, which of Strata's kernels run those formats on each kind of hardware, and how close each file comes to
the Q8_0 reference. Setup and the per-file details: [UD-Q4_K_XL](UNSLOTH_Q4.md), [UD-Q6_K_XL](UNSLOTH_Q6.md),
[MODELS.md](MODELS.md).

## What each file stores

Read from the GGUF headers alone with `tools/quant_formats.py --hf unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF 38bb39ee... <dir>`
(HTTP range requests, nothing else is downloaded; on local shards: `tools/quant_formats.py <shard glob>`).

The routed experts (gate, up, down; 512 per layer, 10 used per token) are where the files differ:

| File | Download | Routed gate / up | Routed down | Routed experts | Per token (10 experts x 48 layers) |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| UD-IQ4_XS | 93.7 GB | IQ3_S (IQ4_XS in layer 2) | IQ4_NL (Q8_0 in layers 2, 4, 30, 46, 47) | 55.4 GiB | 1.16 GB |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | 111.3 GB | Q4_K (Q5_K in layer 2) | Q5_1 (Q8_0 in layers 2, 4, 30, 46, 47) | 71.7 GiB | 1.50 GB |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | 158.3 GB | Q5_K (Q6_K in layer 2) | Q8_0 | 91.6 GiB | 1.92 GB |
| UD-Q6_K_XL | 169.2 GB | Q6_K (Q8_0 in layer 2) | Q8_0 | 101.7 GiB | 2.13 GB |
| Q8_0 | 188.2 GB | Q8_0 | Q8_0 | 119.5 GiB | 2.51 GB |

Everything else is the same in all five: the attention, SSM, hyper-connection and shared-expert projections, the
PLE key/value and the token embedding are Q8_0 (the small vectors, norms and the router F32; the QSA indexer BF16),
the output head is Q8_0 (Q6_K in UD-IQ4_XS). The PLE table (`per_layer_token_embd`) is IQ4_NL (26.8 GiB) in UD-IQ4_XS
and UD-Q4_K_XL and Q8_0 (50.7 GiB) in UD-Q5_K_XL, UD-Q6_K_XL and Q8_0. The dense side the GPU reads once per verify
window is about 4.8 GB in every file.

UD-Q5_K_XL, UD-Q6_K_XL and Q8_0 share their shards 2 (the output head) and 3 (the PLE table) byte for byte (the same
SHA-256), so a PC that has one of them can link those two shards instead of downloading them again.

## Kernels per format and backend

| Format (role) | CUDA decode (grouped experts) | CUDA prompt | CPU pool | AMD (HIP) decode | AMD prompt | Intel (SYCL) decode | Intel prompt |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q4_K (gate/up) | yes | FP16 path; MMQ with `STRATA_MMQ_KQ=1` | ggml AVX2 dot; multi-token AVX2 (`STRATA_KQ256=1`) | yes (CUDA layout; `STRATA_EXPERT_V2K=1` bitwise) | FP16 path; MMQ with `STRATA_MMQ_KQ=1`; gfx11 fused (`STRATA_PF_FUSED_KQ=1`) | kernels built, not run with these files | FP16 path |
| Q5_K (gate/up) | yes | as Q4_K | ggml AVX2 dot | as Q4_K | as Q4_K | kernels built, not run with these files | FP16 path |
| Q6_K (gate/up) | yes (since this change; was `-DSTRATA_Q6K_EXPERTS=ON`) | FP16 path; MMQ with `STRATA_MMQ_KQ=1` | ggml AVX2 dot | yes (CUDA layout) | FP16 path; MMQ with `STRATA_MMQ_KQ=1` | kernels built, not run with these files | FP16 path |
| Q5_1 (down) | yes | as Q4_K | ggml AVX2 dot; multi-token AVX2 (`STRATA_KQ256=1`) | yes (CUDA layout; V2K) | as Q4_K | kernels built, not run with these files | FP16 path |
| Q8_0 (gate/up, down) | yes | MMQ | ggml AVX2 dot; multi-token AVX2 down (`STRATA_KQ256=1`) | yes (CUDA layout; V2K down) | MMQ | kernels built, not run with these files | FP16 path |

- "FP16 path": the prompt's experts dequantized to FP16 and multiplied by the BLAS library. It works for every format
  above but reads each expert as ~10 MB of FP16.
- **Formats cost nothing unless used.** The engine loads every kernel of its own binary when it starts (so that no
  kernel needs VRAM later, mid-prompt), which is why kernels for formats a model does not have used to take expert
  slots from every model. The Q6_K expert kernels are now part of every build: one more instance per grouped kernel,
  +19 KB of sm_60 code, and the expert-cache slot counts measured unchanged (IQ3_XXS: 6,028 slots on a P100, 15,878
  and 1,980 on an R9700). The K-quant MMQ prompt kernels (Q4_K, Q5_K, Q5_1, Q6_K: ~3.8 MB of sm_60 code, 3 IQ3_XXS
  slots on the P100 when they were in the engine) are on CUDA a library of their own next to the engine
  (`libstrata_kq.so` / `strata_kq.dll`), opened only for a model with these experts and `STRATA_MMQ_KQ=1`; without the
  file those experts take the FP16 prompt path. On AMD a code object loads on first use, so they stay in the engine.
- `STRATA_MMQ_KQ=1` is opt-in because MMQ rounds the prompt's products differently from the FP16 path (the output
  differs at the rounding level); its speed and KL are measured before it becomes a default.

## Quality: the yardstick

`tools/quant_quality.py` scores a quant against Q8_0 on one fixed text set (`data/quant_quality/v1`: code, docs,
English prose, German/French/Japanese/Chinese, an agent transcript; 5 x 1,000 tokens in `set.ids.json`). Every token
is read through the decode windows (teacher-forced) with the experts on the CPU (one VRAM slot), no expert
adaptation, no PCIe share, no route tail skip, FP16 K/V; per position the engine writes the log-probability of the
text's next token and its 64 most likely tokens (`STRATA_LOGPOS`, `STRATA_LOGPOS_TOPK=64`). Top-1 agreement: the
same most likely token as Q8_0. KL: KL(Q8_0 || quant) over Q8_0's 64 most likely tokens.

```sh
python tools/quant_quality.py run --config strata-<quant>.json --out <quant>.tsv
python tools/quant_quality.py compare q8_0.tsv <quant>.tsv --segments
```

Measured on the AMD box (EPYC 7452, R9700, HIP, engine at 0601072d; 4,995 positions; Q8_0 against itself in a second
run: byte-identical rows):

| Quant | Same top token as Q8_0 | Mean KL | KL p99 | Perplexity (Q8_0: 4.052) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| UD-Q6_K_XL | 94.61% | 0.033 | 0.494 | 4.020 |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | 94.55% | 0.038 | 0.636 | 4.024 |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | 93.09% | 0.056 | 0.829 | 4.068 |
| UD-IQ4_XS | 88.91% | 0.101 | 1.596 | 4.120 |
| IQ3_S | 87.69% | 0.144 | 1.975 | 4.097 |
| IQ3_XXS | 84.46% | 0.202 | 2.433 | 4.119 |
| Q2_0 | 80.60% | 0.315 | 3.643 | 4.475 |

The same file on another backend is not the same answers: UD-Q4_K_XL on an RTX A4000 (CUDA, the RAM
budget mode of a 62 GB PC) against UD-Q4_K_XL on the R9700 is 94.5% the same top token (KL 0.038), mostly near-ties.

**The prompt path:** `tools/quant_quality.py prompt` / `pcompare` score the batched prompt path the same way (20 prompts
of 256-1,000 tokens of the set, the full vocabulary's KL of the next token's distribution against Q8_0's): every
quant above picks Q8_0's top token after all 20 prompts. The K-quants' MMQ kernels (`STRATA_MMQ_KQ=1`) against the FP16
path on the R9700: UD-Q4_K_XL mean KL 0.095 / median 0.0027 (FP16: 0.081 / 0.0047), UD-Q5_K_XL 0.038 / 0.00055 (FP16:
0.025 / 0.0016), UD-Q6_K_XL 0.028 / 0.00029 (FP16: 0.029 / 0.00069) - a better median everywhere, a worse mean on Q4/Q5
(a few prompts), so it stays opt-in.

## Speed, and the bound

Measured on the AMD box: one Radeon AI PRO R9700 (32 GB, capped at 225 W), EPYC 7452 (32 cores, 8 channels of
DDR4-2400: 106 GB/s read by `rdbw` at 32 threads), every expert in RAM (setup's rule below), `--expert-cache auto`,
40K context, 8-bit K/V, MTP drafts; `rbench.py` cases, the second of two requests; prompt speed varies between runs on
this box by up to 2x (the range is given).

| File | Short story (tok/s) | Code (tok/s) | After a 6K document | Prompt 32K (tok/s) | llama.cpp 8bb3cf0d2 (same card, `-ngl 99 --n-cpu-moe 38-48`): decode / prompt 4K |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| IQ3_S (for comparison) | 75 | 95 | 77 | 1,555 | - |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | 63-64 | 85-88 | 70-72 | 1,110-1,320 | 18-20 / 198-257 |
| UD-Q5_K_XL | 57-60 | 81-83 | 62 | 810-1,260 | 17-18 / 226-270 |
| UD-Q6_K_XL | 54 | 76 | 61 | 1,020 | - |
| Q8_0 | 53-57 | 66-74 | 54-55 | 1,230-1,300 | 16-18 / 186-225 |

**Where a decode window goes** (`STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1 STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1`, UD-Q4_K_XL, the short story, 2.0
tokens per window, 34.3 ms per window): the bandwidth bound of what a window must read is ~12.5 ms - the routed
experts in VRAM (~2.7 GB at 644 GB/s: 4.2 ms bound, 6.0 measured), the dense Q8_0 projections (2.84 GB: 4.4 ms bound,
7.2 measured), the hyper-connections (0.67 GB: 1.0 ms bound, 4.0 measured), router and shared expert (0.5 GB: 0.8 ms
bound, 3.7 measured), the head (1.05 bound, 1.26 measured), the CPU pool's experts at RAM bandwidth in parallel
(1.2 ms), plus the MTP draft (5.8 ms measured). Decode runs at ~35-40% of that bound for every file, IQ3_S included:
the formats' own kernels are near their bandwidth (VRAM-resident experts ~70%, the CPU pool 84-97% of RAM bandwidth,
the head 83%); the rest is the per-window latency of the small kernels and the draft, the same for every model.

The CPU pool's expert rows (`kq_cpu_bench`, the engine's own calls on T threads over 4 GB of experts):

| Pair | EPYC 7452, 32 threads, 1 token per expert | 3 tokens | Ryzen 5600X, 6 threads, 1 token | 3 tokens | Xeon E5-2643 v3, 12 threads, 1 token | 3 tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q4_K / Q5_1 | 97% of RAM bandwidth | 80% | 100% | 85% | 94% | 36% |
| Q5_K / Q8_0 | 97% | 89% | 100% | 95% | 98% | 47% |
| Q6_K / Q8_0 | 97% | 93% | 100% | 100% | 99% | 63% |
| Q8_0 / Q8_0 | 96% | 90% | 100% | 100% | 99% | 64% |

One token per expert (most of decode) is at the RAM bound on all three; older CPUs fall behind with several tokens per
expert (ggml's dot decodes the weights once per token; `STRATA_KQ256=1`, bit-exact, takes 11-20% off Q4_K at 3-4
tokens).

**Dense Q8_0 GEMVs** (`q8_gemv_bench`, the engine's shapes, 2-4 columns): one row per block where it was measured
faster, the same bits as two (R9700: 2560 -> 10240 / 6144 / 12288 at 76-86% of 644 GB/s instead of 51-80%; RTX A4000:
+1-4%, and 6144 -> 2560 at 6 columns 70% -> 76%). UD-Q4_K_XL decode +1.0-2.7% on the R9700, the same text.

**NVIDIA with the RAM budget** (RTX A4000 16 GB, Xeon E5-2643 v3, 62 GB: UD-Q4_K_XL with 39 GiB of its experts in RAM,
the rest read from an NVMe SSD at 2.1 GB/s): 14-20 tokens/s and a 4K prompt at 134-144 tokens/s, bound by the SSD;
llama.cpp on the same PC and file 14.8-16.5 / 117-123. `STRATA_PROMPT_DIRECT=1` (Linux, opt-in) reads the prompt
path's experts unbuffered while decode keeps the file cache: the same output (6 of 6 prompts identical with fixed
flags), the 4K prompt 152 -> 315 tokens/s, a 20K prompt 217 -> 500, decode +2-15% (5 interleaved pairs, page cache
dropped before each run). On a second PC with more file-cache room (the R9700 box held to 64 GB) it was mixed: a 6K
document's prompt +8%, a 4K prompt -15% and the answer after the document -38%, because the buffered reads had left
the document's experts in the file cache. So it stays opt-in. Reading everything unbuffered (`STRATA_UNBUFFERED_LOAD=1`) doubled the prompt too but cost
decode 9-13%; a larger or smaller RAM budget, more fetch threads, a deeper read-ahead or a wider look-ahead did not
help.

**Several cards** (R9700 box, every expert in RAM, layer split, 2 runs each): UD-Q4_K_XL on 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 cards writes
63 / 64 / 55 / 52 tokens/s on the short story and 88 / 96 / 123 / 96 on code, and reads a 32K prompt at 1,110 /
1,275 / 1,987 / 2,381 tokens/s; UD-Q5_K_XL 57 / 60 / 62 / 46 and 83 / 94 / 101 / 89, prompt 1,264 / 1,177 / 1,767 /
2,067. llama.cpp on 3 / 4 cards: 24.5 / 28.2 tokens/s and 497 / 800 (4K prompt) for UD-Q4_K_XL. More cards read
prompts faster; for short answers the split's per-stage cost outweighs the experts it keeps in VRAM, since one card with
every expert in RAM is already fast (`--pipeline-windows 0` helps short answers at 3-4 cards, x1.3, and costs code
6-20%).

**Every expert in RAM against the old RAM budget** (setup's new rule, R9700 box, UD-Q4_K_XL, 5 interleaved pairs, the
old config's `--resident-budget-gib 71` holding the same experts read from the GGUF in place): decode x1.34-1.40 (short
story 39.5 -> 53.3 tok/s, code 60.1 -> 80.4, after a 6K document 49.0 -> 68.8, 5/5 each), prompt 4K x2.07, 6K x1.58,
32K x1.03.

**The route tail skip** (`STRATA_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP=7`, the default since 0.1.42: a missed expert every token of a window
routes at rank 7 or lower is skipped) costs these files more than the 2-3-bit packs: UD-Q4_K_XL's yardstick KL against
Q8_0 goes from 0.056 to 0.086 with every expert in RAM (R9700, the auto cache) and from 0.053 to 0.115 in the RAM
budget mode (A4000, 1,500 GPU slots), for +4-10% decode in RAM and +26-67% in the budget mode (5 pairs each).
`STRATA_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP=0` in a config's `"env"` turns it off.

**The hyper-connections on NVIDIA:** the pack's `--compat-bf16` copy of the Q8_0 HC projections rounds them to BF16
(and doubles their bytes). `STRATA_HC_Q8=1` reads the file's own Q8_0 instead (on AMD gfx12 it is the default): on the
A4000 UD-Q4_K_XL then comes closer to Q8_0 (yardstick KL 0.0562 -> 0.0526, p99 0.925 -> 0.716) and to the same file on
AMD (KL 0.038 -> 0.033). Opt-in until decided.

## Images

Every Unsloth file reads pictures with the model's own encoder: setup's `mmproj-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-BF16.gguf` (from
ISTA-DASLab's repository) has the same 334 tensors, byte for byte, as Unsloth's `mmproj-BF16.gguf`. Run end to end
with a test picture (a line of text and three coloured shapes), two questions through `/v1/chat/completions`: on an RTX
A4000 with the GPU encoder (UD-Q4_K_XL, IQ3_XXS) and on an R9700 with the CPU encoder (UD-Q4_K_XL, UD-Q5_K_XL,
IQ3_XXS), every answer had the text and the three shapes right, as llama.cpp's `mtmd-cli` did on the same GGUF and
mmproj. The GPU encoder keeps ~1.3 GB of VRAM free (UD-Q4_K_XL on 16 GB: 2,331 expert slots instead of 2,741); the CPU
encoder takes none. Setup turns images on by default for these files on an NVIDIA card of 16 GB or more, and on AMD
(Linux, the CPU encoder) where every expert stays in RAM.


## docs/QWEN36.md

# Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: pictures, several requests at once and speed

Strata runs [Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) (35B mixture of experts, 3B active, 256 experts, top-8) from
[Unsloth's GGUFs with the MTP layer](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MTP-GGUF) (UD-Q4_K_XL, UD-Q6_K_XL, Q8_0) on its own
engine path (`src/qwen35`; `strata` switches to it from the file's architecture). Pick it in the app's model list, in `strata launch` or in setup (`--family qwen36`). Besides text it
reads **pictures** and serves **several requests at once**, the same two options the Flash-Next models have.

Measured on an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 32 GB (HIP, Linux, UD-Q4_K_XL, every expert in VRAM) and on an RTX 3060 12 GB (CUDA, 20 threads,
UD-Q4_K_XL in the hybrid mode: 22-37 of 256 experts per layer in VRAM, the rest on the CPU), llama.cpp 972b5fc on the same files.

## Pictures

The vision encoder is Unsloth's `mmproj-F16.gguf` (0.9 GB, pinned revision, SHA-256 checked by setup): a 27-layer ViT with a 2x2 merger,
the same projector family as the Flash-Next models' (`qwen3vl_merger`; only its output width differs: 2048 here, 2560 there). Strata runs
it with the same helper (`strata-vision`, llama.cpp's `mtmd`), so the encoder choices are the Flash-Next ones
([Images](DETAILS.md#images-vision)). Pictures are on by default, the same rule as for every model on NVIDIA and AMD cards:
the CPU reader under 24 GB of graphics memory (a few seconds per picture, no VRAM), the card's reader from 24 GB (GPU encoder,
~1.2 GB of VRAM at up to 1,024 image tokens; on AMD it is `strata-vision-hip`, with the CPU reader as its fallback).
`--vision yes|no|gpu|cpu` and `--vision-tokens N` work as there; what you ask for is kept, with a note. The Mac engine does
not run this model.

| Encoder | Time per picture (640x400 = 260 tokens / 800x450 = 350 tokens) | VRAM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPU, RTX 3060 | 0.10 s / 0.15 s | 1,179 MiB at up to 1,024 tokens (1,337 MiB at 2,048), CUDA context included |
| CPU, 32 threads (R9700 box) | 0.9 s / 1.1 s | none |
| CPU, 10 threads (3060 box) | 1.6 s / 2.1 s | none |

A picture becomes up to 1,024 tokens of the context (the CPU default is 300). The engine puts the encoder's rows where the prompt has
`<|image_pad|>` tokens and gives every row its 2-D position, interleaved M-RoPE exactly as llama.cpp does for this model (rotary sections
11 / 11 / 10, a picture's rows at (t, h, w) = (p, p + row, p + column), the text after it continuing at p + max(columns, rows)).

**Checked against llama.cpp** (its `mtmd` and its own graph, the encoder on the CPU on both sides, the same prompt ids, the answer
llama.cpp gives fed to both so the logits are compared step by step, 24 steps; the "floor" is llama.cpp's CPU backend against its own
