HIP run, the noise two correct engines have on this model):

| Picture and question | Prompt tokens | First token | Mean KL, llama.cpp HIP vs Strata | Floor (llama.cpp CPU vs HIP) |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 640x400, text in the image | 288 | same | 0.029 | 0.056 |
| 640x400, list the shapes | 294 | same | 0.035 | 0.039 |
| 800x450, text in the image | 378 | same | 0.021 | 0.031 |
| 800x450, describe the shapes | 381 | same | 0.0005 | 0.0019 |
| 1024x1024, the title (1,024 image tokens, read in 3 chunks) | 1,042 | same | 0.0022 | 0.0026 |
| two pictures in one request, the text in each | 655 | differs (a near tie: the floor's KL at this step is 0.16 too) | 0.014 | 0.022 |

The answers are the same text as llama.cpp's: `STRATA 42` (with llama.cpp's own spelling ` STRATA42`), `CODE 4217`, `Red circle / Blue square
/ Green triangle`, `A red square is positioned on the left ... A blue circle is positioned on the right ...`. With the picture options on,
a request without pictures gives the same tokens as without them (10 prompts x 128 greedy tokens, identical).

Pictures work with several requests at once, with the MTP drafts and with the conversation cache: the same conversation sent again (a chat
app resends its pictures) continues from the held state when its pictures are the same (they are matched by the server's key for each
picture); a different picture starts that conversation again.

## Several requests at once

`"parallel": N` in the model's config (`strata-qwen36-<size>.json`, or `--parallel N` at setup) makes the engine keep N conversations open
(`--batch N`, up to 8) and decode them together: every window carries one token of each conversation, so the dense weights, the head and
every routed expert two conversations share are read once for all of them. The server needs no change: it speaks the same engine protocol
as for Flash-Next ([BATCHING.md](BATCHING.md)). A request that arrives while another is read waits only for that read: the prompt of a
new request is read **between** the decode windows of the others, and a conversation continues in the slot that holds its start (or the
engine copies the longer held start from another slot). A 3,008-token prompt read in 0.95 s (3,200 tok/s, 6 chunks) beside three decoding
slots: each of them paused at most 160 ms (one chunk) instead of the whole read, and produced 20 tokens meanwhile (one window per chunk,
the default); `STRATA_Q36_READ_WINDOWS=4` gives them 65 tokens during a 1.14 s read (more of the time, a slower read).
A request that runs alone (the solo path, with its MTP drafts) and is moved into a batch slot when another arrives, and back when it is
alone again, gives the text it gives running alone (the server's hand-over reuses the held state).

Aggregate decode speed, N requests at once, same prompts, greedy, 128 new tokens each, wall time from the first request to the last
answer, **R9700 32 GB, UD-Q4_K_XL, llama.cpp `llama-server -np N`** (5 interleaved pairs, median; Strata `--batch 8 --mtp 0`):

| Requests at once | Strata | llama.cpp | Ratio | Pairs faster |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 83.9 tok/s | 73.8 | 1.14 | 5/5 |
| 2 | 173.5 | 107.4 | 1.61 | 5/5 |
| 4 | 252.0 | 165.0 | 1.53 | 5/5 |
| 8 | 325.4 | 208.1 | 1.56 | 5/5 |

**RTX 3060 12 GB, UD-Q4_K_XL in the hybrid mode** (each engine with the slots it needs: `--batch N` takes room from the expert slots; llama.cpp
`llama-server -np N -ncmoe 28 -t 8`, the best split of a sweep on this card; 5 interleaved pairs, medians; the box was shared with other
jobs between runs, never during one):

| Requests at once | Strata | llama.cpp | Ratio | Pairs faster |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 64.0 tok/s | 41.1 | 1.56 | 5/5 |
| 2 | 85.1 | 52.5 | 1.62 | 5/5 |
| 4 | 99.3 | 63.0 | 1.58 | 5/5 |

Every slot's tokens equal the tokens of the same request alone (the base engine's), at 2, 4 and 8 slots, with a 2.5K-token prompt read beside
decoding slots, with slots reused for later requests, with pictures and with sampling (same seed). Through the server: four concurrent chat
requests give the texts of the same four one after the other.

**MTP drafts.** A request that has the engine to itself keeps its MTP drafts (the server sends it alone while nothing else runs). With
several requests the batch window has no drafts unless `--batch-mtp` is in the config's `args` (opt-in): every slot's window then also
carries the proposal its MTP block made (one per slot, up to the rows to spare in the 8-row window) and a confirmed proposal moves two
tokens in the window. Same prompts, 5 interleaved pairs, R9700:

| Requests at once | `--mtp 0` | `--mtp 2 --batch-mtp` | Ratio | Pairs faster |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 83.7 tok/s | 134.0 | 1.60 | 5/5 |
| 2 | 173.1 | 207.0 | 1.20 | 5/5 |
| 4 | 251.0 | 275.0 | 1.10 | 5/5 |
| 8 | 324.0 | 320.5 | 0.99 | 0/5 (no row to spare: no proposals) |

The text is the same with and without it (every slot equal to its solo tokens).

**What a slot costs.** Each slot keeps its own cache in VRAM: 1.5 GB at a context of 32K (fp32 keys and values of the 10 attention layers
and the MTP block, 45 KB per token) and 0.07 GB of recurrent state. Setup writes the context for one conversation, so N slots take N times
that from the room the experts would have: on a card that does not hold every expert (12 and 16 GB, the hybrid mode) that is room the
expert slots lose, and a batch reads more distinct experts from RAM. Setup **offers `--parallel`** where the sessions do not eat the experts' room: up to 3-4 where every expert still fits (3 on a 32 GB card at
32K), and on a card that does not (the hybrid mode) the count whose sessions take at most 35% of the room the experts would have, so it
depends on the context you chose (12 GB: 4 slots at 8K, none at 32K; 16 GB: 2 slots at 32K). It says the price in the same breath, asks
"How many requests at once?" (Enter keeps one at a time), and any number you give is kept. Measured on the hybrid cards (UD-Q4_K_XL, medians of 5
interleaved pairs, `--mtp 2` as setup writes it; "together" = total tokens per second of N simultaneous requests, against ONE request at a time
with the draft layer):

| card, context | slots | one request alone, vs 1 slot | N together, vs one at a time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| RTX 3060 12 GB, 8K | 2 / 4 / 8 | -3.5% / -4.3% / -12% | 0.99x / 1.15x / 1.10x |
| RTX A4000 16 GB, 32K | 2 / 4 | -10.6% / -29.9% | 1.03x / 0.76x |
| Tesla P100 16 GB, 32K | 2 / 4 | -7% / -23% | 0.98x / 0.81x |

Without the draft layer (`--mtp 0`) the same slots give 1.26-1.64x together (3060 at 8K: 4 slots 1.64x for -5.5% alone), but a single request
with drafts is already about 1.6x as fast as one without, so on a small card the main gain is that a second user starts at once; the
speed gain is small. On a card that holds every expert (R9700 32 GB, 8K prompts) 4 slots run 1.45x one-at-a-time-with-drafts (1.59x with
`--batch-mtp`). The engine says what the sessions take before it allocates them and refuses (with the numbers) a count that cannot fit.

In the hybrid mode the text of a request can differ a little between running alone and running beside others: the experts that sit on the
GPU or on the CPU change with the routing of all the requests, and the two compute with different rounding. With the slot tables fixed (`STRATA_Q36_FIXED_SLOTS=1`, a test setting) every slot equals its
solo run there too, with and without `--batch-mtp`.

## Speed (0.1.45)

Decode and prompt kernels of this engine path were rewritten for speed; **every change on the decode path gives the old kernels' bits**
(`STRATA_Q36_VERIFY=1 strata ... --no-graph` runs the old kernel beside each new one on the real activations and compares them bit for bit:
0 mismatches in 18,360 / 8,187 / 6,399 comparisons on the R9700 and the RTX 3060; `STRATA_Q36_OLD_KERNELS=1` switches them all off). The
10 parity prompts (greedy 128) give the base engine's tokens, plain and with `--mtp 2`. Where the prompt's chunk size changes, the numbers
change a little: see "Prompt chunk".

**What was slow** (rocprofv3, R9700, UD-Q4_K_XL, plain decode, 11.25 ms of kernel time per token): the big Q8_0 products (attention, GDN
projections, head: 1.9 GB per token) run at 530 GB/s, the memory bound. The rest did not: the shared expert's and the attention k/v products
(140 per token) at 18 us, the Q4_K gate/up kernel at 250 GB/s, `k_moe_out` (one block) 17 us, `k_group` (one thread walking 256 experts) 9 us.
Now: those products one warp per row (a launch of 2048 warps took 21 us on gfx1201 where 1024 warps took 5 us, so the grid is capped), shared
gate+up+SwiGLU+q8_1 in one launch, the MoE end with 1024 threads and the next layer's q8_1 image, add+norm+q8_1 in one launch, router top-k and
grouping in one launch, the router and the shared gate in one product, Q4_K gate/up on the V2K kernels (`STRATA_EXPERT_V2K`, gfx12 default).
The prompt's GDN conv runs in tiles of 16 tokens side by side and the delta rule loads one token ahead with two barriers per token (both exact).

R9700 32 GB (p620, HIP gfx1201), UD-Q4_K_XL, base = the engine before this work, 5 interleaved pairs, 3 repetitions each, medians; llama.cpp
972b5fc HIP on the same file (`-fa 1`, best of `-ub` 512 / 2048):

| | base | 0.1.45 | ratio | pairs faster | llama.cpp |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| decode tg128 | 83.2 tok/s | 117.8 | 1.42 | 5/5 | 81.9-82.1 |
| prompt pp4096 | 3,453 | 6,220 (chunk 4096) | 1.80 | 5/5 | 3,794 (-ub 2048) / 3,042 (-ub 512) |
| `--mtp 2`, 10 prompts greedy 128 | 167.7 | 183.7 | 1.10 | 3/3 | 129 (draft-mtp, n-max 2, earlier run) |
| 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 requests at once (`--batch 8 --mtp 0`) | 85.2 / 182.4 / 271.9 / 361.1 | 122.4 / 205.1 / 303.3 / 386.9 | 1.44 / 1.12 / 1.12 / 1.07 | 5/5 | |

UD-Q6_K_XL on the same card (every main layer's experts in VRAM, so the prompt chunk stays 512): decode 80.4 -> 106.9 tok/s (1.33), pp4096
2,160 -> 2,200 (llama.cpp 3,486 at -ub 2048, 2,738 at -ub 512; decode 81.1), `--mtp 2` 154.7 -> 167.3. `--chunk 2048` there moves the experts
to the hybrid placement (205 of 256 per layer in VRAM): prompt 3,500 tok/s, decode 94 - an option, not the default.

RTX 3060 12 GB (P2003, CUDA sm_86, 20 threads), UD-Q4_K_XL in the hybrid mode (37 of 256 experts per layer in VRAM): the GPU part of a
token is the dense Q8_0 at the card's bandwidth (6 ms of the 17) and the rest waits for the CPU pool (9 ms of experts), so only the small
kernels' share is gained: decode tg128 58.5 -> 59.7 tok/s (+2%), pp2048 1,958 -> 2,022 (+3.3%), 10/10 identical, plain and `--mtp 2`
(84.3 -> 84.7). llama.cpp 972b5fc CUDA (`-ncmoe 26 -t 8 -ub 2048`): pp2048 1,328, tg128 48-52.

**Prompt chunk (the default changed).** The MoE prompt kernels read every expert once per chunk, so a bigger chunk feeds them more rows per
expert: R9700 pp4096 at chunk 512 / 1024 / 2048 / 4096 = 3,453 / 4,786 / 5,766 / 6,223 tok/s. With every expert in VRAM the engine now takes the
largest of 4096 / 2048 / 1024 that fits beside the experts, the 0.77 GiB reserve and the sessions' caches without giving the packed decode
copies back (8K-64K context: 4096, 100K: 2048, 131K: 512; `--batch 2..4`: 1024 at most so the other slots are not held for a whole chunk,
`--batch 8`: 512). The hybrid mode keeps 2048 (a bigger chunk takes expert slots: RTX 3060 chunk 4096 reads prompts 5% faster and decodes 13%
slower) and goes down to 1024 / 512 on a card with 7.5 / 5.5 GiB free. **`--prefill 512` (or `STRATA_Q36_CHUNK=512`) gives the old size, and
then the text is the base engine's, bit for bit.** The chunk size changes the GEMM tiles the BLAS picks and with them the last bits of the
prompt state: KL against the 512 chunk on six real 1.5-3.2K-token documents (48 teacher-forced rows each): chunk 1024 4.0e-3, 2048 4.2e-3,
4096 3.6e-3 (per prompt 2.3e-3 .. 5.9e-3), top-1 agreement 44-48 of 48 rows - the size of the llama.cpp CPU-vs-HIP difference on the same
file (4.2e-3), not a quality loss. Greedy 64 tokens after those six documents: the default chunk gives the base engine's text for 2 of 6,
`--prefill 512` for 6 of 6. A prompt shorter than the chunk (every chat turn after the first) is one chunk either way: unchanged.
The maintainers keep the new default's reference outputs (six documents, greedy 64) and check later changes against them.

**Tried and dropped.** The MTP drafts' head over a subset of the vocabulary (`--draft-vocab N`, kept as an opt-in; the answer never
changes): the first 16K-131K rows gain 5-8% on English and code but lose 10-15% on Chinese / Russian / Arabic / Hindi (70% of a Chinese
prompt's token ids are above 65,536), and a candidate list built from the tokens seen so far loses on both. The shared expert on a second
stream (captured into the decode graph) decodes at 36 tok/s instead of 117 with this ROCm. Chunked (WY) GDN and the PCIe-assisted hybrid decode
were not attempted.

## Not done / limits

- Eight slots at most (the window holds 8 rows); `--batch-mtp` shares those rows between slots and proposals.
- A sampling request in a batch decodes one token per window without proposals. `logit_bias` is not available on this engine path: the
  server refuses a request that has it (as it does with `--batch` for Flash-Next).
- A slot that stopped being alone goes back to the solo path only through the server's own hand-over; the MTP block's cache has holes for
  the tokens a slot decoded in batch windows (the drafts of a later solo stretch are a little worse; the text is not affected).
- Intel Arc (SYCL) does not run this family.

## Testing

The gates are in `tools/qwen35/` and talk to the engine through its serve protocol (no server needed); run them under the box's GPU lock:

- `q36_solo_gate.py` + `q36_cmp_gate.py`: the 10 parity prompts x 128 greedy tokens through `GEN`, compared with another build's.
- `q36_batch_gate.py --slots N --waves --long 2500`: every slot's tokens equal its solo tokens, slots reused, a long prompt read beside
  decoding slots. `q36_proto_edge.py`: `max_new` 1, `BSTOP`, a busy slot, `STOP` during a prompt read, held-state reuse, sampled requests,
  the context's end. `q36_interleave_probe.py`: what the decoding slots see while a long prompt is read.
- `q36_vision_cmp.py` (with `q36_mtmd_dump.cpp` built against llama.cpp): the picture comparison above; `q36_vision_proto.py`: pictures through
  `GENI` / `BGENI` (solo, in a batch, the conversation cache); `q36_vision_serve.py` and `q36_serve_par.py` / `q36_serve_handoff.py`:
  the same through the server.
- `q36_par_bench.py`: the aggregate-throughput A/B against `llama-server -np N`.


## docs/RADEON_780M.md

# Radeon 780M / 760M (Ryzen 7040 / 8040, gfx1103): build from source on Linux

The Radeon 780M (Phoenix / Hawk Point, RDNA3, `gfx1103`) runs Strata through the same HIP backend as the Radeon
cards in [AMD_HIP.md](AMD_HIP.md). **Status: experimental and opt-in** (`STRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_GFX1103=1`): the port
is measured on one machine (the numbers below), the maintainers have not run one, and the chip is not Strix Halo.
Everything here was measured on a Ryzen 7 8745HS (8 cores, AVX-512), Radeon 780M (12 CUs), 60 GB DDR5, GTT at
50 GiB, Ubuntu kernel 7.0.0-38, `cwsr_enable=0`, engine 0.1.43 built from this tree by hand, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
GSQ-RCO Q2_0 with the MTP draft layer, 32K context, Int8 KV.

## 1. What the port changed

- **Native dot4.** gfx1103 was outside the `dp4a` guard in `hip_compat/intrinsics.hpp`, so every quantized dot
  product ran a four-step byte loop instead of `v_dot4_i32_iu8`. gfx1103 now compiles the native instruction
  (decode +55% measured: 8.70 -> 13.44 tok/s at a 32K prompt, same greedy token ids as before).
- **gfx11 WMMA kernels.** gfx1103 was outside the `__gfx11xx__` list of the prompt attention, block scorer,
  prompt GEMMs and prompt experts, so those fell back to hipBLAS / portable kernels. It is now in the list and
  the parity tests run on it (`hip_prefill_wmma_gemm_parity`, `hip_prompt_attn_wmma`, `hip_prefill_fused_moe`,
  `hip_prefill_fused_iq`, `qsa_*`, `hip_gemm_f16_io_parity`, `hip_prefill_mmq_parity`).
- **A hipBLASLt table** for gfx1103 + hipBLASLt `100401`: `tools/hip/gfx1103-hipblaslt-100401.txt` (section 3).
- **The gfx1103 exact speed switches** (section 4), written into the config's `env` by setup for the opt-in install
  (the engine keeps gfx1103 out of its exact-switch arch defaults (the prompt set of section 5 is separate), as it does for gfx1150). Whether the chip leaves the
  `STRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_GFX1103=1` opt-in is the maintainers' call; the numbers here are what they need to make it.

## 2. Toolchain and build

ROCm 10.1 (`rocm/dev-ubuntu-24.04:10.1.0-full`) is what this build and the table were tested with: HIP
7.16.26385, hipBLASLt 1.4.1 (`100401`), clang 24. Its hipBLASLt carries gfx1103 kernels. setup's TheRock index
for `gfx110X-all` has no 10.x (its newest is 7.14.0a20260612); the gfx1103 opt-in keeps setup's nightly pin, and
the wheel route was not exercised by the numbers below - they come from a hand build.

By hand, the steps of [STRIX_HALO.md](STRIX_HALO.md) with the architecture and the paths changed:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build-780m -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DSTRATA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF -DSTRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON \
  -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1103 \
  -DCMAKE_HIP_COMPILER=/opt/rocm/lib/llvm/bin/clang++ -DCMAKE_HIP_COMPILER_ROCM_ROOT=/opt/rocm \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/rocm \
  "-DCMAKE_HIP_FLAGS=--rocm-path=/opt/rocm --rocm-device-lib-path=/opt/rocm/lib/llvm/amdgcn/bitcode"
cmake --build build-780m -j 12
ctest --test-dir build-780m
```

`ctest` on this machine: 57 passed, 2 skipped (`hip_prefill_hcd_exact_parity`, `hip_prefill_hipblaslt_gemm` -
they run and pass with the table set), 2 environmental failures (`ple_parity` needs the `bench/micro` fixtures,
`platform_memory_test` needs a memlock limit above 8 MiB; this host's hard limit is 8 MiB).

The model: a GSQ-RCO Q2_0 pack (`tools/iq_pack.py`, the experts read from the GGUF in place), the PLE table on
the SSD (`--ple-io direct`), `--mmap-experts --expert-cache 24576`, `--prefill auto`, MTP from
`tools/mtp_fetch.py` + `mtp_pack.py` + `mtp_rt.py`. GTT must be raised for this model (`ttm.pages_limit`; setup
changes no host setting).

## 3. The hipBLASLt table

```sh
export STRATA_HIPBLASLT_TUNING=$PWD/tools/hip/gfx1103-hipblaslt-100401.txt
```

setup hands it over automatically when the installed hipBLASLt reports 1.4.1. It was calibrated with
`tools/hip/tune_hipblaslt` over the gfx1150 table's 144 GEMM cases at T = 64..16384 (the same case list the 890M
run used), two passes, 32 MiB workspace, each row the solution with the lowest median of all six repetitions: 143
rows (the `bf16 N=1 K=2560 T=64` shape has no candidate faster than plain hipBLAS and is left out), 1.05-23.30x per
GEMM, geometric mean 4.95x. `hip_prefill_hipblaslt_gemm` reports `fallbacks=0`; `hip_prefill_hcd_exact_parity`
skips because the table picks no 1176 / 1177 for the HC down GEMM (the gfx1150 table gets the same skip).

## 4. The exact speed switches

With `STRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_GFX1103=1` setup writes the 17 exact switches below into the config's `env`, the same way
it writes the hipBLASLt table; turning the opt-in off takes them out again. The engine keeps gfx1103 out of its exact-switch
arch defaults (`arch_default_env("gfx1103")` stays empty, checked by `arch_defaults_test`). Measured on the 780M:
+13% to +15% prompt with the table (183-186 -> 211-212 tok/s at 4K) and +3.2% decode (16.63 -> 17.17 tok/s, 640
greedy tokens, 3 of 3 pairs), with the greedy token ids unchanged. They are the gfx1151 table less
`STRATA_HCD_EXACT` (which needs hipBLASLt solutions 1176 / 1177; the gfx1103 table picks others).

| Switch | What it does |
|---|---|
| `STRATA_GDN_HEAD`, `STRATA_GDN_PP=2`, `STRATA_GDN_CONVL2`, `STRATA_GDN_NOY`, `STRATA_CVEC_FUSE` | the prompt's gated-delta-net recurrence and the steered layer's fused write |
| `STRATA_PF_PAD` | padded GEMM row strides (acts with `STRATA_PF_GEMM`; inert without it) |
| `STRATA_Q8_PACKED`, `STRATA_Q6_PACKED`, `STRATA_MMVF_ROWS`, `STRATA_ATTN_LANECELL` | decode layouts and kernels (packed Q8_0 / Q6_K weights, 4-row BF16 GEMV, one-cell-per-thread attention scores) |
| `STRATA_EXPERT_V2`, `STRATA_TSUM`, `STRATA_LFUSE`, `STRATA_GDN_SPLIT`, `STRATA_QFUSE`, `STRATA_PLE_BATCH`, `STRATA_SH_STREAM` | grouped decode experts, butterfly warp sums, fewer launches, the GDN step over four blocks per head, producer-written activation images, batched PLE projections, the shared expert on its own stream |

## 5. The matrix-core prompt set (on by default on the 780M; it changes bits)

On by default on the Radeon 780M (`gfx1103`, integrated, Linux; AMD_HIP.md, "Integrated GPUs"): the engine sets `STRATA_HIP_WMMA`, `STRATA_PF_GEMM`,
`STRATA_PA_FAST`, `STRATA_SELECT_WMMA` and `STRATA_HC_UPMIX` itself. `STRATA_IGPU_PROMPT_SET=0` turns the whole set off, `NAME=0` one switch. The 880M / 890M
(`gfx1150`) and Windows keep it off (no hardware / not tested); `STRATA_IGPU_PROMPT_SET=1` turns it on there. `STRATA_PF_FUSED` stays opt-in.

Measured (021-minipc, P2006, Q2_0, fresh engine per run, 10 interleaved rounds, 6 complete pairs): prompt 1K 98.5 -> 157.3 tok/s (x1.60, 6/6 pairs faster),
4K 115.1 -> 233.3 (x2.03, 6/6), decode 22.02 -> 21.99 (code) and 15.09 -> 15.05 (story) (x0.999), greedy token ids identical in 6 of 6 pairs.

**GPU resets.** The 780M's current Ubuntu firmware (gc 11.0.1 MES) can still reset the GPU now and then, with or without this set: when the kernel moves memory that the
GPU has registered, the process's queues are evicted, and a kernel that sits in a barrier at that moment never answers. The engine recovers
("device wedged, but recovered through reset") but the running request fails. In the same runs the default engine crashed 4 of 10 times and the set 0 of 10, so it did
not add resets. Until AMD fixes the firmware a mini PC may still see them; the engine does not touch the firmware. A newer `linux-firmware` is the thing to try.
The prompt levers need the table to pay: with the table, the WMMA set
read 248 tok/s at 4K against 186 without it, and at 32K 272 against 178. No KL was measured on this chip.

```sh
export STRATA_HIP_WMMA=1      # prompt attention on matrix cores
export STRATA_PF_GEMM=1       # the prompt's FP16 projections on the WMMA GEMM
export STRATA_PA_FAST=1       # prompt attention with single FP16 q and p
export STRATA_SELECT_WMMA=1   # the block scorer on matrix cores
export STRATA_PF_FUSED=1      # the prompt experts on matrix cores (neutral at 4K here: 246 vs 248)
export STRATA_HC_UPMIX=1      # the hyper-connection up projection with its epilogue
```

## 6. Engine flags

`--spec 2` is the best MTP window on this chip: 15.65 tok/s decode at a 4K prompt against 14.18 at `--spec 4` and
11.16 at `--spec 6` (greedy, 256 tokens, medians of three interleaved restarts). `--lookup-chain 4` adds +2.3% (3
of 3 pairs, byte-identical greedy answers) and setup's `--spec-min-p 0.5` is 4.5% slower here than the default;
`--mtp-q4` is neutral and `--mtp-window 4096` measured +2% at 32K in two pairs (weak). The raw runs are in the
results folder.

## 7. Measured

bench/bench_vs_llama.py, 256 tokens out, temperature 0 and 0.7, interleaved; each cell one round (medians need
more rounds - treat these as one-machine samples):

| arm | cell | prompt tok/s | decode tok/s | TTFT s |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| plain (no table, no opt-ins) | 4K | 90 | 13.1 | 44.9 |
| plain (no table, no opt-ins) | 32K | 90 | 13.1 | 351 |
| table + all opt-ins | 4K | 277 | 13.9 | 14.6 |
| table + WMMA set | 32K | 272 | 14.3 | 118 |

A context ladder on the shipping configuration (131K context, `--spec 2 --lookup-chain 4`) with fresh prompts from
this checkout's own documentation, 128 greedy tokens each: prefill holds ~310 tok/s to 32K (276.7 at 4K, 314.3 /
314.6 at 8K / 16K, 308.7 at 32K), then 258.2 at 64K, 215.5 at 96K and 198.5-221.4 at 128K across two runs - that is
the average over the full read, and the last ~14K tokens at 128K depth read at ~206 tok/s with the prefix cached.
Decode holds ~16 tok/s to 32K, then 12.1 at 64K and 9.8-9.9 at 96-128K (draft acceptance stays ~70%, so it is
context cost, not the drafter). Memory stays flat: 38.1 of 50 GiB GTT at 131K. Raw:
[bench/results/2026-10-12-community-gfx1103](../bench/results/2026-10-12-community-gfx1103/README.md).

## 8. Not tested

- The TheRock-wheel install for gfx1103 (the hand build above is what was measured).
- The opt-in set beyond one round; KL of any bit-changing switch; other models; contexts past 131K.
- CUDA and SYCL were not built here (no toolchains on this box); the added gfx1103 macros are undefined for them.
- Reset stability looks good but is one machine: a 2 h 07 m soak (`tools/serve_load.py`, 924 requests) and the
  reset-prone combination from 7.10 (partial expert cache + `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` + the adaptive tier) both ran
  with zero `amdgpu` resets in the kernel log. The known 780M issue ([DETAILS.md](DETAILS.md)) was seen on ROCm
  7.10; with `cwsr_enable=0` and this stack it did not reproduce.


## docs/RESEARCH_RUNS.md

# One long document, many questions (0.1.40.2, opt-in)

Read a long document once, then ask many different questions without reading it again. All numbers: Tesla P100 16 GB,
IQ2_XS, `--kv int8 --kv-resident 32768`, MTP on, greedy, the 0.1.40 engine unless a row says "pin".

## What the engine already did (0.1.40)

The conversation cache keeps small checkpoints (the GDN and indexer state, about 118 MiB each); the K/V of the document
stays in the session, so a question that starts from a checkpoint reads only what lies past it.

| 262K document (258,655 tokens) | time to first token |
|---|---|
| first question (cold read) | 904 s (286 tok/s) |
| questions 2-20, engine with a turn boundary at the document's end | 0.53 s median (0.44-0.72) |
| the same through the server's chat API (no turn boundary at the document's end) | 55.5 s each (15 measured): the engine re-reads up to `--prompt-cache-every` (16,384) tokens from the last periodic checkpoint |
| `parallel` 2 through the server | the first two questions 918 s and 979 s; the next pair read the document again from token 0 |

Checkpoint RAM: +804 MiB resident after the first read (6 checkpoints); each later question adds at most 10 MiB. The
K/V of 262K takes 3.06 GiB of pinned RAM, once per session (`--batch` slots each take their own).
Identity (greedy, 64 tokens): questions 1 and 12 on a fresh engine give the same tokens as in the 20-question run.
Caveat: IQ models are not byte-reproducible at temperature 0 between runs unless `STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN=1` (DETAILS.md);
some answers differ between two runs of the same prompt for that reason, with or without the field below.

## `strata_prefix` (and the engine's `pin=N`)

`"strata_prefix": {"messages": 1}`, `{"message": 0, "chars": N}` or `{"tokens": N}` marks the start of the prompt as the
shared document. The checkpoint at its end is pinned: never evicted, kept in the parked-conversation budget, kept by
`SAVE`, and a question that resumes from it does not park the branch it leaves.

| 64K document (P100) | no field | with the field |
|---|---|---|
| engine, raw prompts, questions 2-5 | 48.6 s | 0.35-0.53 s |
| a 100K-token branch between two questions, then a question | 149 s | 0.55 s |
| another 20K prompt between (`--conversation-cache-mib 8192`) | 49 s | 0.97 s (restored), then 0.44 s |
| server, 18K-token document, split messages / one message | 8.8 s | 0.6-0.8 s |
| server `parallel` 2, six questions | 730 s (every pair re-reads) | 220 s (questions 3-6: 2.5-3.8 s) |

Copy-on-write K/V pages across `--batch` slots are NOT built: each slot keeps its own K/V (3.06 GiB at 262K, about 12 GiB
at 1M), and admitting a branch copies the prefix K/V (3 s at 262K). The pinned prefix removes the re-read, not the copy.

`tools/research_run.py` runs a document and a question list against a server with and without the field.

## R3: expert slots against K/V blocks (P100, IQ2_XS)

64K document, 5 questions. Prefill, then median first token of a short question, then decode:

| expert slots (GiB) | prefill | first token | decode |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2,083 (2.81) | 230 s | 0.69 s | 27.5 tok/s |
| 3,500 | 200.7 s | 0.61 s | 30.9 |
| 5,000 | 200.7 s | 0.55 s | 34.2 |
| 7,000 | 200.7 s | 0.51 s | 36.7 |

Marginal value of VRAM: decode 0.31-0.41 s per GiB per 200-token answer between 2,000 and 5,000 slots, 0.15 above;
prefill gains only below the prompt loan's floor. K/V cells in VRAM (`--kv-resident`): 4096 / 16384 / 32768 / 65536 give
34.05 / 34.06 / 34.21 / 34.92 tok/s at 64K; at 262K (5,000 slots) 8192 / 32768 / 131072 give 29.54 / 29.46 / 29.49 tok/s
(block hit rate 92.6 / 94.5 / 95.7 %). So the K/V block cache is worth nothing per GiB, experts only help decode, and the
read is already served by the loan. A split planner would gain almost nothing, so none was built. The one real lever in
the read is the chunk: `--prefill 16384` with 7,000 slots reads 64K in 186.4 s against 200.7 s (-7%), and 4096 takes 228 s;
it needs the larger loan and changes the chunking, hence the rounding, so it is not a placement-only change.


## docs/SAFETY.md

# Is Strata safe and private?

This page says what Strata downloads, where from, when it uses the internet, what stays on your PC and how the downloads
are checked. Everything here comes from reading the code of this version. Each section names the files, so you or anyone
you trust can check it. Where Strata does less than you might hope, the page says so.

## At a glance

- **Your chats, prompts, files, pictures and models stay on your PC.** They leave only when you choose it: you add an
  outside model service, you open the server to other devices or to the internet, or the agent searches the web or opens a page
  (see [What the agent can do](#what-the-coding-agent-can-do-on-your-pc)).
- **There is no telemetry.** Strata sends no usage data, no crash reports and no analytics, and has no account to sign in to.
- **Starting and running a model never downloads anything.** Downloads and updates are separate steps that you start.
- **The server listens on your PC only.** Reaching it from another device needs an API key.
- **Once a model is downloaded, Strata runs without internet.** Starting, loading, serving and chatting need no
  connection. Only things you ask for use it: the agent's web search and web pages, an outside model service, the tunnel,
  and installs and updates (a first model install also fetches llama.cpp's preparation scripts).
- **Downloads are checked.** Updates come from a signed feed. Every model file has a fixed SHA-256 and size, and an install
  stops if the pinned version of a file is gone (the details are [below](#how-downloads-are-checked)).
- **In its default mode the coding agent asks before it changes anything**, and once per chat before its first web search or web page.
- **The code is open.** Anyone can read it, and security problems go to [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

## Does Strata phone home?

No. A search of the app, the Terminal, the engine server and the installers found no analytics library, no crash
reporter and no code that reports usage anywhere. The app's privacy notes say the same
(`apps/host/src/components/PrivacyNotes.tsx`: "Strata sends no usage telemetry").

Some things sound similar and stay on your PC:

- The Monitor, `/metrics` and `/v1/telemetry` show hardware readings (temperature, speed, memory) to you. They are served
  from your own PC, and they need your API key when you set one.
- When the app window crashes (Linux) or the app fails to start (Windows, Mac), a crash log is written to a folder on your disk
  (on Windows, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Strata\logs`). Nothing sends it. **Save logs**
  (Settings, Engine, Diagnostics) puts a text file in your Downloads folder, and you decide whether to attach it to a bug report.
- The coding agent is a separate component (the DeepSeek Harness, MIT). It has its own telemetry switch, and Strata starts it
  with that switch off (`apps/host/server/agent/harness-runtime.mjs`).

Like any download, each connection below shows the other side your IP address and the file you asked for.

## When Strata uses the internet

| What | Where it goes | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model files, the picture reader, the speed-up layer (MTP) | huggingface.co, or the mirror in `HF_ENDPOINT` if you set one | When you install a model |
| The same files from ModelScope, for PCs that cannot reach Hugging Face | modelscope.cn | Only if you ask for it (`--source modelscope`). Strata never switches to it by itself |
| Engine, Terminal and Control updates | The signed feed on GitHub Releases of Niko1221/Strata | When you install an engine, press **Update engine** or **Check for updates**, or run `strata update`. Opening **Settings, Engine** does not connect: it shows the result of your last check |
| App updates | `latest.json` on the same GitHub Releases, through Tauri's updater | When you press **Check for updates** or **Update Strata** |
| llama.cpp source code (a fixed commit) | github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp | During a model install, if it is not on your PC yet. Strata uses only its model-preparation scripts |
| Web search and web pages | DuckDuckGo, with Bing as the second source; or Exa, Perplexity or DeepSeek if you save a key for them. Any page the agent is asked to open goes to that page's site | When the agent uses its search or "open web pages" tool. In Manual mode it asks you first, once per chat |
| Outside model services | The service you add (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, a server on your network and others) | Only for chats with that model, and only after you add its key |
| Cloudflare tunnel | Cloudflare, through the `cloudflared` program | Only while you have the tunnel on, and Strata makes an API key for it unless you pass `--no-api-key` (then it warns that anyone who finds the address can use your model) |
| Tailscale, local network | Not Strata's traffic. Strata only reads Tailscale's status and shows the address | Only if you choose that access in `strata launch` |
| An image link in an API request | The address in the link | Only when a program sends your server a request with an `http(s)` image link. `--offline` refuses it |
| Remote tool servers (MCP) | The address you put in the run config | Only when you add one |
| A website you open in the app's preview pane | That website | Only when you type an address into **Open a website** |
| Share to X or Reddit (Monitor screenshot) | Your browser opens x.com or reddit.com with a caption and a link to the Strata page | Only when you click it. The screenshot is saved to your disk, not uploaded |

That is the full list found in the code. Some details:

- **Nothing checks for updates in the background.** The app does not check when it starts, and not when you open Settings,
  Engine either: that screen shows the result of your last check, or nothing if you have not checked. The checks in the table
  run when you press a button or run a command. With no connection, the check says so and nothing else happens. The Terminal fetches an engine by itself only when none is
  installed, and `strata launch` asks first.
- **Starting and serving never download.** `strata serve` and the app's load button fetch nothing. The app sets
  `STRATA_PACKAGED=1` and `STRATA_NO_ACQUIRE=1` for its parts (`apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/main.rs`), and the downloaders
  refuse to run under them (`strata_control/acquisition.py`, `apps/host/server/acquisition.mjs`). That is why the app
  never downloads `cloudflared` for you while it runs.
- **The engine itself has no network code.** The part of Strata that runs the model (`src/`, `include/`, `sycl/`, `metal/`)
  contains no networking. The app's own pages load no fonts, scripts or trackers from the internet.
- **Building from source** reaches more places. Python from python.org or winget (`START-HERE.bat`), a standalone Python
  from GitHub on a Mac (`setup.sh`), Python packages from PyPI (`requirements.txt`, pinned versions), NVIDIA's CUDA libraries
  from PyPI and, on Ubuntu and Debian, NVIDIA's apt key and packages, AMD's ROCm wheels, the Vulkan SDK from LunarG, and
  llama.cpp and stable-diffusion.cpp source from GitHub. These run only while you run the setup.

## What stays on your PC

- **Chats, prompts, attached files and pictures** are handled by the engine on your PC. The app keeps chats in its own
  storage on your disk. Models are in the folder you chose.
- **API keys** you save for outside services are kept in a file that only your user account can open. They are not
  encrypted. (`apps/host/server/model-providers.mjs`)
- **The server listens on `127.0.0.1`**, this PC only. The app fixes that address (`STRATA_BIND=127.0.0.1`), and the engine
  server's default is the same (`serve/server.py`, the `--host` option).
- **Sharing needs a key.** The app's "Share with other devices" and the Cloudflare tunnel will not start without an API
  key, and the shared port answers only `/v1/models`, `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages`
  (`apps/host/server/local-share.mjs`, `cloudflare.mjs`). `strata launch` makes a key for you when you pick anything wider than
  this computer. The bare engine server (`serve/server.py`) only prints a warning if you open it to your network without a key,
  so set one yourself in that case.
- **When you use an outside model**, the conversation (and the instructions of skills you switched on) go to that service.
  The app says so in its privacy notes. The service's own rules then apply.
- **Programs you connect** (Claude Code, Codex, and so on) are separate programs with their own network behaviour. Strata
  does not control what they send.

The server also has browser protections (a host check, an origin check, no CORS by default). They are in
[SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md#what-the-server-exposes).

## How downloads are checked

**Updates for the engine, the Terminal and Control.**

1. The release publishes `strata-feed.json` and `strata-feed.json.sig`, signed with an Ed25519 key. The matching public key is
   inside every installed Strata (`strata_control/update_keys.json`). The private key is kept offline by the owner.
2. Before it uses the feed, your PC checks the signature, that the feed has not expired and that it is not older than the
   last feed it accepted (so an old feed cannot be replayed).
3. Each engine package is checked against its SHA-256 and its signed manifest, then every file in it against its own hash,
   then it is checked to fit your PC.
4. The new engine is test-started before Strata switches to it. If anything fails, you keep the engine you had.

Updates never replace your models or saved tuning. The full description is in [packaging/UPDATES.md](../packaging/UPDATES.md).

**The app.** Its updates are signed with a separate key (Tauri's minisign), and the public half is in the app
(`apps/desktop/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`). The updater refuses an installer whose signature does not match. The Terminal
checks the same signature when you run `strata update --app`.

**Model files.** Every model file that `setup.py` downloads has a fixed SHA-256 and size, written in the code, so the check
needs no network: the main Qwen3.8-Flash-Next files (Q2_0, IQ2_XS, IQ3_XXS, IQ3_S), Swift 1.5, the Coder, the Unsloth sizes,
the Gyro files, Qwen3.6, the NVFP4 packs, the picture reader, the image model files and the speed-up layer (MTP, tensor by
tensor). A file that does not match is deleted and the install stops. A file whose size on the server is not the pinned
size stops it before the download starts.

- If the pinned version of a file is gone from Hugging Face, the install stops and says to update Strata. It does not take
  the repository's current file instead. A tester can set `STRATA_ALLOW_UNPINNED=1` to take the current file anyway, without
  the check. It is off by default, and setup says so when it is set.
- Starting a model does not check its files, and running setup again for a model you have does not download or hash them
  again. A file installed before these hashes existed is kept as it is.
- Files from ModelScope are checked against the same fixed SHA-256. ModelScope serves a repository's current files, so a file
  it has changed fails the check. A file without a pin is checked against the hash ModelScope publishes, and setup warns
  when it publishes none.
- The app installs these models by running the same setup, so it has the same checks. The app's host also keeps a short
  starter list of its own (`apps/host/server/real-model-catalog.mjs`). It is for display only. The host refuses to download
  from it, because its files have no hash, and says that models come from the Models screen.
  (`setup.py`: `REPO_PINS`, `download`, `verify_sha256`; `tools/mtp_fetch.py`; `apps/host/server/image-models.mjs`.)

**Engine in the source route.** `setup.py` checks the engine zip against the SHA-256 that GitHub's API publishes for that
release file. If GitHub cannot say (offline, rate limit), setup warns and installs anyway. `STRATA_SKIP_SHA256=1` switches the
check off, and it is never on by default.

**The one-line install** (`curl ... | sh`, `irm ... | iex`) checks the Terminal archive's SHA-256 and the signed feed with the
Terminal it just unpacked. The checksum and the key come from the same release as the archive, so the first install trusts
HTTPS and the `Niko1221/Strata` release itself. What that means, and how to read the script first, is in
[SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md#how-far-to-trust-curl--sh-and-irm--iex). Later updates are checked against the key already on
your PC.

**Code signing.** The Windows installer is not code-signed yet, so Windows shows "Windows protected your PC". The signing and
Apple notarisation of the Mac builds is set up in `packaging/mac/` and runs on the maintainer's Mac. A Mac build that has not
been notarised shows macOS's "damaged" warning ([MAC.md](MAC.md)).

**What the checks do not cover.** They catch a damaged or swapped download and a feed nobody signed with the release key. They
cannot protect you if someone who can publish a release (or who holds the signing key) publishes something harmful.

## What the coding agent can do on your PC

The app's chats run through an agent that can read files, run commands, edit files, search the web and use tools you
connect. What it may do without asking depends on the **Mode** menu (`apps/host/server/agent/README.md`).

| Mode | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Manual** (the default) | Anything that changes something asks first, with one **Approve** or **Deny** card, before it runs. |
| **Plan** | Nothing can change. A request to change something is refused, and no card appears. Tools you connect are refused too. |
| **Bypass** | Full access, no questions. |

In **Manual**:

- **These ask:** writing or editing a file, any command that is not on a short list of look-only commands, and every tool
  you connect. In the browser tool, opening a page, clicking and typing ask.
- **These do not ask:** reading files, listing and searching folders, and look-only commands such as `ls`, `cat` and
  `git status`. A command with a redirect, a chain (`;`, `&&`), a variable or anything else the check does not recognise asks.
- **Web search and opening web pages ask once per chat.** The first one in a chat shows a card with the search words and the
  service they go to, or with the address of the page. **Approve** covers the rest of that chat. **Deny** tells the assistant
  you did not allow the web, and it carries on without it. Plan and Bypass do not ask. The model picks the search words and
  the address, so words from your conversation can end up in a search or a web address, which is why the first one asks.
  In Settings, Tools you can switch the web tools off, or turn on **Let the assistant search the web without asking**, which
  is off by default. A scheduled task in Manual mode cannot answer the card, so its web call is refused unless that switch is
  on (`strata-gate.mjs`).
- **The chat folder is only where the agent starts.** Manual mode does not confine it there. What you
  approve can touch anything your user account can touch, so read the card before you press Approve.
- **Your keys stay out of its commands.** The agent's shell does not get environment variables whose names contain KEY, TOKEN,
  SECRET, PASSWORD, CREDENTIAL or AUTH.
- **Scheduled tasks** run in Plan mode by default. With nobody at the screen, a request for approval is answered "no".
- **Stop** ends a chat's run. Closing a tab does not.

The agent runs on a loopback address with a random token, so other programs on the network cannot reach it.

## Open source and reporting a problem

Strata is MIT-licensed and the whole code is at [github.com/Niko1221/Strata](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata). Read it, build
it and compare. Strata has not had an outside security audit yet.

To report a security problem, use GitHub's private reporting (the repository's **Security** tab), as described in
[SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md). Ordinary questions and ideas can go to an
[issue](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata/issues).

## docs/SECOND_GPU.md

# CUDA1–3 expert experiment

CUDA0 keeps the dense layers, KV/state, MTP and its existing expert cache. Up to
three independent expert caches fill CUDA1, CUDA2 and CUDA3 in that order. Each
expert has one owner: CUDA0, one secondary GPU, or the CPU pool. Each secondary
GPU computes its rows while the CPU pool works; the results return through
private pinned host buffers before CUDA0 continues the layer. The GPU launches
can overlap, but each layer waits for all three.

The shipped profile ranks 8,000 `(layer, expert)` pairs. CUDA0 takes its usual
`--expert-cache auto` allocation. With only CUDA1, it takes the first remaining
pairs. When CUDA2 or CUDA3 is enabled, the remaining profiled pairs are assigned
round robin to the secondary GPUs. The ranked list is then extended with all
other pairs in expert-then-layer order and distributed in the same way. This
fills the additional VRAM and lets all secondary GPUs see frequent experts, but
unranked experts may hardly ever be routed. The startup
log reports slots and GiB per card; each request reports the number of expert
entries actually computed on each secondary GPU. Remote outputs are packed
before returning over PCIe/USB4: the request log compares MiB transferred
with the previous full-row transfer. The input and routing metadata use pinned
host staging. This reduces transfer traffic and launch overhead, but does not
release the expert arena in system RAM or significantly change VRAM use.

The optional `--gpu-placement layer` gives each layer to exactly one secondary
GPU (layer number modulo the number of enabled cards). It fills that card with
the most frequently routed experts of its layers first, then the unranked ones.
This can reduce USB4 device switches and synchronization when several secondary
cards serve the same layer in the default `stripe` mode. All three cards still
keep their requested expert slots; the primary CUDA0 cache and CPU fallback
continue to work. The log counts active layer launches on each card, so the
tradeoff can be measured alongside tokens per second. This placement is
experimental and may be slower if a given layer needs more than one card's
compute capacity.

The experiment requires the corresponding visible CUDA devices and a CUDA
enabled build. Each card must keep at least 512 MiB free. Tiers must be enabled
in order. Under WDDM (Windows, WSL2), CUDA registration of the host expert arena is capped at
8 GiB to leave room for the contexts and MTP on CUDA0 (`STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB` overrides it; on Linux the whole
arena is registered). The rest remains
available to the CPU pool; the PCIe expert path is available only for the
registered layers. Without secondary GPUs, the original uncapped registration
behavior applies.

On an existing Linux installation, apply the patch to its source tree, then run:

```sh
./setup.sh --setup --gpu1-experts 5000 --gpu2-experts 5000 --gpu3-experts 5000
```

On Windows, from PowerShell in the installation folder:

```powershell
.\START-HERE.bat --setup --gpu1-experts 5000 --gpu2-experts 5000 --gpu3-experts 5000
```

To test the layer placement instead, add `--gpu-placement layer` to the setup
command. To go back, run the same command with `--gpu-placement stripe`. After
the new engine is built, the mode can also be changed without a rebuild: edit
`--expert-cache-remote-placement` in `strata-iq3_xxs.json` from `layer` to
`stripe` or vice versa and restart the server. If the argument is absent, the
default is `stripe`.

Choose the same model, size, context and image settings as your current
installation when prompted. Setup recompiles the engine, updates its server
configuration, and starts it. Later starts keep those settings. To tune the
slots without recompiling, edit the values after `--expert-cache-device1`,
`--expert-cache-device2` and `--expert-cache-device3` in the stored
`strata-iq3_xxs.json`, then restart with `.\run-iq3_xxs.bat`.

Compare identical requests at one, two and four GPUs, preferably with several
repeats. VRAM use alone does not show useful offload: compare the per-request
CUDA1–3 counts and tokens per second. More GPU contexts and synchronization
may lower the speed. Prompt prefill still uses CUDA0; secondary GPUs serve
decode, including MTP verification. No peer-to-peer access is required.

Longer contexts reserve more KV/state memory on CUDA0, which reduces its
automatic expert cache. On a 64 GB PC `setup.py` limits IQ3_XXS to 128K even
if 262K was selected; the secondary caches still require the host expert arena.
To try 262K on 64 GB, choose Q2_0 or IQ2_XS instead and check that CUDA0 still
has enough free VRAM after loading. Benchmark long prompts separately from
short decode requests.

The existing warning about the CUDA0 expert-cache GPU hit path still applies:
its outputs diverge from cache-off runs. Treat performance as experimental
until the generated tokens have been validated.

## Optional helper decode optimization

`--remote-expert-opt` (`--serve` only) optimizes the CUDA1-3 helper caches
above. The engine's default is off; since 0.1.39b setup adds it to a config on
two or more GPUs (`--gpus`, or "use both" at start). It acts only when a helper
cache is configured; a layer split runs exactly as before. To leave it out:
setup's `--no-remote-expert-opt`, or `"remote_expert_opt": false` in the
model's `strata-*.json` (kept when setup runs again). Measured by the PR's
author: dual RTX 4090 +63% mixed / +132% code decode over the plain helper
path; RTX 5090 + 4090 +28% / +63%. The primary cache avoids admitting experts already held
by a helper, and helpers replace cold experts with frequently routed CPU
misses using their existing same-layer slots. Each helper reduces its expert
outputs to a weighted partial sum on its GPU before returning one vector per
token. Tokens with no CPU expert work skip CPU activation quantization.

For an existing server configuration with CUDA0 as the primary and CUDA1 as a
helper, use these engine arguments alongside the model and profile arguments:

```text
--expert-cache auto --expert-cache-device1 auto --remote-expert-opt
```

`--expert-cache-device1`, `--expert-cache-device2` and
`--expert-cache-device3` now also accept `auto`: fill each helper from its
assigned ranking using actual aligned expert bytes and free VRAM, retaining
the existing 512 MiB allowance. Explicit numeric budgets still work. This is
startup capacity sizing, not throughput balancing; with several helpers a
card's truncated candidate tail is not redistributed to another card.

The optimization uses the existing host scheduling and pinned-host transport,
not P2P or tensor parallelism. Each layer still waits for its participating
helpers. It changes floating-point summation order, so enabled output is not
claimed to be bitwise identical. Only two-card CUDA operation has been measured
by its author; a community machine measured two cards on HIP (2x RX 6900 XT,
PCIe 4.0 x8 each, IQ3_S): there the expert plan's PCIe share had been taking
experts the helper already held, which made the primary card wait 43 ms per
verify window instead of 19 (decode 40 instead of 66 tok/s). #854 keeps a
helper's experts out of that share; before it, `--pcie-frac 0` avoided the
cost ([bench/results/2026-10-04-rdna2-helper-pcie-share](../bench/results/2026-10-04-rdna2-helper-pcie-share/README.md)).
Three/four cards have not been validated. Without the switch, the
existing decode path remains in use. This does not optimize the separate
`--peer-device` path below or change its existing incompatibility with helper
caches.

## Peer tier (`--peer-device`)

`--peer-device N` puts a second adaptive expert cache on CUDA device N. It
takes the ranked pairs CUDA0's cache does not hold, as many as fit. The peer
computes the rows of its own experts, for decode windows and for prompt
chunks; the activations and the results cross NVLink or another P2P path. The
tier adapts while the server runs, like the primary cache. It is an
alternative to the CUDA1-3 caches above, not a third tier beside them.

- `--peer-device N` (default off): enable the tier on CUDA device N (N >= 1).
- `--peer-reserve-mib M` (default 600): leave M MiB free on the peer card; the
  cache takes what remains. The prompt-path buffers need this headroom.
  Keep a few hundred MiB free on both cards beyond this: the prompt path loads its kernels and cuBLAS on first use
  (a start with 5 MiB left on the peer and 485 MiB on the primary stopped at the first prompt with "cuBLAS status 14").
- Whether the two cards can really exchange data is tested once at start (#2666): two RTX A4000 behind a host
  bridge reported peer access, enabled it, and `cudaMemcpyPeerAsync` then copied nothing, so the peer computed on
  zeros and the first prompt came back NaN. A test copy each way now decides; if it arrives wrong the log says so
  and the prompt path uses the host route (the one without P2P: activations and rows through mapped host memory).
  `STRATA_PEER_NO_P2P=1` asks for that route by hand.
- `--peer-slots N` (default 0): cap the tier at N experts; 0 = as many as fit.
- `--peer-adapt-swaps N` (default -1): swaps per adaptive round on the peer;
  -1 uses the primary's `--adapt-swaps`.
- `--peer-prefill-rows N` (default -1): the share of each prompt chunk's rows
  the peer computes; -1 is half of chunk x top-k, 0 keeps prompt rows on the
  primary.

Through the server, list both cards in the config's `"gpu"` (e.g. `[0, 1]`, numbered as nvidia-smi numbers them)
and add `--peer-device 1` to its `"args"`; the number is the card's position in that list (with `"gpu": [2, 0]`,
`--peer-device 1` is nvidia-smi's card 0). Several GPUs in `"gpu"` are otherwise a layer split: the server adds
`--layer-split` only when `--peer-device` is not among the args.

`--peer-device` requires `--expert-profile` and an enabled expert cache, and
the device must be visible; it refuses otherwise. It also refuses
`--layer-split` (a different second-GPU mode: use one or the other) and
`--expert-cache-device1..3` (the peer tier already caches experts on that card):

    strata generate: --peer-device cannot be combined with --layer-split (use one or the other)
    strata generate: --peer-device cannot be combined with --expert-cache-device1..3 (the peer tier already caches experts there)

Without `--peer-device` the binary is unchanged; its output is byte-identical
to the release. With `--peer-device` and the same expert set split across the
two cards, the generated tokens are byte-identical to the single-GPU run under
the exactness gate.

With a peer the prompt path keeps the MMQ path; the fused int8 prompt path is
not yet combined with the peer's rows. Mapped host buffers gain
`cudaHostAllocPortable` only with a peer, since only then does a second
context write them. The tier size is manual for now (`--peer-reserve-mib`,
`--peer-slots`); automatic sizing on small cards wants the buffer lending of
#216 and is a follow-up.

## The resident RAM mode with the helper caches

`--resident-experts` (the low-RAM mode) works with the helper caches: the
experts a helper holds are left out of the RAM copy as a split stage's are, and
the helpers' refills read through the source - the RAM copy when it holds the
bytes, the files otherwise. Measured here on an RX 6800 (gfx1030, 16 GB) + RX
6600 (gfx1032, 8 GB), Windows 11, an i5-11400F and 32 GB of RAM (the 6800 alone:
~37.5 decode tok/s, the same worker configuration): the 6600's 3.4-3.8k-expert
cache lifted decode to ~40.6 / 44.2 tok/s on 8K-token requests at 3800 slots,
with the CPU pool's share of the experts down from ~2.9 to ~0.4 entries per
layer-window. The helper's rows cost about 0.3-0.6 ms per layer on the pool's
critical path - usually less than the CPU rows and page faults they replace,
which is why the 6600 (about 2-3x the 6800's cost per row) still pays off as a
cache tier.

**Size a helper against the card's *real* free VRAM.** `--expert-cache-device1
auto` reads `cudaMemGetInfo`, which on Windows reports the *process's* WDDM
budget: it cannot see the desktop, the vision encoder (a separate process), a
streaming host or other apps on that card.  A helper auto-sized on a card that
also drives the display or the encoder over-commits, WDDM backs the excess with
system RAM ("shared GPU memory"), and that memory leaves the machine's RAM - on
a 32 GB PC it pushed the resident complement into the pagefile and made the
helper read its own cache over PCIe.  An explicit count
(`--expert-cache-device1 3800` here, of ~4100 that fit an empty card) kept the
cache in real VRAM; freeing another app's sticky allocation on the same card
was worth about the same again.  Prefer explicit counts on a card that shares
its VRAM with anything else.

## Choosing the primary device on Windows (`STRATA_PRIMARY_DEVICE`)

The engine runs the model on the device the runtime numbers 0.  Windows' HIP
runtime enumerates the cards in a fixed order that `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` only
filters - it cannot reorder - so on a PC whose faster card comes second (an RX
6800 after an RX 6600, say) a run with both visible could only put the model on
the slow one.  `STRATA_PRIMARY_DEVICE=N` picks another visible ordinal as the
primary; unset or 0 is upstream's behavior.

- the helper caches (`--expert-cache-device1..3`) take the visible devices
  other than the primary, in order;
- the peer tier's cross-device checks use the same ordinal;
- a layer split is refused with this set (its later stages must be > 0, and
  stage 0 is the primary);
- NVIDIA cards do not need it: `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` with
  `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID` already reorders.

Measured on RX 6800 + RX 6600, Windows 11; the report accompanies this change.


## docs/STRIX_HALO.md

# Strix Halo (Ryzen AI Max, gfx1151)

Strata runs on the Ryzen AI Max "Strix Halo" APUs (Radeon 8060S / 8050S, RDNA3.5, `gfx1151`, one pool of LPDDR5X shared by the
CPU and the GPU) through the same HIP backend as the Radeon cards in [AMD_HIP.md](AMD_HIP.md). **Status: experimental.**
Everything here was built and measured on one machine, the maintainers' Strix Halo box (Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 128 GB,
Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0, ROCm 7.14.1). Setup (`setup.sh`, `START-HERE.bat`) recognizes it from 0.1.40, by its PCI id (`1002:1586`, one id for the 8060S, 8050S and 8040S) and by
`gfx1151` exactly: a Strix Point (890M / 880M, gfx1150), Krackan (860M / 840M, gfx1152) or Phoenix / Hawk Point (780M / 760M, gfx1103) Radeon is
named as what it is and not supported. On Linux setup compiles the engine for gfx1151 itself (the steps below are the same, by hand). The 0.2.0-beta release also has ready-made packages: `Strata-0.2.0-beta-linux-amd-strixhalo.AppImage` (engine `halo`, gfx1151, ROCm 7.14.1) and, on Windows, `Strata-0.2.0-beta-windows-hip-rdna3.exe` (engine `rdna3`: gfx1100, gfx1101, gfx1102 and gfx1151, ROCm 10.2.0a20260930); any app installer plus **Update engine** (or `strata update`) fetches the same package. What was run: both packages were built, linked and scanned, and the Linux package refuses to start on a card of another family (tried on an RX 9000 card); the maintainers have no Strix Halo and ran neither on one. The measurements on this page come from source builds on Linux (the maintainers' earlier box and community machines). Nobody has run a Strix Halo on Windows. The packaged engines do not carry the hipBLASLt table of section 3 yet (planned for 0.2.1), so their prompt reading is slower than the numbers below until then. A Windows zip of the 0.1.x START-HERE route without gfx1151 code is refused with a message, never used. Setup counts the GPU's memory as the BIOS carve-out plus the shared memory
(the GTT pool; on Windows half the RAM) and recommends UD-IQ4_XS from about 80 GB of memory; it changes no BIOS or kernel setting.

**Windows start-up (0.2.1.2).** On a Strix Halo under Windows the engine no longer registers the expert arena with the GPU driver: registering it took all free VRAM (91 GiB before, 0 after, on a 64 GB carve-out + 32 GB shared PC), the expert cache got no slots and the engine stopped with "the embedding buffer failed" (0.2.1 and earlier). The arena stays in RAM, held by the working-set lock, and the cache gets its normal slots. `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB=N` (or `0`) registers it as before, `STRATA_UMA_REGISTER=1` too. Linux is unchanged.

What the engine does differently on this chip:

- **Unified memory.** The GPU's "VRAM" is the GTT pool of the same RAM. `device_free_bytes()` (the figure `--expert-cache auto` and
  the memory plan use) counts what Linux can give back (`MemAvailable` less 6 GiB for the system, `STRATA_UMA_HEADROOM_GIB`
  changes the 6) instead of only `MemFree`, per device, for any integrated GPU on Linux (this applies to a DGX Spark too).
- **gfx11 matrix cores.** The prompt attention, the block scorer, the prompt GEMMs and the prompt experts have WMMA kernels for
  gfx1100 / 1101 / 1102 / 1103 / 1150 / 1151. A gfx11 part outside that list (gfx1152) is not given them: it takes the portable path.
- **The hipBLASLt table** `tools/hip/gfx1151-hipblaslt-100401.txt` (ROCm 7.14.1's hipBLASLt 1.x `100401`), including the prompt shapes
  at `--prefill 16384` (T 16383 / 16384). Setup's own ROCm for gfx1151 (the 7.14.0a20260608 wheels, hipBLASLt 1.4.0) takes
  `tools/hip/gfx1151-hipblaslt-100400.txt`: the same shapes, calibrated against that library (docs/AMD_HIP.md, Tuning table).
- **The expert cache and the RAM budget share the RAM.** For a model with a RAM budget (UD-IQ4_XS, UD-Q4_K_XL) setup writes a number for `--expert-cache` (the RAM less 24 GB less the budget), not `auto`: `auto` counts all the memory the OS can give back at start, and with a 55 GiB budget and a desktop open it took the room the OS needed (#1715, a global OOM on a 128 GB box). The number is in the config's `args`; `--expert-cache N` there sets it. An engine run by hand should pass one too.

## 1. The toolchain (no root needed)

ROCm 7.14.1 for gfx1151 from AMD's TheRock builds, extracted into a folder of your own:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/rocm && cd ~/rocm
curl -LO https://repo.amd.com/rocm/tarball-multi-arch/therock-dist-linux-gfx1151-7.14.1.tar.gz   # 1.7 GB
sha256sum therock-dist-linux-gfx1151-7.14.1.tar.gz   # c40e8f2bd6630a7d11557c762b99c6fa8afb04c9bd0e51ed1675ee1ca24afb00
mkdir install && tar -xzf therock-dist-linux-gfx1151-7.14.1.tar.gz -C install
export SDK=$HOME/rocm/install
export ROCM_PATH=$SDK HIP_PATH=$SDK HIP_PLATFORM=amd
export PATH=$SDK/bin:$SDK/lib/llvm/bin:$PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$SDK/lib:$SDK/lib/rocm_sysdeps/lib:$SDK/lib/llvm/lib:${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}
```

You also need CMake 3.24+, Ninja, git and a C++ host toolchain with libstdc++ headers (`sudo apt install build-essential cmake ninja-build git`).
The maintainers' box has no system compiler: they point ROCm's clang at a user-space copy of gcc 15 with
`--gcc-toolchain=<dir>/usr` (added to `CMAKE_HIP_FLAGS` below; leave it out when the system has one).

The kernel's amdgpu driver and `/dev/kfd` access (your user in the `render` and `video` groups) are all the GPU side needs.
To let the GPU use most of a 128 GB machine the maintainers' box boots with `ttm.pages_limit=29360128 ttm.page_pool_size=29360128`
(a 112 GiB GTT; the default is about half of the RAM) and `amd_iommu=off`; both are host settings the engine does not need to run,
only to have the room.

## 2. The engine

llama.cpp's `ggml` sources are pinned by this repository: CMake fetches the revision it needs. For an offline build, point
`STRATA_GGML_DIR` at a checkout of exactly that revision.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata.git && cd Strata
cmake -S . -B build-halo -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DSTRATA_ENABLE_HIP=ON -DSTRATA_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF -DSTRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON \
  -DCMAKE_HIP_ARCHITECTURES=gfx1151 \
  -DCMAKE_HIP_COMPILER=$SDK/lib/llvm/bin/clang++ -DCMAKE_HIP_COMPILER_ROCM_ROOT=$SDK \
  "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$SDK;$SDK/lib/rocm_sysdeps;$SDK/lib/llvm" \
  "-DCMAKE_HIP_FLAGS=--rocm-path=$SDK --rocm-device-lib-path=$SDK/lib/llvm/amdgcn/bitcode"
cmake --build build-halo --target strata -j 8        # about 25 minutes the first time
```

`gfx1151` is "unvalidated" in the build's own wording (it warns). `STRATA_PREFILL_MMQ=ON` builds ggml's MMQ kernels the prompt
experts need. The tests: `cmake --build build-halo -j 8` builds them all, `ctest --test-dir build-halo` runs them;
`hip_prefill_hcd_exact_parity` and `hip_prefill_hipblaslt_gemm` need the table (next section) and skip without it.

## 3. The prompt table, and running

Hand the engine the table (`setup` does it for the supported cards; for gfx1151 you do it): without it the prompt's dense matrix
products use plain hipBLAS and are slower.

```sh
export STRATA_HIPBLASLT_TUNING=$PWD/tools/hip/gfx1151-hipblaslt-100401.txt
```

The engine accepts it only for the architecture and the hipBLASLt version named on the table's second line
(`STRATA_HIPBLASLT_TUNING_V1 gfx1151 100401`: ROCm 7.14.1) and says so at start-up (`prefill gemm: hipBLASLt tuning enabled (90 rows,
gfx1151, version 100401)`). Then run `strata` with the same arguments as on any other card (the model packs, `--serve`, the
settings of [DETAILS.md](DETAILS.md)); a pack of the Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS or UD-Q4_K_XL GGUFs is what the numbers below used.

## 4. What is on by default on gfx1151

At start the engine looks at GPU 0; on a gfx1151 it sets the switches below unless you set them yourself
(`STRATA_GFX1151_DEFAULTS=0` turns the whole table off, and the start-up line names what was set). **Every one of them gave
byte-identical output on the maintainers' box** (the same token ids, 4K / 32K / 64K and four models, and a bitwise harness per kernel):
they change speed, not answers. Nothing here applies to CUDA or to another AMD architecture.

| Switch | What it does |
|---|---|
| `STRATA_GDN_HEAD`, `STRATA_GDN_PP=2`, `STRATA_GDN_CONVL2`, `STRATA_GDN_NOY` | the prompt's gated-delta-net recurrence: four lanes per column, two columns per lane, the convolution and the norms fused |
| `STRATA_HCD_EXACT` | the hyper-connection down projection (N 320, K 10240) in a WMMA kernel that reproduces hipBLASLt solution 1176 / 1177's summation order (`hip_prefill_hcd_exact_parity` checks it bit for bit); it runs only where the table makes hipBLASLt pick one of those two, and says once if it cannot |
| `STRATA_CVEC_FUSE`, `STRATA_PF_PAD` | a steered layer's write, control vector and next norm in one pass; padded GEMM row strides |
| `STRATA_TOPK_REG_MIN_BLOCKS=4096` | the prompt's QSA top-k uses the register kernel from 16K cells of context instead of 28K (the original kernel is slower there; the selected cells are identical, `qsa_topk_parity` checks it) |
| `STRATA_Q8_PACKED`, `STRATA_Q6_PACKED`, `STRATA_MMVF_ROWS`, `STRATA_ATTN_LANECELL` | decode layouts and kernels (packed Q8_0 / Q6_K weights, 4-row BF16 GEMV, one-cell-per-thread attention scores) |
| `STRATA_EXPERT_V2`, `STRATA_TSUM`, `STRATA_LFUSE` | the grouped decode experts (IQ3_S / IQ4_NL), single-butterfly warp sums, fewer launches around the shared expert and the KV append |
| `STRATA_GDN_SPLIT`, `STRATA_QFUSE`, `STRATA_PLE_BATCH` | the GDN step over four blocks per head, activation images written by their producers, the PLE key / value projections of a verify window at once |
| `STRATA_SH_STREAM=1` | the shared expert on a second stream beside the routed experts. It is off by default on other AMD cards (#816), but it pays on gfx1151: decode +1.8% (UD-IQ4_XS) and +6.7% (UD-Q4_K_XL) at 8K |

## 5. What is not on by default (it changes bits)

**Five of the switches below (`STRATA_PF_GEMM`, `STRATA_HC_UPMIX`, `STRATA_PA_FAST`, `STRATA_HIP_WMMA`, `STRATA_SELECT_WMMA`) are one opt-in on an integrated Radeon: `STRATA_IGPU_PROMPT_SET=1` ([AMD_HIP.md](AMD_HIP.md), "Integrated GPUs"). It was measured on a Radeon 780M only, where it is the default.** `STRATA_PF_FUSED`, `STRATA_PF_SWITCH_MIN_T` and `STRATA_PREFILL_STREAM_MIN` stay opt-in as well. `STRATA_HC_Q8` is on by default on gfx1151 (below); `STRATA_HC_Q8=0` turns it off.

These are faster on gfx1151 and **round differently** from the default path (a different summation order or a half-precision
intermediate), so they are opt-in and the maintainers gate them with KL against the default (`STRATA_PF_SWITCH_MIN_T=4096` keeps
the short prompts on the default numerics, since these pay on long ones). The maintainers' fast configuration sets all of
them:

```sh
export STRATA_PF_FUSED=1        # the prompt experts on the matrix cores (IQ2 / IQ3 / IQ4_XS gate/up, Q2_0 / IQ4_NL / Q8_0 down)
export STRATA_PF_GEMM=1         # the prompt's FP16 projections on the 128 x 256 WMMA GEMM
export STRATA_HC_UPMIX=1        # the hyper-connection up projection with its epilogue
export STRATA_PA_FAST=1         # the prompt attention with single FP16 q and p
export STRATA_HIP_WMMA=1        # the prompt attention on matrix cores
export STRATA_SELECT_WMMA=1     # the block scorer on matrix cores
export STRATA_PF_SWITCH_MIN_T=4096
export STRATA_PREFILL_STREAM_MIN=128   # prompt reads of 128-1,023 tokens on the fused experts too (below)
```

`STRATA_HC_Q8` (on by default on gfx1151 since 0.2.2; `STRATA_HC_Q8=0` restores the bf16 read) measured on the Strix Halo (IQ3_S, gfx1151, 2026-10-21, MTP 4 drafts / min-p 0.5): **+8.4%**
on `json_extract` at fixed windows (53.55 -> 58.03 tok/s), at the cost of **94 of 250 output tokens differing** from
the BF16 read (first at 60). It halves the hyper-connection weight bytes (13.29 -> 7.15 MB per read; cold read
93.8 -> 20.3 us, 142 -> 352 GB/s). The answers are not bit-identical to the bf16 read; how far they move is in docs/AMD_HIP.md ("Strix Halo: 8-bit hyper-connection weights").

`STRATA_PF_FUSED=1` reaches only chunks of `STRATA_PREFILL_STREAM_MIN` tokens or more (1,024 by default, the floor measured on
a discrete card, where a smaller chunk does not pay for streaming every expert); a smaller read runs its experts through MMQ.
With every expert in the unified memory nothing streams, and MMQ is the slow part: an agent's turn - a tool result of ~1,000
tokens on a cached conversation - read in 3.1-6.0 s at 1,024 and 0.9-2.5 s at 128 (C2T8, `--no-prefill-borrow`; 12-turn
replay 3.4 -> 2.1 s per turn). Its output is the fused path's, which reads of 1,024 tokens or more already take; it is not
under `STRATA_PF_SWITCH_MIN_T`, which gates only the hyper-connection and padding switches. A UD-Q4_K_XL or other K-quant
pack takes the fused experts only with `STRATA_PF_FUSED_KQ=1` as well.

`STRATA_PF_F16=1` (gfx11 only; add it to the list above) runs the covered prompt experts on the F16 matrix cores instead of
the int8 ones: K-quant gate/up and Q5_1 down (with `STRATA_PF_FUSED_KQ=1`), IQ2 / IQ3 / IQ4_XS gate/up, Q2_0 / IQ4_NL / Q8_0
down. One layer, 16,384 tokens: Q4_K / Q5_1 85.3 -> 53.5 ms, IQ3_S / IQ4_NL gate/up 11.65 -> 9.87 and down 6.11 -> 4.71 ms.
It rounds differently from the int8 kernels. First-token KL against a run with no switches, 12 natural-text prompts of
1.5K-24K tokens (Strata's own docs and sources), top-1 the same in 12 of 12: UD-Q4_K_XL mean 0.0068 (median 0.0021) against
0.0031 (0.0024) for `STRATA_PF_FUSED=1 STRATA_PF_FUSED_KQ=1` without it; UD-IQ4_XS 0.0085 (0.0036) against 0.0068 (0.0032). One
1.5K prompt carries most of the Q4_K_XL mean (0.049).

`STRATA_REFILL_PARTS=1` (opt-in, exact; HIP and CUDA, a GGUF read in place) refills the expert-cache slots a prompt borrowed straight from the GGUF mapping (an expert's gate, up and down tensors) instead of through an assembled 4 MB copy per expert: the same bytes in the slot (checked against the assembled blob on 162 slots), 0.1 to 0.3 s less at the end of a prompt; gfx1151, UD-Q4_K_XL and UD-IQ4_XS: a 4K-8K prompt +2.3% to +3.5%, 32K +1.1%. It is not in the table above because only gfx1151 has measured it.

Two engine flags help on long contexts and are not Strix-specific: `--mtp-window 8192` (the draft layer attends to the last 8,192
cells: 64K output +3.5%, 32K -0.4%) and `--spec`, `--lookup-chain`, `--mtp-q4` (see [DETAILS.md](DETAILS.md)).

## 5b. The desktop, the RAM, and a discrete card beside the Strix Halo (Linux)

The Strix Halo chip usually draws your desktop, and its graphics memory is your RAM. Two things follow, and the engine now takes both into account.

- **One memory, counted once.** The expert cache of an integrated GPU lives in the same RAM as the expert arena. The automatic cache size is the smaller of
  what the GPU reports free and what the OS reports available, less a reserve for the desktop (the larger of 8 GiB and 8% of the RAM; the start-up line says so
  when it changes the size). `STRATA_UMA_RESERVE_GIB=N` sets the reserve (`0` = the old sizing, nothing kept back); `--expert-cache N` is never changed.
- **A card of its own beside the chip** (for example a Radeon AI PRO R9700). A card of its own is the recommended Main card and the chip stays Off in the card roles.
  If you name the chip in a layer split anyway (`--gpus 0,1`, or the config's `"gpu": [0, 1]`), the split runs as asked, the chip is placed on the first layers and
  never on the last stage (the output head, the draft layer and the check of its guesses), the picture reader is started on the card of its own, and the
  start prints one plain line about it. `"gpu_order": "as_given"` and a manual `layer_split` keep your order. `setup --gpus all` leaves the chip out
  when two cards of their own are present; name it by number to use it.
- **The CPU.** On Linux with built-in Radeon graphics the engine starts at nice +5, so the desktop keeps its share of the CPU while the engine's workers spin.
  `STRATA_ENGINE_NICE=0` turns it off, `STRATA_ENGINE_NICE=N` sets another value.

What is not known yet: how much of the screen freeze a long compute job on the same chip causes, and whether registering the whole expert arena with the driver
(the Linux default on gfx1151; Windows uses the unregistered arena since 0.2.1.2) hurts when the GTT is small. `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB=none` runs the unregistered
arena on any OS; reports with `amdgpu_top` and `dmesg` are welcome.

## 6. Measured

Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (128 GB, gfx1151), the maintainers' fast configuration of section 5 on top of the defaults of section 4, `--spec 4`,
`--mtp`, `--lookup-chain 3`, `--mtp-q4 all`, `--prefill 16384`, int8 KV, all experts in the unified memory. Prompt tok/s is
(prompt tokens - 1) / prompt time, output tok/s is the tokens / decode time; medians of 3 runs, one fresh process per run, the two
engines interleaved. "Before" is the maintainers' earlier engine branch (the same switches set by hand), "now" is this release.
Every pair printed the same token ids.

| Model | Context | Prompt before -> now | Output before -> now |
|---|---|---|---|
| UD-IQ4_XS | 8K | 1,212 -> 1,293 (+6.7%) | 51.7 -> 53.8 (+4.0%) |
| UD-IQ4_XS | 128K | 1,241 -> 1,320 (+6.4%) | 49.3 -> 51.4 (+4.2%) |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | 8K | 1,136 -> 1,169 (+2.9%) | 50.6 -> 52.6 (+3.9%) |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | 128K | 1,220 -> 1,248 (+2.4%) | 41.6 -> 43.3 (+3.9%) |
| IQ3_S | 8K | 1,202 -> 1,242 (+3.4%) | 56.2 -> 59.7 (+6.3%) |
| IQ3_S | 128K | 1,254 -> 1,312 (+4.6%) | 40.6 -> 42.8 (+5.5%) |
| IQ3_XXS | 8K | 1,237 -> 1,238 (+0.1%) | 48.8 -> 51.5 (+5.6%) |
| IQ3_XXS | 128K | 1,259 -> 1,252 (-0.6%) | 48.4 -> 50.9 (+5.1%) |

UD-IQ4_XS at 4K / 32K / 64K (5-6 interleaved pairs): prompt +9.2% / +6.0% / +5.3%, output +5.0% / +3.9% / +4.6%.
IQ3_XXS at 8K was measured again with 6 interleaved pairs (an earlier 3-run set had read 5% low while other jobs shared the GPU): prompt equal, output +5.6%. With the defaults off the same build's prompt is 8% lower (1,137), so the table helps there too.

### Re-measured on the merged 0.1.40 code

The same box and method, no environment switches at all (the arch defaults only), on the final merged tree. 4 interleaved pairs per cell,
medians; "j" is the build of the table above (the Aurora port before the other 0.1.40 work was merged), "merged" is the release
code. Every run printed the same token ids, and the ids also match `strata-int29` (the v4.2 config) on UD-IQ4_XS and UD-Q4_K_XL at
a8 / 4K / 64K.

| Model | Context | Prompt j -> merged | Output j -> merged |
|---|---|---|---|
| UD-IQ4_XS | 8K | 1,260 -> 1,159 (-8.0%, spread 1,070-1,320) | 53.94 -> 53.14 (-1.5%) |
| UD-IQ4_XS | 128K | 1,317 -> 1,299 (-1.4%) | 51.38 -> 50.72 (-1.3%) |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | 8K | 1,163 -> 1,104 (-5.0%, spread 890-1,240) | 52.66 -> 50.47 (-4.2%) |
| UD-Q4_K_XL | 128K | 1,252 -> 1,211 (-3.3%) | 43.28 -> 42.64 (-1.5%) |
| IQ3_S | 8K | 1,283 -> 1,265 (-1.4%) | 59.81 -> 59.10 (-1.2%) |
| IQ3_S | 128K | 1,311 -> 1,310 (-0.1%) | 42.74 -> 42.09 (-1.5%) |
| IQ3_XXS | 8K | 1,127 -> 1,212 (+7.6%) | 51.64 -> 50.95 (-1.3%) |
| IQ3_XXS | 128K | 1,252 -> 1,250 (-0.1%) | 50.88 -> 50.22 (-1.3%) |

The prompt numbers at 8K swing by more than the differences (other jobs share this box), so read them as unchanged. The output
column moved by a steady -1.2% to -1.5% (-4% on UD-Q4_K_XL at 8K, where the default arm also had slow runs): since 0.1.39 the
shared-expert stream fork is off by default on HIP (#816). It overlaps the shared expert with the routed experts on a second
stream and does help on gfx1151, so 0.1.40 turns it on there by default (section 4). It changes no bits (same ids). 4 interleaved pairs at 8K, merged
code with the fork off -> on: UD-IQ4_XS output 53.1 -> 54.05 (+1.8%), UD-Q4_K_XL 49.5 -> 52.8 (+6.7%, the default arm ranged 46.0-52.1),
prompt unchanged. With the fork on, the merged code's output is at or above the j build's (IQ4_XS 54.05 vs 53.94).


## docs/TERMINAL.md

# Strata terminal commands

`strata launch` (guided setup, serve and monitor) and `strata connect` (setup for your coding apps): see [TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md](TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md).

For the shortest path, use the [terminal quick start](TERMINAL_QUICKSTART.md). The Terminal installs with one line (see [TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md](TERMINAL_LAUNCH.md#install-one-line)) and gives you the `strata` command; every command below is typed as `strata ...`. In a source checkout, run `python strata.py ...` from the repository root instead (use `python3` where there is no `python`).

Read a server, watch it and start one:

```sh
strata status --url http://127.0.0.1:8095
strata status --url http://127.0.0.1:8095 --json
strata monitor --url http://127.0.0.1:8095 --once
strata serve --profile path/to/strata-model.json --port 8095
```

Discover setup-written model run configs in an installation without loading the engine:

```sh
strata models list --installed --output json
strata models inspect MODEL_ID --output json
